The stunningly detailed gold cape is unique in Europe and may have belonged to a high-ranking woman.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The gold accessory was found in a Bronze Age grave near the town of Mold in Wales.

Where it is from: Bryn yr Ellyllon (Goblins' Hill), Wales

When it was made: Circa 1900 to 1600 B.C.

In 1833, stone quarry workers discovered an ancient burial mound at Goblins' Hill near the town of Mold in Wales. At the center was a stone-lined grave that contained a fragmented skeleton and a gold, cape-like accessory that had been crushed over time. The Mold gold cape has a unique shape and style, and it is one of the finest examples of prehistoric goldwork ever found, according to the British Museum, where the artifact is on display.

The cape dates to Britain's Early Bronze Age (2500 to 1200 B.C.), a time that saw a metalworking revolution as artisans shifted from crafting flint tools to making weapons and jewelry out of gold, copper and bronze.

When the cape was originally unearthed, experts assumed that it had belonged to an ancient warrior, chief or religious leader, due to the spectacular design of the object, Benjamin Roberts, then curator for the European Bronze Age collections at the British Museum, told the BBC in 2010. But after the broken pieces of the cape were put back together, the small size of the artifact suggested it may have been worn by a woman or a child.

The Mold gold cape measures roughly 9.3 inches (23.5 centimeters) tall and 18.3 inches (46.5 cm) wide. It weighs about 1.2 pounds (560 grams) and was probably crafted from a single lump of gold about the size of a ping-pong ball.

The gold ingot was beaten incredibly thin, fashioned into a cape, and then embellished with decorations that mimicked beads or necklaces, according to the British Museum. Additionally, several hundred amber beads were found on the cape in the grave, which likely added to the gilded appearance of the accessory. Perforations around the neck opening suggest the cape originally had a lining made of leather or another perishable material that did not survive.

Because the gold cape, when worn, would restrict a person's upper arm movements, it may have been a ceremonial accessory that conferred religious authority and was worn only on special occasions. But experts are still unsure why the cape was buried in a grave. Nor can they confirm whether the person it was interred with was male or female, as the skeleton was not recovered by the quarry workers in the 19th century.

"The cape is unique — there is really nothing to compare it to in the whole of Europe," Roberts told the BBC. "This makes it more difficult to understand why it was made and what significance it had."

#6622. The Cheesecake Factory Drama, Explained

Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly column covering the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered Italy’s looming food shortage.

Well, it’s over. Last Ditch, the bar in Greenfield, Massachusetts, that became the center of a tornado of scrutiny, ridicule, discourse, and, er, media coverage a few weeks ago is now closed as it searches for new co-owners, or to sell the bar to new owners. If your memory needs a refresh, the TL;DR is that the bar relaxed its COVID-conscious mask restrictions, and it tore the local community apart.

The Boston Globe covered the drama, and the story quickly went viral. But despite—or perhaps because of—its newfound infamy, the bar couldn’t attract enough clientele to stay open. Could new owners resurrect the beleaguered business?

Also in the discourse this week: Washington, DC residents will be voting on a foie gras ban which has prominent chefs coming out as firmly pro-foie, despite public backlash. José Andrés argues that the American food system also mistreats many other animals—and that we have bigger issues, like child hunger, to address.

Also in today’s Open Tab: why The Cheesecake Factory has made headlines this week, how salmon could decide Alaska’s midterm elections, a delivery platform acquisition for the ages, and a look inside LA’s buzzy Skywalker Grill.

This week the Cheesecake Factory’s name was splashed across headlines in a handful of national magazines and newspapers—a feat that hasn’t happened since…ever? It’s hard to say.

This story starts last weekend, when former president Barack Obama made a joke at a campaign rally in Ohio. “[President Trump’s] got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere,” he said.

Trump himself responded on Monday. “For you to say it’s a Cheesecake Factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president,” he told reporters. The White House X account followed up with some AI-generated trolling.

Rick McCormack, the chain’s former vice president of design, also weighed in. “I think it’s a little bit sad that the pettiness of politics would create that sound bite, knowing all our challenges going on in the country today,” he said.

Is the Cheesecake Factory designed to look like it was done by an Egypt-obsessed kid with an unrestricted budget and a lot of ambition? Yes. But that’s part of its charm. You need a maximalist setting to match a maximalist menu, a maximalist experience. As I see it, The Cheesecake Factory is designed as it is so that ordering an “all day morning cocktail” (?), or a slice of “Brownie Crunch Choc-o-Lot Cheesecake” suddenly doesn’t seem so crazy. The Cheesecake Factory, as we were reminded again and again this week, is an American institution. So, unfortunately, is a quips-based, sound-byte-heavy political system.

And don’t feel too bad about the beleaguered corporate chain, which operates 200-plus locations. The C-suite is laughing their way to the bank: Stock analysts were quick to point out it is among the highest performing stocks on the market.

A few weeks ago a friend who grew up in Alaska told me nonchalantly that the state’s upcoming primary would be decided by salmon. “It’s the only thing that matters,” he said.. According to a recent feature in the New Yorker, it looks like he was right.

For many Alaskans fishing is both a job and a way to nourish their family. The democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, even settled on the slogan ““Fish, Family, Freedom.” But in recent years, runs of king salmon and chum salmon have collapsed, and don’t seem to be recovering. Experts point to climate change, but activists point to the practice of trawling—a method of fishing that includes pulling an enormous net behind the boat— for pollack which also catches millions of salmon which get killed and discarded by fishermen.

“This is an ecological crisis, a cultural trauma, an economic emergency and a public-health disaster,” reads one op-ed in an Alaskan paper.

Today in sentences that a Victorian tween wouldn’t understand a single word of: Delivery platform DoorDash, most recently in the news for its new fleet of drones, will buy Instacart for $17 billion.

It’s hard to overstate just how enormous this deal will be. Instacart is among America’s dominant platforms for grocery delivery, and DoorDash corners the market on the country's restaurant delivery apparatus.

The size of the acquisition would, under most administrations, attract FTC scrutiny. This is a pretty big consolidation in the field, after all. But the Trump administration has been particularly permissive of giant companies coming together to maximize their joint slay. In this case “joint slay” means market share and monopoly.

Museums must have a buzzy restaurant attached these days, and Los Angeles’s Lucas Museum of Narrative Art is no different. That’s where you’ll find Skywalker Grill, which, despite its monied environs, features a menu that’s surprisingly approachable. As Bon Appétit contributor Khushbu Shah tells us, it’s quickly become one of the city’s hottest tables. She takes us inside the restaurant to break down its surprisingly accessible menu.

#6620. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

Archaeologists have uncovered the 1,500-year-old burial of an elite toddler from the Moche culture in Peru.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The child was buried alongside two ceramic objects depicting defeated warriors about to be sacrificed.

Archaeologists in Peru have found an elaborate 1,500-year-old tomb that may hold the remains of a high-status toddler from a pre-Inca civilization.

The burial, which is from the Moche culture, also contained vessels depicting prisoners with rope around each of their necks and a sculpture of a human-bird deity.

Moche (also known as Mochica) culture developed along the northern coast of what is now Peru from the third to the ninth century. They created agricultural lands in the region's desert landscape, and their archaeological record includes monumental temples, water canals, pottery, metallurgy, textiles and a distinctive form of art. The Moche didn't have a written language, but they left behind thousands of realistic portrait vessels, which are somewhat similar to the prisoner sculptors found in the toddler's burial.

In the newfound tomb, the team unearthed a small skeleton, which is likely the remains of a toddler who was, at most, 2 years old, Carlos Rengifo-Chunga, director of the University of Trujillo's Huacas de Moche Archaeological Project, told Live Science. The child's sex is unknown.

The child was buried alongside 32 ceramic objects associated with Moche culture.

Rengifo-Chunga and his colleagues also found two copper objects in the burial: a mask-like disk covering the child's face, and a half-moon object on their feet. In addition, the burial contained 32 ceramic objects associated with Moche culture, including those depicting the prisoners and the deity.

The tomb was large compared to the child's small size, and could have easily held an adult, Rengifo-Chunga said. It dates to the sixth or seventh century, he added.

The team unearthed the tomb inside the Uhle Platform at the Huacas de Moche archaeological site in northern Peru. The Uhle Platform is a mausoleum, attached to the Huaca de la Luna temple, with a patio archaeologists call the Patio of the Serpents. Of the more than 80 burials previously uncovered there, the tomb represents the only known child to receive this sort of lavish burial.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The elaborate funerary treatment, including the use of copper, and the location of the tomb all suggest that the child belonged to an elite class of Moche society, Rengifo-Chunga said.

The two prisoner sculptures are associated with the "ritual of combat," a common theme in Moche art. In this sort of imagery, two warriors fight each other, and the loser is stripped of his clothes and weapons, tied around the neck with a rope and offered as a human sacrifice, Rengifo-Chunga said. The prisoners depicted on these two vessels were the losing warriors, and their presence in the burial of a child is rare.

"One would normally presume that these kinds of vessels represent something related to the deceased's life," Rengifo-Chunga said. For example, a vessel like this might signify that the individual took part in combat.

One of the ceramic objects depicts a presumed deity with human and bird features.

An archaeological team discovered a likely elite child burial at the Huacas de Moche archaeological site in Peru.

One of the two ceramics depicting prisoners that archaeologists found in the toddler's burial.

But a toddler couldn't have taken part in such an activity. In general, archaeologists wouldn't expect to see elements of an adult ritual in the burial of a child. "This expands our knowledge on Moche funerary practices," he added.

The sculpture of the presumed deity depicts a human body with bird wings and a bird tail, although for some scholars it might be interpreted as a god in transformation, Rengifo-Chunga said. The deity holds a square shield in one hand and a goblet in the other, and is flanked by two bird "assistants" wearing ceremonial garments.

Researchers will have to investigate whether the deity is a known Moche god, or a newfound addition to the pantheon. Either way, the object joins a contentious debate over whether the Moche pantheon consists of many gods, or just a few that can transform into many different versions, Rengifo-Chunga said.

The artifacts are now in the laboratories of the Santiago Uceda Castillo Museum in Peru, where they will undergo conservation treatment.

Margherita is a trilingual freelance writer specializing in science and history writing with a particular interest in archaeology, palaeontology, astronomy and human behavior. She earned her BA from Boston College in English literature, ancient history and French, and her journalism MA from L'École Du Journalisme de Nice in International New Media Journalism. In addition to Live Science, her bylines include Smithsonian Magazine, Discovery Magazine, BBC Travel, Atlas Obscura and more.

#6617. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

#6615. Crispy Rice Omelet

On mornings when there’s almost nothing in the refrigerator, this crispy rice omelet is the back-pocket meal that’s even faster than turning to a drive-thru. Although it’s ready in just 10 minutes and made in a single pan, you’ll forget it was a struggle meal after just one bite of its craveable crunchy outside and soft, cheesy center. The perfect crispy rice omelet features gorgeously crunchy toasted rice and egg that’s well cooked through without becoming rubbery, and this recipe promises the perfect bite.

Use leftover cold rice:Rice dries out as it cools, making it easier to crisp up in the pan. If you try to use freshly cooked rice, it will still have a lot of extra moisture, making it prone to clumping up—and it might even burn before it completely crisps up.

Use the right pan:Either a nonstick or cast iron pan will work here. In testing, I found that cast iron gives a more consistent golden color and crunchier result, but can result in rice that’s almost too crunchy (if that’s a thing!)—and there was always the *tiny* risk of the rice sticking. The nonstick pan, on the other hand, gave that extra bit of insurance against sticking, and while it didn’t yield such a picture-perfect color, it did result in consistently crispy rice. Whichever you use, I highly recommend sticking to one that’s 8″: It’s the perfect size for this amount of rice and egg.

Pre-salt your eggs:Seasoning the eggs 5 to 10 minutes before they hit the pan allows the salt time to unravel the proteins, resulting in more tender eggs. I recommend this tip anytime you’re making scrambled eggs, and it’s an easy tip to incorporate here if you whisk and season the eggs before starting the rice.

Watch the heat:While it’s best to crisp the rice on medium-high, it’s important to drop the temperature before the eggs go in. If you cook them too hard and fast, they’ll be rubbery.

Delish Official:Eggland's Best Eggs are the Official Eggs of Delish. That means they're the only eggs we're using in our recipe content.

Storage:This omelet is actually great left over, since the rice remains crisp, even after refrigerating. Store in an airtight container for up to 3 days. You can rewarm it (gently!) in the microwave, or eat it cold.

#6613. Apple Juice Bread

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

While rare, colorectal cancer is becoming more common in kids, teens and young adults, and the disease appears particularly aggressive in this age group.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

More children, teens and very young adults are being diagnosed with colorectal cancer in the United States, and new research suggests they often experience aggressive forms of the disease.

While diagnosis rates are rising, the disease is still rare among young people. Colorectal cancer, which affects the lower intestines and rectum, is largely a disease of age: 55% of all colorectal cancers are diagnosed in people over 65, and only 16% occur in people ages 49 or younger, according to a 2026 study published in the flagship journal of the American Cancer Society. Only a few hundred cases per year are diagnosed in people under age 21 in the U.S.

Nevertheless, the numbers of cases in the very young are rising, even as colorectal cancer rates decline or hold steady in older individuals. This increase coincides with an overall rise in colon and rectal cancer rates in people under 50.

The reasons for this schism aren't entirely understood. People over 50 receive routine colonoscopies in which precancerous polyps are removed, and that likely accounts for much of the decline in colorectal cancer diagnoses in older adults. But researchers suspect that environmental factors, such as ultraprocessed foods and sedentary lifestyles, might be behind the growing rates in young people.

Scientists are looking to the gut microbiome for clues about why colorectal cancer is on the rise in young people.

"Most of the research has really focused on the gut microbiome," the community of bacteria and other microbes that live in the gut, said Dr. Christopher Lieu, a professor of medical oncology at the University of Colorado Anschutz and a medical adviser to the nonprofit Colorectal Cancer Alliance.

Microbiome disruptions may spur inflammation, which, in turn, may trigger DNA mutations that cause cancer. But these mechanisms are complicated, Lieu told Live Science, and there likely isn't one simple reason young people's microbiomes may be getting disturbed.

"It's going to be extraordinarily more complex than that," he said.

What researchers are starting to learn is that colorectal cancer in people in their early 20s or younger tends to be a more aggressive disease than that often seen in older people.

"We do feel like it is a bit of a distinct disease than what we're seeing in older adults," said Dr. Erica Arnold, a pediatric surgery research fellow at Nationwide Children's Hospital in Columbus, Ohio. In October, Arnold presented new research on colorectal cancer in people ages 21 or younger at the annual meeting of the American Academy of Pediatrics.

Arnold and her colleagues analyzed the cases of 84 patients diagnosed between 2012 and 2023. They found that the median age of diagnosis was 16 years old and the median duration of symptoms before diagnosis was only 12 weeks long.

Only about 20% of the patients had a close relative with colorectal cancer, suggesting that for many of these young people, the disease did not necessarily emerge due to hereditary factors.

If you want my honest opinion, it does suggest that these cancers are developing differently.

Eighty percent of the study participants were diagnosed with Stage III or Stage IV disease, meaning the cancer had already spread locally and to lymph nodes or to other, distant organs when the patients were diagnosed. For comparison, in colorectal cancer patients of all ages, 60% are diagnosed in Stage III or IV, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

In addition, Arnold said, one-third of the patients in their study had cellular markers of particularly aggressive cancer.

"Some of that might be related to delays in diagnosis," Lieu said, "but if you want my honest opinion, it does suggest that these cancers are developing differently."

The study's data was not nationally representative, but a recent analysis of CDC data has also found that colorectal cancer rates in youth are on the rise. In 1999, the diagnosis rate in kids ages 10 to 14 was 1 in a million. By 2020, it had risen to 6 in a million. For teens between 15 and 19, the rate of diagnosis went from 3 in a million to 13 in a million in that same time frame.

There is no definitive reason for this rise, Lieu said. Research on the microbiome has suggested that processed food, antibiotic exposure in childhood, stress, reduced exercise and other lifestyle factors may contribute to this increased risk of colorectal cancer.

Some microbes may play a particularly strong role, at least in some cases of colorectal cancer. For instance, a specific variant of the common gut bacterium Escherichia coli is strongly associated with colorectal cancer; the variant carries a genetic segment and produces compounds that are toxic to genes. But this variant alone cannot explain all colorectal cancer cases in young people. Nor is it clear why the gut microbiome might be undergoing a shift in the first place.

"It may be a combination of food, antibiotic use and environmental exposures," Lieu suggested.

Regardless of the exact causes behind the cases, Arnold's new research pointed to the symptoms that deserve closer scrutiny in young people. Among the 84 patients in the study, 75% reported experiencing back and abdominal pain before their diagnosis, 45% had changes in their bowel movements, 43% experienced unexplained weight loss and 38% had rectal bleeding.

These are classic colorectal cancer symptoms, Arnold said, but they might be overlooked in this young age group because these same symptoms can have more common causes.

Parents should know that in most cases, stomach pain and gastrointestinal disruptions in kids are not caused by colorectal cancer, Lieu said, calling the cancer an "extraordinarily rare event." Nevertheless, pain or gastrointestinal upset that doesn't ease or that worsens over time needs a checkup, and symptoms like weight loss and blood in the stool are very unusual in kids and deserve extra attention.

"It's just important to investigate it to make sure we're catching colorectal cancer earlier rather than later in these patients," Arnold said.

#6611. Snickers Apple Salad

Candy in salad might seem contradictory, but this Snickers apple salad is here to prove it can be done. Chopped apples are tossed with Snickers in a creamy vanilla dressing and drizzled with caramel for a cool and sweet dessert that will surprise and delight everyone at bonfire night. Trust me—it’s a Midwest classic for a reason.

What People Are Saying:“Childhood favorite! ❤️” - NanaManda2025

Start by making a salt water bath for the apples. In a big bowl, stir together water and salt in a bowl until the salt is dissolved. Keep the bowl nearby while you cut the apples into 1/2″ pieces, adding the apples to the salt bath as soon as they’re cut—this will stop them from browning. When all the apples have been cut and fully submerged in the water, drain the apples and transfer about one-eighth of them to a small container—these will be for topping the salad. Cover and refrigerate them until you’re ready to serve the salad.

In a large bowl, whisk together the milk and pudding mix until thickened (this won’t take longer than a minute). Use a flexible rubber spatula to gently fold in the Cool Whip.

Then fold in the remaining apples and most of the chopped Snickers until incorporated.

Transfer the salad to a serving bowl and chill in the refrigerator until it’s cold—1 hour should be just fine. When you’re ready to serve, top with the remaining apples and chopped Snickers, and drizzle with caramel sauce.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

While you can technically keep Snickers apple salad up to 3 days in the refrigerator, it’s really best the day it’s made. The longer it sits, the looser it gets. By day 3, it’s basically Snickers apple soup.

#6610. Pumpkin S’mores Cookies

Recipe by Lauren Habermehl, Pewaukee, Wisconsin

Preheat the oven to 350°F and line two sheet pans with parchment paper.

Melt the butter in a medium saucepan over medium heat. Cook, stirring often with a whisk, until the butter has melted, begins to foam, and turns a rich golden brown color. Remove the saucepan promptly and pour the butter into a bowl of a stand mixer. Cool the brown butter at room temperature for 10 to 15 minutes. (This is important! You don’t want the butter to scramble the egg when it’s added to the bowl in the next step.)

Editor’s Tip: Keep a close eye on the butter, as it can burn easily if you’re not careful. Browning butter typically takes 3 to 5 minutes and is ready when the butter has a warm, nutty aroma.

Add the brown sugar and granulated sugar to the cooled brown butter. Stir to combine, and then whisk in the vanilla and room-temperature eggs. Beat everything until the mixture thickens slightly and turns paler in color, 3 to 5 minutes.

Add the all-purpose flour, baking powder, baking soda and salt to the wet ingredients. Gently fold in the dry ingredients using a rubber spatula until just combined—a few streaks of flour are OK.

#6609. Brûléed Kheer (Rice Pudding) With Mango Sorbet

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

#6608. 21 Easy Weeknight Dinners for November

As daylight dwindles and the November chill settles in, dinner calls for something cozy. Think chicken thighs nestled into caramelized onions, pasta slicked with brown butter, and hearty soups that practically demand a hunk of crusty bread. It’s time to lean into comfort food.

The good news? You don’t need to spend your whole Sunday cooking to make dinner feel special, so you’ll have plenty of time for that When Harry Met Sally rewatch. These 21 easy weeknight dinners deliver all the comfort without the commitment. There’s a three-ingredient pumpkin soup, gochujang chicken that gets a quick blast under the broiler, and a smoky one-pan pasta made with pantry staples. Plus a few Thanksgiving-adjacent flavors—sage, stuffing, squash—because the holiday is right around the corner.

Greek yogurt tenderizes the chicken quickly, but the real weeknight win is the broiler: just 15 minutes under high heat, and you’ve got dinner.

Juicy chicken meatballs and crisp-tender sesame green beans roast on opposite sides of the same sheet pan, streamlining both dinner prep and cleanup.

This speedy stir-fry recipe brings together thin strips of boneless pork shoulder and crisp-tender bok choy for a satisfying, weeknight-ready dinner.

Savory ground beef, fluffy scrambled eggs, and crisp vegetables turn a bowl of steamed rice into a satisfying Japanese dinner that’s ready in 35 minutes.

Give boxed stuffing mix a new lease on life with this clever, holiday-inspired crust. Mixed with Parmesan, lemon zest, parsley, and butter, it gives tender fish a golden, crispy topping. Genius.

Brushed with a sticky, sweet teriyaki sauce, then hurled under the broiler, this salmon develops a glossy, caramelized finish in a matter of minutes.

This easy sheet-pan dinner pairs tender cod with a savory chorizo topping. Big flavor, minimal effort, and only one pan to wash.

Canned chickpeas and frozen spinach make this richly spiced saag quick to prepare—and any leftovers taste even better the next day.

Inspired by satay, this saucy, lip-smacking tofu dish comes together in 30 minutes in just one skillet—so cleanup is a breeze.

Cheesy, creamy, and deeply comforting, these fondue-inspired beans bring a little alpine indulgence to an ordinary Tuesday. Serving them over crusty bread is a must.

Nutty brown butter, crunchy pecans, and hot Italian sausage make this an easy dinner bursting with fall flavors. One reader reports, “Made me feel like a 5-star chef.”

Buttery, garlicky shrimp scampi meets pasta in this weeknight-friendly dinner. A splash of white wine and a pinch of red pepper flakes make the sauce sing.

Canned butternut squash purée (find it by the canned pumpkin!) makes this cozy, cold-weather recipe come together in a snap. Vegetable broth and certified vegetarian parm keep it meat-free, but chicken broth works if that’s what you’ve got.

Four ingredients are all you need for these grown-up buttered noodles. Toasted almonds and parsley are totally optional, but add welcome texture and zing.

Pumpkin purée adds richness, body, and a gentle orange hue to this speedy ground beef chili, letting the flavors of the spices and aromatics shine.

Roasted squash, crispy bacon, and crunchy walnuts turn chopped salad into a proper fall dinner. Use pre-cut butternut squash to streamline prep.

This comforting chicken noodle soup is ideal for chilly evenings or sick days. Chicken breast, kabocha squash, and tiny ditalini cook right in the broth.

A vegetarian spin on the classic Reuben swaps in hearty kale for the meat but keeps the melty cheese and tangy sauerkraut. One reader reports, “I didn’t miss the pastrami one bit.”

Made almost entirely from pantry ingredients—S&B curry powder, red lentils, crushed tomatoes, and coconut milk—this cozy soup is, as one reviewer puts it, “way more delicious than it should be.”

When dinner needs to get on the table pronto, a tuna melt is hard to beat: pantry-friendly, cheesy, and comforting.

This fiery soup has a shockingly trim ingredient list: curry paste (we like Maesri), a can of pumpkin purée, and coconut milk. Perfect for busy November weeknights.

#6607. Wildly Delicious Weeknight Dinners To Keep You Cozy All November Long

There’s more than just Thanksgiving to plan for.

November is the month when comfort food season really kicks into full gear. It’s the last month that really feels like fall before those pleasantly chilly evenings turn teeth-chattering, the leaves are still colorful and on the trees, and, of course, we can’t forget about Thanksgiving, so we’re not letting it get away without celebrating all it has to offer. Join us this November as we cook up cozy, comforting meals for both weeknights and special occasions. We’ve got 40 recipes to help inspire you to make dinner this November—one for every day of the month, and then some.

We’ve included a good mix of entirely new recipes, like our lasagna alla vodka skillet and our sheet-pan chicken tagine, as well as some old cold-weather classics like our chicken & dumplings, our broccoli cheddar gnocchi soup, and our chili mac.

Looking for cozy recipes for November? Check out our favorite one-pan fall dinners, under-an-hour comfort foods, and easy comfort food recipes.

Lasagna and penne alla vodka are two Italian-American staples that go hand in hand. Because our one-pot lazy lasagna skillet is a weeknight favorite, it only felt right to consolidate these two classics in one pan.

This version of chicken biryani is inspired by Hyderabadi biryani, which is one of the most popular and iconic dishes in South Asia. This streamlined version stays as true as possible to the authentic flavors, using readily available grocery store ingredients, but cuts down on the time by finishing things in the oven.

We can never get enough of beef and broccoli. In this easy, hands-off version, we’re cooking thinly-sliced steak low and slow in a rich broth until it’s fall-apart delicious, and then throwing in the broccoli near the end so it cooks just long enough to become tender.

This sheet-pan chicken tagine is the ultimate glow-up, transforming the complex, slow-simmered flavors of the classic North African dish into a streamlined meal perfect for busy evenings or an effortless dinner party.

This pumpkin pot pie is basically a pumpkin coconut curry baked beneath a flaky, golden crust that turns out equal parts comforting and festive. The carved Jack-o'-lantern top transforms a simple pot pie into a showstopping centerpiece that's almost too cute to cut into.

Carbonara always feels like a luxurious dish, but it's made with the simplest ingredients: eggs, spaghetti, Pecorino Romano, and pork. Add a bottles of Shaoxing and soy sauce, and you've got yourself an unforgettable meal.

In the world of all of our Marry Me Chicken variations, this just may be our new favorite version. We have a soft spot for risotto because it feels elevated, but it’s also soothing to stand there and stir until the rice hits the right tenderness. This version is extra luxurious with sun-dried tomatoes and a touch of cream.

Pizza is our guilty pleasure, but sometimes we want the flavors of the classic dish with a little more protein, without ordering a meat lovers. This vegetarian dinner has everything you love about pizza—slightly sweet tomato sauce, Italian herbs, and plenty of cheese—but makes a protein-packed swap by substituting the crust for cannellini beans.

One spoonful instantly made me think of my childhood. This easy comfort food recipe is perfect on a cold night, and simple enough to whip up when you don't feel like making anything (like on a weeknight after a weekend full of potlucks and Friendsgivings).

Slow-cooked turkey legs are this year’s ultimate Thanksgiving hack (we're not stopping you the rest of the month either!). No basting, no inevitable dry meat—no fuss at all. All you have to do is make an easy festive herb butter, wrap everything in foil, and let it roast unsupervised.

When you combine chili and mac and cheese, incredible things happen. We started with our preferred chili variation—white chicken chili, of course—and added in all the creamy, cheesy goodness of mac and cheese for the perfect weeknight dinner for indecisive families.

This recipe combines the rich, smoky flavors of traditional barbacoa with a cheesy topping and buttery biscuits for an irresistible meal. At the heart of this dish is succulent beef chuck roast, slow-cooked in a blend of fire-roasted tomatoes, chipotle chiles, and a medley of spices.

If you love stovetop mac 'n' cheese, you’ve got to try this creamy butternut squash orzo. Butternut squash and Parmesan join forces with orzo to create a cheesy pasta skillet that hits every nostalgic note.

The real magic in this sheet-pan dinner is in the savory-sweet, spoonable sauce that the onions transform into. Blending the chicken fat-roasted, charred onions with butter, sweet white vinegar, and crushed red pepper yields a creamy, umami-rich sauce that makes the chicken even more succulent.

If you’re looking for a vegetarian dinner centerpiece, then you can’t beat a whole roasted cauliflower. Gorgeously browned outside and meltingly tender in the middle, its stunningly simple goodness can’t be topped at any vegetarian Thanksgiving dinner.

Nothing satisfies a meat-and-potatoes craving quite like a classic, hearty shepherd’s pie. In this comfort food staple, ground beef is cooked with aromatics and red wine before being combined with corn and peas, all covered with velvety, rich mashed potatoes and topped with Parmesan before being broiled until golden brown.

Want taco night without the multiple pans and (semi-?) controlled chaos of a build-your-own dinner? Make this taco skillet. Saucy, spiced sweet potatoes and black beans are tossed with crushed potato chips and topped with melty cheese for a simple one-pan meal that will be your new weeknight go-to this November.

The heavy cream cuts the robust, earthy pumpkin in this soup, making it one of the most comforting soups for a chilly fall day. Load up on the garlic, cook the tomato paste to eliminate any rawness and release its sweet side, and get ready to thoroughly enjoy this pumpkin tortellini soup (in under 30 minutes!).

Broccoli cheddar soup is the ultimate comfort food—it’s rich, creamy, and packed with cheesy goodness—and we're taking it to the next level with pillowy gnocchi, making it heartier and more satisfying without any extra hassle. The gnocchi cooks right in the same pot, so you’re not stuck washing another dish.

This one-pot meal is a perfect way to warm up during the colder months, so go ahead and make it in the dead of winter to awaken your soul and grab a spoon to dig in! The best part? This hearty favorite is ready to enjoy in just 30 minutes, making it the perfect go-to weeknight dinner.

#6606. Japanese Sweet Potato Chaat

Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

To a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

To a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

#6605. Apple Butter Snack Cake

Recipe by Margaret Knoebel, Milwaukee, Wisconsin

Made with apples and apple butter, this easy fall cake is just the thing when you need a sweet snack.

I know I’ve fallen into the autumnal magic of a fall farmer’s market when I walk away with too many apples, a jar of apple butter and no real plan for either. Luckily, our recipe tester Maggie Knoebel figured out how to combine both spoils into one super easy bake: an apple butter snack cake, complete with a brown butter glaze and cinnamon-sugar topping.

Preheat the oven to 350°F. In a large bowl, use a hand mixer or stand mixer to beat the eggs, sugar, apple butter, canola oil and vanilla extract.

In a separate bowl, whisk together the all-purpose flour, cinnamon, baking soda and salt. Add the flour mixture to the egg mixture and stir just until no streaks of flour remain. Fold in the apples and pecans.

Pour the batter into a greased 13×9-inch baking dish. Bake the cake until a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean, 50 to 55 minutes. Cool the cake on a wire rack to room temperature.

Meanwhile, in a small, heavy saucepan, melt the butter over medium heat. Cook the butter until the milk solids are golden brown, stirring constantly, about 5 to 7 minutes. Immediately pour the brown butter into a mixing bowl to stop the cooking process or the butter will burn. Let the brown butter cool to room temperature.

Editor’s Tip: At some point during cooking, the butter will start to foam up. Don’t panic, it’s completely normal! Continue to stir while cooking, making sure to keep an eye on the butter’s color so you know when to take it off the heat.

Use a hand mixer or stand mixer to beat in the confectioners’ sugar until it’s fully combined with the brown butter. Spread the brown butter over the cake, then sprinkle the cinnamon-sugar mixture over the top before serving, if desired. Enjoy!

Store your apple butter snack cake in an airtight container in the fridge for up to four days. You really want to keep it well covered, so the glaze doesn’t absorb lingering fridge smells. If you want to keep the cake in the pan, cover the pan with storage wrap.

Yes, you can freeze apple butter snack cake. If you’re freezing the cake unfrosted, allow it to cool completely to room temperature, then cover the cake in storage wrap followed by aluminum foil. To freeze the glazed cake, place it in the freezer, uncovered, until the glaze is hard, about 30 minutes. Cover the cake with storage wrap and aluminum foil. Freeze the cake for up to two months and thaw overnight in the fridge.

Yes, you can bake an apple butter snack cake in a different-sized pan. Instead of a 13×9-inch baking dish, divide the batter evenly between two 8-inch square or two 9-inch cake pans. The baking time and temperature should be the same.

Yes, you can absolutely make this apple butter snack cake gluten- and/or dairy-free! Replace the all-purpose flour with a good gluten-free flour blend—one that’s designed as a cup-for-cup (or measure-for-measure) replacement. The cake is naturally dairy-free, but you’ll need to replace the butter in the glaze with vegan butter. You won’t be able to brown the vegan butter, so take 2 tablespoons off the measurement. That’s about how much liquid evaporates from butter when it’s browned.

There's a new type of landslide affecting northern latitudes, and it could affect more areas as the planet continues to warm.

These landslides, called permafrost detachment slides, occur in areas with relatively thin permafrost and seem to be a long-term impact of wildfire in these environments, according to a paper published Sept. 23 in the journal Geophysical Research Letters. Such slides have not been observed in the region before and may be unprecedented over the past 10,000 years or more, said study leader Joseph Young, who completed the work as part of his doctoral degree at the University of Alberta.

"It has been stable, and then it just flipped a switch, essentially," Young told Live Science.

Young and his colleagues were doing field observations in Canada's Northwest Territories when they noticed large landslide scars in valleys that have long hosted stable permafrost, which is sediment that remains frozen year-round. They began using satellite imagery to map the changes and also conducted fieldwork, which revealed that the slides weren't standard melting permafrost.

"Typically with permafrost, everything just thaws and melts in a slurry and moves like a mud downslope," Young said. "But with these large landslides, we found blocks of frozen material in the debris."

Some of these blocks were 33 feet (10 meters) tall, the height of a two-story house. The researchers ran an electrical current through the ground to determine the depth of the permafrost on the slopes.

They focused on two slides. One, in the Johnson River Valley, took place in 2017 and moved more than 636 million cubic feet (18 million cubic meters) of soil and rock. The other, in the Redstone River Valley, moved almost 159 million cubic feet (4.5 million cubic meters) of debris in 2018. The smaller slide left a scar three-quarters of a mile (1.2 kilometers) long, while the larger one gouged nearly 2 miles (3.2 km) out of the hillside.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The researchers then used the data they'd collected to build a model of how these icy slides occurred. The permafrost in this area has been warming by about 0.54 degrees Fahrenheit (0.3 degrees Celsius) per decade since 1980, when monitoring began, and there were also severe wildfires nearby in 1995.

The researchers found that instead of a top-down melting process by which the permafrost thawed to a muddy slurry from above, the slides were instead caused by a combination of fire-related thaw and warming temperatures, leading to cracks near the top of the slopes. These cracks allowed the thaw to penetrate deeper, eventually melting the bottom of the permafrost layer. This propagation can take 20 years to penetrate 66 feet (20 m), which is exactly what happened in the Johnson River and Redstone River valleys.

"We had a fire in '95 and then 20 years later, we start to get a lot of these widespread disturbances," Young said.

The two large slides the researchers studied are among more than 150 in the area, Young said. The others are smaller, but they still typically move over 35 million cubic feet (1 million cubic meters) of land apiece. Canada's Northwest Territories are remote, so the permafrost detachment slides have yet to damage any infrastructure. But the two in the study did dam rivers, creating brand-new lakes and rapidly dumping sediment into the waterways downstream, Young said.

There are many other places in Canada and Alaska where the permafrost is 66 to 130 feet (20 to 40 m) deep and thus vulnerable to the same type of slide. This is especially true given the increasing intensity of wildfire at northern latitudes, Young said.

"This is almost a potential glimpse into the future of what we might be able to expect in these areas with changing forest fire dynamics," he said.

Young, J. M., Van Der Sluijs, J., Kokelj, S. V., Gruber, S., Herring, T., Rudy, A. C. A., Alvarez, A., & Froese, D. (2026). Permafrost detachment slides: a distinct High‐Magnitude Permafrost mass wasting process. Geophysical Research Letters, 53(18). https://doi.org/10.1029/2026gl124103

Stephanie Pappas is a contributing writer for Live Science, covering topics ranging from geoscience to archaeology to the human brain and behavior. She was previously a senior writer for Live Science but is now a freelancer based in Denver, Colorado, and regularly contributes to Scientific American and The Monitor, the monthly magazine of the American Psychological Association. Stephanie received a bachelor's degree in psychology from the University of South Carolina and a graduate certificate in science communication from the University of California, Santa Cruz.

#6603. A Diwali Menu That’s Full of Joy (and Sticky Chicken Wings)

Growing up, I remember a steady stream of guests coming in and out of our home in the weeks leading up to Diwali. The season would start with Navratri, a nine-night Hindu festival celebrating the divine feminine, Shakti, through the worship of Goddess Durga. Our celebrations were led by women, my grandmother, mother, and aunts, who would meticulously clean the house and spend weeks preparing snacks and sweets. They taught me the art of hosting and how to share the joy of food with our community.

I came to associate Diwali with that sense of abundance, care, and graciousness. There was always more food than we needed, and always room for more people. When I moved to New York, I started to miss that deeply, so I began a tradition to share Diwali with my chosen family here, many of whom were experiencing the holiday through food for the first time.

I’m the kind of host who likes to enjoy her own party, which means being strategic about the menu. I lean on dishes like my homestyle chicken kari, which can be made ahead and tastes even better the next day. And then there are dishes that bring a little theater to the table, like the creamy rice pudding which gets torched before serving. I want food that feeds a crowd, feels special, and lets me spend less time in the kitchen and more time with the people I love.

Guests always ask me for this crowd-pleasing app. Japanese sweet potatoes have a creamy texture that pairs beautifully with the spicy, crunchy elements of chaat. Best of all, the spuds can be cooked ahead, with the toppings added just before serving. One less thing for you to do on the big day.

Wings reign supreme when it comes to a party appetizer, and these tamarind-glazed ones deliver tangy punch in every bite. The marinade combines tamarind purée, fish sauce, brown sugar, red pepper flakes, and cumin, with extra glaze brushed on for maximum flavor and char. Be sure to finish with fried onions for bonus crunch.

This tastes like you spent hours cooking, but actually it comes together in less than an hour. The best part? It’s even better the next day, making it ideal for hosting. Gently reheat the kari before guests arrive, letting the warm, heady spices fill your home before everyone gathers around the table.

Mushrooms are an underrated ingredient in Indian cooking, and this creamy masala puts the earthy veg front and center. Sautéing them in batches gives the shrooms beautifully caramelized edges, while deglazing the pot captures all those flavorful browned bits. Serve the masala with rice or warm flatbread to sop up all the savory sauce.

No Diwali celebration is complete without something sweet, but dessert doesn’t have to be elaborate to feel special. This recipe transforms a handful of pantry staples into a rich, creamy rice pudding. For a playful twist, finish it with a crackly brûléed sugar crust and serve with a scoop of mango sorbet.

#6602. Failproof Homestyle Chicken Kari

This recipe is inspired by the garam masala my mother used to make back in India. Just a pinch adds incredible depth and flavor to both meat and vegetable dishes—it’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional. And now you can use it too! This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again. If you prefer a sweeter blend, add more cinnamon and fennel seeds; if you want a spicier kick, increase the black pepper and cloves.

In a small bowl, toss 12 dried bay leaves, 12 whole cloves, 5 black cardamom pods, 4 whole star anise pods, three 3" (7.5-cm) cinnamon sticks, 1 whole nutmeg, 3 Tbsp. coriander seeds, 3 Tbsp. whole mace fronds, 2 Tbsp. cumin seeds, 1 Tbsp. black peppercorns, and 2 tsp. white poppy seeds to combine.

Heat a medium dry skillet over low heat until hot. Add the spice mixture and toast until slightly fragrant, about 45 seconds. Transfer back to the bowl and let cool.

Transfer the whole nutmeg to a mortar and break into smaller pieces with a pestle (this is just to make it easier to grind, so don’t worry about being too precise!). Repeat with the cinnamon. Tear the bay leaves into smaller pieces. Transfer all of the spices to a spice grinder and grind into a fine powder (it will be slightly warm when you remove the lid). Transfer to an airtight container (do not cover yet) and let cool completely. Then close the lid.

Do Ahead: Garam masala can be made 1 month ahead. Cover and store in a cool, dark place.

To a small heatproof bowl, add 1 medium yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, 2 Tbsp. lime juice, 2 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 2 tsp. chaat masala, ½ tsp. cayenne powder, and ½ tsp. fine sea salt.

In a small pan over medium-high heat, warm 2 Tbsp. peanut oil or any vegetable oil or avocado oil until it shimmers. Add 1 tsp. cumin seeds and cook until fragrant and they start to turn brown, about 1 minute. Be careful not to let the seeds burn or they will taste bitter. Remove from the heat and pour the hot oil over the onions. Toss to coat the onions in the spice mixture.

Serve immediately or let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

To a mortar and pestle or food processor, add one 2" (5-cm) piece fresh ginger, chopped, 4 garlic cloves, peeled, and 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, chopped, and pound or pulse into a chunky paste. To a medium bowl, add 2 lb. (910 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, excess fat trimmed, cut into 2" [5-cm] pieces, along with the ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp. fine sea salt and toss to combine. Cover and place in the refrigerator to marinate for a minimum of 1 hour or overnight.

In a medium heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-low heat, warm ⅓ cup (80 ml) vegetable oil or avocado oil, then add 1 tsp. cumin seeds, ½ tsp. black mustard seeds, ½ tsp. black peppercorns, 5 whole cloves, 1 fresh or dried bay leaf, 1 star anise, and one 3" [7.5-cm] cinnamon stick, broken into small pieces, and lightly toast and until fragrant, about 1 minute. Increase the heat to medium, add 1 medium red or yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), finely chopped, cover, and cook until the onion is translucent and beginning to turn brown around the edges, stirring halfway through, about 10 minutes.

Add 1 Tbsp. ground coriander, 1 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 Tbsp. Garam Masala, 2 tsp. cayenne powder, and 1 tsp. powdered turmeric. Stir to combine and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Drain off the excess marinade from the chicken, then add it to the pot along with 3 Tbsp. tomato paste, 1 Tbsp. packed fresh fenugreek leaves, and remaining 1½ tsp. fine sea salt and stir until everything is mixed thoroughly and the chicken is covered with the spices and tomato paste. Add ½ cup (120 ml) water and mix again. Cover and cook until the chicken is cooked through and tender, 30 minutes, stirring halfway through.

Remove from the heat and sprinkle with the remaining 1 tsp. Garam Masala, remaining 1 tsp. fresh fenugreek leaves, and cilantro leaves. Serve immediately with lime wedges, Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions, and steamed rice or Indian flatbread.

Do Ahead: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or in the freezer for up to 1 month.

#6601. Fall Harvest Minestrone

Recipe by Margaret Knoebel, Milwaukee, Wisconsin

Our fall harvest minestrone trades summer’s vegetables for autumn’s produce. Break out the slow cooker!

You may be familiar with the usual cluster of summer vegetables in classic minestrone, but any Italian will tell you that real minestrone changes with the season. Italians like to prioritize whole, nutritious, in-season produce—especially those living in Italy’s blue zone, where some of the longest-living people eat minestrone every single day.

As we dive into fall, we’re taking our classic minestrone recipe with us and giving it a couple of tweaks. Our fall harvest minestrone ditches the zucchini, green beans, parsley, basil and spinach, and reflects what’s growing in the garden right now: sweet potatoes, onions, kale, sage and rosemary. We included Italian sausage, too, to enrich the broth and add a big boost of protein—enough for this fall soup to officially be considered dinner.

In a large skillet, cook the sausage over medium heat until it’s no longer pink, six to eight minutes, breaking it into crumbles with a wooden spoon. Drain the liquid from the skillet, then transfer the meat to a 6-quart slow cooker.

Stir in the beef broth, sweet potatoes, canned tomatoes, kale, onion, carrot, garlic, sage and rosemary. Cook the minestrone, covered, on low until the vegetables are tender, five to six hours.

Editor’s Tip: The sweet potatoes should be fork-tender before moving on to the next step.

Stir the pasta into the minestrone. Cook everything, covered, on low until the pasta is tender, 20 to 25 minutes longer.

Ladle the soup into bowls and serve. If desired, top the fall harvest minestrone with Parmesan cheese, red pepper flakes or fresh sage or rosemary.

Allow leftover fall harvest minestrone to cool completely to room temperature in under two hours. Transfer the soup to an airtight container and store it in the fridge for up to four days.

Yes, you can freeze fall harvest minestrone. Let the soup come to room temperature in under two hours, then ladle it into freezer-safe, airtight containers. Freeze the soup for up to two months. Thaw it overnight in the fridge before enjoying it again.

Yes, you can make fall harvest minestrone gluten free. Buy a box of good gluten-free pasta and make sure the Italian sausage is gluten free, too. I like to cook the gluten-free pasta separately when I suspect I’ll have leftovers. I add the pasta to individual bowls, then top it with the soup. Gluten-free noodles will absorb too much broth overnight, breaking down and becoming mushy.

The fall harvest minestrone has everything: vegetables, carbs and meat. It doesn’t really need anything else, but if you want to stretch the meal a bit, serve the soup with cornbread, biscuits (I love our garlic bread biscuits) or slices of crusty sourdough bread. Something like a vinegary salad will cut the richness a bit and bring in fresh flavor.

A hypothetical particle could have briefly held more energy than everything else in the infant universe combined, which could help explain how matter won out over antimatter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A neglected "ghost particle" may have dominated the universe right after the Big Bang ‪—‬ changing how the cosmos expanded in its first moments and reshaping the conditions under which matter won out over antimatter, a new study suggests. In other words, it may explain why anything exists at all.

The particle, a hypothetical "right-handed" neutrino, briefly could have held more energy than everything else in the infant universe combined, which would have sped up cosmic expansion and delayed key particle interactions, the study proposes. The research was published Sept. 8 in the journal Physical Review Letters.

Neutrinos are ghostly particles that rarely interact with anything. A typical neutrino from the sun could pass through a slab of lead a light-year thick — about 5.9 trillion miles (9.5 trillion kilometers) — before striking a single atom. Neutrinos come in three types, or "flavors," and switch between them as they travel, making use of a subtle quantum effect that works only if they have mass. Yet the Standard Model of particle physics predicts they should be massless.

One popular fix involves "right-handed" neutrinos. Particles spin a bit like tiny tops, and physicists call them left- or right-handed depending on how they spin relative to their direction of travel. A right-handed particle rotates like an ordinary screw being driven in, turning clockwise as it moves away from you. Every neutrino detected so far is left-handed and turns counterclockwise as it flies away, like a screw with a reverse thread.

"Right-handed neutrinos are hypothetical particles that do not feel the weak nuclear force, "unlike their left-handed counterparts, which are part of the Standard Model," study co-author Rishav Roshan, a theoretical physicist at the University of Southampton in the U.K., told Live Science via email. "They are characterized by having no electric charge and being much heavier."

"Right-handed neutrinos may mix with left-handed neutrinos, helping to explain the mass of the latter" and why they switch flavors, Roshan said.

The IceCube facility, photographed here beneath the Southern Lights, is Earth's premier neutrino detection facility. The proposed 'right-handed' neutrino has not yet been detected.

In quantum physics, particles that mix can exist as a blend of two identities at once. In a theoretical framework called the seesaw mechanism, each ordinary neutrino carries a faint trace of a heavy right-handed partner, and that trace gives it a tiny mass. The heavier the partner, the fainter the trace and the lighter the ordinary neutrino — hence the name, after the playground ride whose ends move in opposite directions.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The particles could solve other puzzles, too. They "aim to address several issues, including the origin of neutrino masses, the matter-antimatter asymmetry of the universe, and the nature of dark matter," Roshan said.

The Big Bang should have made equal amounts of matter and antimatter, which would have annihilated each other, forbidding the universe as we know it from ever taking shape. Right-handed neutrinos play a crucial role in models' proposals that the "observed matter-antimatter imbalance arose from processes involving these neutrinos in the early universe," Roshan said.

In this picture, decaying heavy neutrinos left behind a slight excess of leptons — the particle family that includes electrons — that later became today's surplus of matter, he explained.

The seesaw framework usually includes three right-handed neutrinos, but because two are enough to explain the data, physicists often ignore the third, assuming it is too heavy or interacts too feebly with matter.

In the new study, Roshan and Sudipta Show, a physicist at the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur, examined what this neglected particle — which, in the team's main example, was about 100 trillion times as heavy as a proton — would have done after the Big Bang.

At first, the particle would have zipped around at nearly light speed, so its energy would have faded like that of light, which would have both spread out and stretched to weaker wavelengths as space expanded. But as the cosmos cooled, the particle would have slowed down and most of its energy would have become locked in its mass, which would have been only spread out. Its share of the cosmic energy therefore would have grown until it dominated, and the long-lived particle would have stayed in charge until it decayed into other particles, according to the team's computations.

The study reveals that the neglected right-handed neutrino "significantly impacts the early universe's expansion dynamics, driving a period of early matter domination," Roshan said. This change "affects various Standard Model interactions"‬ that could help to explain the matter-antimatter asymmetry, Roshan added.

Each interaction would have switched on only once it outpaced the expansion of space. Because a universe dominated by the heavy neutrino would have expanded faster, the interactions would have had to wait until it cooled further.

These interactions would have let the early universe distinguish lepton flavors, which would have affected how the matter surplus formed. Thanks to the delay, the team found, a lighter right-handed neutrino about 100 billion times as heavy as a proton could have produced the observed amount of matter before the flavors could be told apart — even after the heavy neutrino's decay diluted part of it.

The heavy neutrino is far too massive to create in any particle accelerator, so tests must be indirect.

Gravitational waves — ripples in space-time — offer one such route. An era dominated by the heavy neutrino would have left a telltale kink in the background of early-universe gravitational waves, such as those from "cosmic strings" ‪—‬ hypothetical thread-like defects in space. The results can be tested through forthcoming facilities such as the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) and the Square Kilometer Array Observatory (SKAO), Roshan noted.

LISA, a space-based European Space Agency mission, is scheduled to launch around 2035, while SKAO, a giant radio telescope project being built in Australia and South Africa, could catch such waves by timing distant pulsars. Tests could come "as these facilities come online and begin data collection," Roshan said. A faint hum from the hot primordial plasma would carry the era's imprint too, but at frequencies beyond what existing detectors could pick up.

Roshan, R., & Show, S. (2026). Delayed charged Lepton Yukawa equilibration in minimal seesaw. Physical Review Letters, 137(11), 111802. https://doi.org/10.1103/nfkx-q6z7

Andrey got his B.Sc. and M.Sc. degrees in elementary particle physics from Novosibirsk State University in Russia, and a Ph.D. in string theory from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel. He works as a science writer, specializing in physics, space, and technology. His articles have been published in AdvancedScienceNews, PhysicsWorld, Science, and other outlets.

#6598. Apple Cinnamon Bread

Sorry, banana bread, there’s a new quick bread coming for the crown. Bursting with chunks of cinnamon apples, this easy bread is a MAJOR hit come fall. Gone apple picking? It's the perfect baking project to use up some of those goodies. Don't worry, you'll still have enough for apple pie, too. Our secret weapon? Orange juice! This loaf is perfectly balanced, not too sweet, and tender and fluffy. It pairs well with a cup of tea or coffee, but you can also totally eat it by itself as a festive midday snack.

What People Are Saying:"This is a ridiculously delicious recipe! Really might be the best sweet loaf I've ever had/made." -GoldPin

"Wonderful recipe making it today for the third time!" -GreenSnow

Start by preheating your oven to 350° and lining a 9x5-inch loaf pan with parchment paper. Now you are ready to make your apple mixture! First, core and slice your apples into chunks, about 1 inch in thickness. In a large bowl, stir together chopped apples, lemon juice, brown sugar, and cinnamon until your apples are evenly coated in the sugar and spice mixture. Set this bowl aside, and get started on your batter.

In another large bowl, using a hand mixer, cream together butter and sugar until light and fluffy—about 2-5 minutes. Scrape the sides of the bowl continually to ensure everything is evenly combined. Then, add in your eggs and vanilla and beat until smooth. In a separate bowl, whisk together flour and baking powder. Then add this dry mixture to your butter mixture, keeping your mixing on low. Be careful not to over mix, which will result in an overly dense cake! Add in your orange juice and mix until just combined.

Now that your batter is done, scoop half of it into a greased loaf pan, spreading it out with a butter knife or the back of a spoon. Then spoon in half the apple mixture. Top this with the remaining batter, then press in the remaining apples on top.

Now your loaf is ready for the oven! Bake until your loaf is golden and a toothpick inserted into the center of the cake comes out clean, about 1 hour and 15 minutes. Let cool completely. Enjoy!

This apple cinnamon bread can be stored, covered, at room temperature for 3 to 4 days. You can also wrap it tightly in plastic wrap, then wrap it with foil or place it in a freezer-safe zip-top bag, and freeze for up to 3 months.
