#6596. Cranberry Meringue Pie

A big, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you plan to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

We never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling)

Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too quickly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

Spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

#6595. The 15 Cookbooks We’re Most Looking Forward to This Fall

Fall cookbook season is upon us, and in advance of the holidays and cooler nights, that means big-name releases from restaurant-world heavyweights (ahem, Eric Ripert and Kwame Onwuachi) along with topic-based books delving into underrepresented cuisines (Basque, Taiwanese, and plant-based Ghanaian, to name a few) and even specific courses. There’s plenty to choose from this year, which is why we’re presenting a special supersize fall cookbook preview, with 15 of the titles we’re most looking forward to.

Ghanaian author Afia Amoako has amassed hundreds of thousands of followers on social media, where her account @eatwithafia highlights Ghanaian and West African cultural traditions and recipes through a plant-based lens. In her lush, colorful debut cookbook, Amoako builds a deeply researched archive of a cuisine that’s often passed down only orally, and we all benefit from her efforts: More than half of the recipes are traditional and unmodified, not modern interpretations, creating an essential record of Ghanaian foodways. Recipes include classics such as jollof rice and okra stew, plus “roadside snacks” like ofam (a sweet plantain-based snacking cake) and drinks including iced Moringa milk tea. (Avery, Aug. 18)

Pim Techamuanvivit is a legend. A former food blogger turned chef of several Michelin-starred Thai restaurants in San Francisco and Bangkok, she is uniquely poised to help guide home cooks interested in understanding the nuances of Thai cuisine. Teaming up with fellow food writing superstar Andrea Nguyen, Techamuanvivit created more than 100 new recipes covering an expansive range of Thai flavors and techniques, including chapters dedicated to “Grilled, Roasted, Simmered, and Steamed” dishes, along with “Stir-Fried and Deep Fried” delights, plus soups, curries, noodles, and more. (Ten Speed Press, Aug. 25)

Ali Stoner, aka the delightfully named @rovinghaggis on social media, is a Glasgow-born, Melbourne-based home cook and former Masterchef Australia contestant who tackles the flavors of her heritage in her debut cookbook (the title is Scottish slang for a simple, comforting meal). There are plenty of hearty breakfasts and handheld “savouries” (tattie scones and bacon pieces, “wee tongue sandwiches,” and chicken Balmoral sausage rolls), plus sweet puddings (try the Tipsy Laird trifle), soups, and breads. It’s refreshing to see modern Scottish cuisine given the spotlight, especially in such an approachable, home-cook-friendly fashion—with moody, evocative photos, to boot. (Mitchell Beazley, Sept. 10)

PBS host and Mexico City native Pati Jinich is back with a new cookbook (following 2021’s Treasures of the Mexican Table). This time she focuses on the cuisines of the borderlands between Mexico and the U.S. (or, as she prefers to call it, “la frontera”). What that translates to is thoughtfully researched dishes that go far beyond Tex-Mex, including skirt steak and shrimp hot pot, seafood fried rice with asparagus and mushrooms, and smashburger tacos with poblano peppers. Throughout, she intersperses personal stories of growing up between two cultures and challenges readers to think beyond the confines of a single place. (Harvest, Sept. 15)

Enrique Salmón is a Rarámuri (Tarahumara) scholar at Cal State University, East Bay, and an expert in the connection between Indigenous foodways and land-management practices and climate change. In his second cookbook, he explores the concept of “kincentricity,” an Indigenous worldview emphasizing the interconnectedness of all living beings and our responsibility to be good stewards of the planet we share. After a comprehensive introduction, Salmón dives into the history, harvesting, and cooking methods of more than 50 Indigenous ingredients, ranging from huckleberries to black walnuts to wild onions. The result is as much an ethnography as it is a cookbook, from an author with the lived experience to guide the newly kincentric-curious. (Rizzoli, Sept. 15)

In his second cookbook, Kwame Onwuachi, the Bronx-raised chef behind Tatiana in New York and Dōgon in Washington, D.C., promises personal recipes “about how I really eat” at any and all hours of the day. What that translates to is big, bold dishes that aren’t afraid to mash up cultures and cuisines, like Red Stew Chicken Parm and Drunken Noodles Alla Vodka. (“That’s not a thing! Well, it wasn’t a thing, but now it is,” he explains.) There are chapters dedicated to sandwiches, the “Holy Grail of the Bronx” (aka New York Chinese food), and “Goddamn Veggie Sides,” which should give you some indication of the verve and voice behind this raucous collection. (Knopf, Sept. 22)

Dona Murad is the Bahrain-born owner of New York’s beloved Librae, a self-described “third culture bakery” that draws equally from SWANA flavors and Danish technique. With recipes for pastries like rose and pistachio croissants, za’atar and labneh morning buns, and loomi and lemon curd babka, her debut book is aimed at home bakers who revel in a project, but Murad walks readers of all levels through techniques like lamination with a steady, gentle hand. And with step-by-step photos throughout (plus plenty of beginner-friendly bakes), you’ll be turning out pastries that inspire lines down the block, just like Librae, in no time. (Quadrille, Sept. 22)

In his ninth book, Eric Ripert, the celebrity chef and owner of New York’s fine-dining temple Le Bernadin, draws on his travels to Buddhist monasteries across Korea and Japan to put together 75-plus recipes designed to emphasize the joy and mindfulness that cooking with plants can bring. The recipes here hopscotch across Asian, European, and Latin cultures, in chapters introduced by “guiding principles” like gratitude, intention, and joy. That translates to recipes like Radish & Turnip Carpaccio With Yuzu Kosho Vinaigrette, Tamales Rojos, and Seared Tofu With Chili Crisp, among others. Through it all, the boundlessly enthusiastic Ripert encourages home cooks to consider cooking itself as a meditative act and to enjoy the process of nourishing ourselves in both body and spirit. (Random House, Oct. 6)

The crew behind the acclaimed Montreal wine bar Mon Lapin—namely co-chefs Marc-Olivier Frappier and Jessica Noël, along with sommelier Vanya Filipovic and coauthor Mireille Silcoff—team up for a cookbook that’s every bit as chic and vibey as the restaurant that inspired it. With chapters like “What Is a Wine Bar Anyway?” and “Every Vegetable Is a Summer Vegetable in Quebec,” their collective voice shines through, and recipes like White Asparagus Soldiers with Good Anchovies and Eggplant-and-Cantaloupe Ceviche belie a deep understanding of quality ingredients and elegant presentation. As to be expected, there’s plenty of wine writing throughout, making this a must for future dinner parties. (Phaidon, Oct. 7)

Award-winning New York-based pastry chef Caroline Schiff (formerly of Gage & Tollner) makes her cookbook debut with this bright, cheerful baking book, which encourages readers to consider making and eating some form of sweet treat as a daily ritual. Yes, there are a few advanced-level pastries (such as Hazelnut Roche Profiteroles with Glossy Chocolate Sauce), but most of the recipes are approachable and friendly, as outlined in chapters like “Bake Once, Snack All Week” (snacking cakes) and “Little Bakes Just for You (and Maybe a Friend)”. With a section dedicated entirely to doughs, toppings, and crumbs, Schiff equips bakers of all levels with the confidence they need to make dessert a regular part of their day. (Abrams, Oct. 13)

Ernesto’s chef Ryan Bartlow is American, but he spent years living and cooking at the three Michelin-starred Akelarre in San Sebastián, Spain. Despite his fine-dining bona fides, though, what Bartlow really fell for during his time abroad was the rustic, humble side of Basque cooking, codified, as he writes, “on farms, in fishing ports and cider houses.” In his handsome debut with coauthor Laurie Woolever, Bartlow champions recipes with simple ingredients, like a classic tortilla de patatas, callos de Madrileña (a smoky, spicy tripe stew), and a lush crème caramel, along with pintxos and cocktails. This is a book fully steeped in a sense of place, including helpful guides to the Basque language and Basque-Spanish drinking culture, and a travel guide to the region itself, with gorgeous photographs. (Abrams, Oct. 13)

Eric Sze, the chef behind 886 and Wenwen in New York, teams up with veteran food writer Elyse Inamine for a voicey, intimate, and delightfully neon-soaked exploration of the foods of Taiwan, where he was born and raised. The first half of the book focuses on Taiwanese dishes as they’re presented in Taiwan itself, while the second half is more experimental, covering the fusion-y (a term the chef embraces) recipes Sze has perfected cooking at his New York pop-ups and restaurants, such as Mochi Gnocchi with Chili Oil Pumpkin purée and Beef Noodle Soup Ragu). Shot colorfully on location, this is a book brimming with personality—and a sneakily impressive amount of research—on every page. (Hardie Grant, Oct. 20)

Siberia-born, London-based academic and food writer Alissa Timoshkina is the author of two previous cookbooks on Eastern European foodways, though she’s perhaps best known as the founder of #CookForUkraine, a global fundraising campaign supporting humanitarian relief. It’s fitting, then, that her latest title is focused on humble-yet-mighty soups and stews from across a borderless collection of Ukrainian, Jewish, Tatar, Hungarian, Polish, Slovak, and Roma traditions. Organized into “Soups & Broths,” “Stews & Grains,” “Dumplings & Pasta,” and “Sweet Comfort,” the chapters highlight the myriad ways in which foods eaten with a spoon have the power to soothe, surprise, and connect people across cultures and conflicts. (Quadrille, Oct. 20)

Fuchsia Dunlop, who graduated from culinary school in Sichuan Province, is one of the West’s foremost experts in Chinese cuisine, guiding home cooks with a knowledgeable and compassionate hand. The author of several renowned cookbooks on the topic, she’s back with a strikingly illustrated new volume, focused on the five taste sensations (sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and pungent) that a Chinese cook strives to balance harmoniously within a dish. Instead of a dogmatic approach to traditional dishes, she encourages cooks to apply Chinese seasonings and flavoring techniques to “whatever ingredients you have on hand,” assuring readers that “the ways of the Chinese kitchen travel well.” (W.W. Norton, Oct. 20)

#6594. One-Dish Red Curry Noodles

Recipe by Susan Bronson, Rhinelander, Wisconsin

This one-dish red curry noodles recipe is packed with pantry and freezer staples, making it perfect as a dump-and-bake weeknight dinner.

I’m not quite sure where the time goes between school bus drop-off and dinnertime, but I’m pretty sure there’s a fast-forward button involved. Suffice it to say, quick and easy weeknight dinner recipes are life-savers. Easy casserole recipes made with pantry staples are some of my favorites, and dump-and-go recipes—which just require one dish—are even better. This one-dish red curry noodles recipe checks all those boxes: It’s a casserole; it takes just 45 minutes from start to finish; and it’s made with chewy udon noodles, colorful fresh and frozen vegetables, and a rich and spicy red coconut curry sauce.

Easy prep, minimal mess, quick to bake and something my whole family will eat? That’s a real win in my book.

Preheat the oven to 375°F. In a 13×9-inch casserole dish, stir together the vegetable stock, coconut milk, red curry paste, soy sauce, ginger, sesame oil and minced garlic.

Add the udon noodles and use a fork to carefully separate them into a single layer.

Top the noodles with the sliced red pepper, frozen stir-fry vegetables and finely shredded cabbage.

Submerge the noodles and vegetables in the liquid as much as possible.

Cover the dish tightly with foil and bake it for 20 minutes. Uncover the casserole dish and stir the noodles and vegetables. Return it to the oven, uncovered, and cook until the noodles are tender, about 15 to 20 minutes. Top the red curry noodles with green onions and sesame seeds, and serve them with lime wedges.

Editor’s Tip: When you pull the dish out of the oven the first time, take special care to separate any clumped noodles.

Any leftover red curry noodles should be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator.

When stored properly in the fridge, leftover one-dish red curry noodles last up to four days.

For the best flavor and texture, plan to serve this dish directly after baking it. However, you can prep the casserole up to 24 hours in advance, waiting to submerge the noodles in the sauce until just before it goes in the oven.

Unfortunately, this one-dish red curry noodles is not ideal for freezing. There’s a chance that the coconut milk will separate when thawed, leading to a grainy texture. Additionally, the softer texture of the cooked noodles will likely lead to a mushy texture once thawed.

This recipe calls for udon noodles, which are a thick type of Japanese noodle made with wheat flour. These thicker noodles hold up well in the hot oven, and retain their plump and chewy texture. You could also use egg noodles or lo mein noodles—even spaghetti will work in a pinch! Rice noodles are also an option, although the cook time will likely need to be shorter.

Pump up the protein in this noodle dish by adding cubed or shredded chicken, shrimp or ground pork. For plant-based protein, you can add cubed tofu, edamame, chickpeas or cannellini beans.

Whichever veggies you like best! A few of my family’s favorites include sliced bell peppers, broccoli, green beans and sugar snap peas. Frozen veggie stir-fry mixes, which commonly include broccoli, baby corn, water chestnuts and sugar snap peas, are a great short-cut too.

NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has officially ended its mission after more than 20 years, as it approaches a fiery reentry through Earth's atmosphere.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A pioneering NASA space telescope is no more. In sad news for Swifties everywhere, the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has officially ended its mission after more than 20 years of tracking the most powerful explosions in the universe since the Big Bang.

According to a NASA announcement, the Swift team shut down the telescope's science operations Tuesday (Oct. 20) after the observatory fell too low in its orbit to continue taking reliable measurements of the cosmos. In the coming weeks, Swift will drop even further, eventually passing a point of no return and taking a fiery plunge through Earth's atmosphere.

The observatory is the latest victim of intense solar activity, which increases the drag on satellites in Earth orbit and makes it harder for spacecraft to stay aloft. Swift has been losing altitude for a while, but the final straw came in August, when a costly mission to boost Swift's orbit with a private spacecraft failed, ending with the would-be rescue craft burning up in the atmosphere after a series of hardware malfunctions.

Swift is now beyond saving and, orbiting at just 171 miles (275 kilometers) above Earth, can no longer take reliable observations of space. NASA expects the spacecraft to break up upon reentry "in the next few weeks."

NASA knew Swift was in trouble when it went in; soon, it'll be lying on the cold hard ground. However, the Swift mission surpassed its goals by decades. According to NASA, the satellite launched in November 2004 on a primary mission intended to last just two years. In the end, Swift survived for 22 years, surpassing its intended lifespan by more than 10 times.

In that time, Swift made thousands of observations of exploding supernovas, intense gamma-ray bursts, and black-hole-related episodes of stellar destruction, contributing data to about 7,000 scientific papers, according to NASA.

An illustration of a stellar 'mega-flare' detected by Swift. The observatory excelled at catching powerful, fast-acting cosmic events.

Designed as a multiwavelength observatory, Swift watched the sky in optical, ultraviolet and X-ray light that made it well suited to track the aftermath of powerful energy bursts. Its greatest asset, perhaps, was its rapid response time; if an explosion flashed somewhere in the sky, engineers could swivel Swift to study it within minutes, NASA said.

"Swift was designed as a satellite dedicated to studying gamma-ray bursts, outbursts that came and went so quickly that no one could target them with large telescopes to learn more," S. Bradley Cenko, the mission's principal investigator at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, said in the statement.

Swift's fast-acting observations "played a major role in advancing our understanding of the changing universe and was part of a revolution in astrophysics," added Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of the Astrophysics Division at NASA headquarters.

Brandon is the space / physics editor at Live Science. With more than 20 years of editorial experience, his writing has appeared in The Washington Post, Reader's Digest, CBS.com, the Richard Dawkins Foundation website and other outlets. He holds a bachelor's degree in creative writing from the University of Arizona, with minors in journalism and media arts. His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.

#6591. These Immersive Coffee Tours Follow the Beans From Tree to Cup

Travelers who can’t go a day without press-and-go espresso pods or a ­meditative pour-over ritual, rejoice! Coffee tourism is on the rise, and, thanks to expert tour operators with access to the best farms and baristas, your next visit to Latin America, East Africa, or Southeast Asia can be as caffeinated as you want. That could entail lingering with like-minded locals in cafés or stomping on the very soil in which these prized beans grow. If you’re eager to geek out on the whats and hows of it all, immersive education is always on the table—and in the cup.

In the Antioquia region, a custom itinerary with True Colombia Travel balances exclusive access to three of the country’s best producers with myriad adventures (like coffee in a village where locals still get around on horseback). Enthusiasts will marvel at coffee trees on volcanic slopes and learn about fermentation techniques. A visit to Café Cocondo Orgánico, where coffee is cross-­pollinated with mango, avocado, orange, and soursop trees, is especially thrilling.

Known for high-quality ­arabica and robusta beans, this East African nation is paradise for those who crave a brightly flavored brew. Arusha Coffee Lodge by Elewana is conveniently located between Mount Kilimanjaro and the Ngorongoro Conservation Area. It’s also surrounded by 100 acres of coffee trees. Hotel guests can tour the roasting facilities and sample as much of the final product as they’d like. Don’t miss the day’s rotating selection of java-flavored treats, which might include nutty cakes, tiramisu, or scones.

Every year, Augusto Carneiro—founder of Nossa Familia Coffee in Portland, Oregon—leads tours of Guatemala City’s third-wave scene. Travelers start by sharing breakfast with the owners of the trendy café Coffee District, then help with the harvest at a farm partway up Volcán de Agua. Later, they head to Finca San Jerónimo Miramar in the Atitlán region to learn about grafting arabica plants onto robusta roots. There are also many sorts of excursions, from a hike on Acatenango mountain to swimming in Lake Atitlán.

#6590. Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie

The one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so plan ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling)

Whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6589. Countdown to Christmas with Snoopy! The Best Peanuts Advent Calendars

The Lenox Peanuts Advent calendar is both a beautiful luxury gift for loved ones and a nostalgic yearly tradition for families.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Here at Taste of Home, we know all too well that Advent calendars are no longer just for tots. In fact, some of the top-selling picks among our readership over the last few years include wine calendars and other boozy options. Not to mention the bestselling Bonne Maman Advent calendar, which has been voted one of our favorites for three years running! But when it comes to collectible calendars that double as unforgettable gifts, nothing impresses us quite as much as the Lenox Peanuts Advent calendar.

That’s right! The brand behind the iconic Spice Village now has Advent calendars. And yes, the Peanuts Advent calendar is just as gorgeous and nostalgia-filled as you’d imagine. Here’s my experience unboxing this assortment of adorable ornaments. Warning: spoilers ahead!

Boasting 25 ornaments crafted in Lenox's signature porcelain, the Lenox Peanuts Advent calendar is a luxury Advent calendar unlike any other.

The Lenox Peanuts Advent calendar isn’t just your average Christmas countdown. It’s a luxury Advent calendar that unfolds to reveal 25 doors, each housing its own adorable ornament. Because these are made from Lenox’s signature  premium porcelain, they’re meant to be enjoyed season after season. That makes this Advent calendar an extra special gift for Peanuts fans. It also makes a fun yearly tradition for families! Don’t forget to put on A Charlie Brown Christmas as you hang them on your Christmas tree!

This collector’s calendar comes with 25 different tree hangers, each boasting either an iconic wintery scene from the comic strips or one of our favorite classic characters. In total, there are 13 characters and 12 scenic snowflakes, all of which sit at around two inches tall. And these bite-sized heirlooms aren’t found anywhere else—you can only get them inside the Advent calendar, making them a thoughtful gift for collectors.

My experience unboxing the Lenox Peanuts Advent calendar was truly magical. Even before I opened the first door, I was struck by the packaging. While simple, the shiny red box looks classy and expensive. It also feels nice and hefty—a nod to the precious porcelain ornaments nested inside. Once you loosen the gold clasp, the calendar folds open like a book to reveal 25 doors, and each opens to reveal a figurine or snowflake nestled in a protective foam cushion. I love that the box is protective enough to reuse for storage once the season ends, too!

From Lionel to Peppermint Patty to Charlie himself, each of the character ornaments offers extraordinary detail. Despite the small size, they’re slightly heavy, so you can tell they’re also high-quality. Among the figurines are also several iterations of fan favorite puppy dog Snoopy partaking in holiday traditions and lounging on his light-wrapped doghouse.

Even the snowflake ornaments offer their own holiday charm. Each one is carefully painted with a miniature scene from the wintery comic strips. Among the art are ageless, captivating sequences of the gang gathered around a lighted tree, Lucy performing on ice skates and mischievous Snoopy tangled up in a string of vibrant Christmas lights among many others. Adorning each hanging loop is a festive tassel, giving the ornaments a little added flair.

Whether you plan on giving this one as a gift or want to keep it as a holiday heirloom, it’s truly a special collection that the whole family can enjoy. It’s also the perfect way to signal the most wonderful time of the year is here!

While we absolutely love the Lenox Peanuts advent calendar as a yearly tradition, it’s not exactly child-friendly (without parental assistance, that is). For folks seeking an alternative Advent calendar for kids that still offers the same Peanuts charm, we love this Peanuts puzzle Advent calendar. Deputy Editor Katie Bandurski tested it last year and praises its adorable prints, which cover all of the classic characters.

Want something a little sweeter? Sure, you can always opt for a classic chocolate Advent calendar. But for fans of Snoopy, this adorably delicious Advent calendar from Sugarfina makes a showstopping gift. It’s brimming with 24 of the brand’s popular sweet treats, including gummies in fun holiday shapes, peach hearts, sparkling stars, sparkle pops, chocolate biscuits, confetti caramels and so much more.

“This calendar gets major points for its design even before you get into the good stuff,” raves Katie, who enjoyed last year’s edition. “It’s shaped like the iconic red doghouse. It gets even better when you open the doors to the calendar and find a pop-up paper Snoopy.”

This gorgeous Advent calendar will quickly become a yearly family tradition.

Absolutely smitten with the limited-edition Lenox Peanuts Advent calendar? We don’t blame you. Folks wanting to get their hands on one ahead of the holidays can find them on the Lenox website, Wayfair and Macy’s. The calendar retails for around $300, but offers an incredible $500 value, making it a great choice for gifting or adding to your yearly holiday traditions.

One note: We recommend investing in one as soon as you can, because they’re bound to sell out well ahead of Christmas time.

#6587. What Goes Into Making Real-Deal Prosciutto di Parma PDO

There are precious few food products that have been enjoyed for as much of human history as Prosciutto di Parma. The signature silky texture and buttery, sweet-savory flavor of the “King of Hams” is recognized around the world as the result of carefully controlled production methods, dedication to quality, and traditions continued for centuries.

The history of Prosciutto di Parma reaches back more than 2,000 years, to Roman times, when the art of preserving pork through salting and natural drying was already well established in the Po Valley. As early as the 3rd century BC, Cato the Elder described methods for curing pork legs with salt and allowing them to dry and mature. Today, Prosciutto di Parma is produced exclusively in a strictly defined area of northern Italy, in the province of Parma in the Emilia-Romagna region, where local know-how combines with distinctive climatic conditions. Humid breezes from the Tyrrhenian Sea become drier as they flow over the Apennines and down onto the hills. Prosciutto producers discovered that this created an ideal environment for dry aging, and they built storerooms with tall windows that could be opened and closed as necessary, allowing the air to circulate through the racks of hams for gradual drying.

The specifics of aging, like every step in the process, are governed by a consortium—the Consorzio del Prosciutto di Parma—that was founded in 1963 to protect the authenticity of the product. In 1996, Prosciutto di Parma obtained the European Union’s Protected Designation of Origin (PDO). These have a red and yellow seal to show that a product is made in a certain geographical area using time-honored, traditional methods. Grana Padano, a nutty, aged hard cheese also from Northern Italy that’s often paired with Prosciutto di Parma on a charcuterie plate, was awarded a PDO the same year.

Grana Padano PDO and Prosciutto di Parma PDO also share the distinction of being fire-branded—a sign for consumers that you are buying the real thing. Only Parma hams that meet the PDO’s specifications can receive the five-pronged Ducal Crown that signifies a true Prosciutto di Parma.

Well before that brand is applied, production starts with the pigs. Which breeds, where they can be bred and raised (in 11 Italian regions), and what they are fed (a list that also includes whey from local cheesemakers) are all precisely detailed. Within the 28th day from birth, the piglets receive a breeder tattoo that will also appear on the final product along with the crown brand. The fresh pork (hind legs only) sent to prosciutto producers must weigh between 26 pounds and 40 pounds, with a set amount of fat coverage. After they arrive at the production facility, the legs are trimmed to form the characteristic rounded shape, chilled to a precise temperature, and salted by hand with sea salt, which joins the pork as the only two ingredients that go into the making of Prosciutto di Parma PDO.

Following a resting period of at least 90 days, the hams are washed then hung in windowed storerooms to dry slowly. The next step is called sugnatura: The parts of the ham not covered by rind are rubbed with sugna—a mixture of pork fat, salt, and pepper—to keep the meat from drying too quickly. For final aging, the hams hang in cool, dimly lit cellars. From start to finish, the process cannot last less than 14 months (many producers continue aging for 24, 30, or even 36 months and beyond). The last step before inspection may be the most fascinating: The hams are tested using a needle made from horse bone, selected because the bone is able to absorb the aroma and quickly shed it. By inserting the needle into different parts of the cured meat and smelling it, experts can determine if a whole ham leg has the qualifications to be named Prosciutto di Parma PDO.

The Consorzio, which started with 23 producers, now numbers 125, and in 2025 they turned out 6.75 million Prosciutto di Parma PDO hams. Beyond its economic significance to the region, the “King of Hams” is a cultural icon and a tourism magnet. The annual Parma Ham Festival is held in September, and there’s even an entire museum dedicated to the region’s signature product—with a tasting room, of course.

However you experience the exceptional flavor and texture of Prosciutto di Parma—on a visit to the museum or from your local specialty store—look for the crown and PDO seal, and take a moment to remember that you are tasting a distinctly delicious slice of history.

Head to DistinctlyDeliciouslyEuropean.eu to learn more about Prosciutto di Parma PDO and Grana Padano PDO.

#6586. Carne Guisada

Recipe by Margaret Knoebel, Milwaukee, Wisconsin

With its warm spices and a rich gravy, this slow-braised carne guisada is perfect in tacos or on a bed of rice.

Carne guisada, a classic Mexican beef stew whose name translates to “stewed meat,” has a rich culinary backstory. Its roots stretch across northern Mexico and into Texas, where slow-braised beef dishes are a staple of home kitchens, taquerias and Tex-Mex restaurants alike. Tender beef simmers in a chili-based sauce, then is often served as a taco filling with soft flour tortillas. Some versions (especially in Texas) include potatoes to make it a one-pot meal. Others focus solely on the fall-apart meat and the smooth, peppery sauce built from dried chiles. You win either way.

For our carne guisada recipe, we keep the signature slow-cooked, deeply seasoned beef and rich gravy, but say yes to the potatoes for extra body and comfort. The use of beer, Worcestershire sauce and tomato paste brings layered depth that complements the traditional spices like cumin and chili powder. We aren’t claiming this is the only version because, honestly, that doesn’t exist. But this dish absolutely captures the spirit of classic carne guisada: tender meat, bold flavor and something meant to be shared.

In a large bowl, toss the beef with 1/4 teaspoon of salt. In a separate large bowl, combine the flour and paprika. Add the beef to the flour a few pieces at a time, tossing to coat them.

In a Dutch oven, heat the oil over medium heat. Brown the beef in batches, adding additional oil as necessary. Remove the pieces with a slotted spoon.

Editor’s Tip: Those browned bits stuck to the bottom of the pot are called fond, and they’re flavor gold. Don’t even think about washing them away.

To the same pan, add the onion. Cook and stir until it’s tender, three to five minutes. Stir in the tomato, jalapeno and garlic, and cook until they’re fragrant and the color starts to darken slightly.

Add the browned beef back to the pan. Add the beer, and bring it to a boil, scraping the bottom to release the browned bits. Simmer until the liquid is reduced by half, about five minutes.

Stir in the broth, Worcestershire sauce, crushed red pepper flakes, chili powder, cumin, bay leaf and the remaining 1/2 teaspoon of salt, and bring the mixture to a boil. Reduce the heat, then cover the pot and simmer the stew until the meat is almost tender, about 1 hour and 30 minutes.

Add the potatoes and red wine vinegar. Cover the pot and simmer the stew until the meat and vegetables are tender, about 30 minutes longer.

Discard the bay leaf. Using the back of a spoon or ladle, slightly mash the potatoes. If desired, shred the beef slightly with two forks. Serve with tortillas, rice, lime and cilantro.

Let the carne guisada cool completely before transferring it to an airtight container. Store it in the refrigerator, where the flavors will actually deepen and improve overnight. It’s one of those dishes that might taste even better the next day. Carne guisada lasts up to four days in the refrigerator.

Carne guisada freezes very well. Store it in freezer-safe containers for up to three months, and thaw it overnight in the refrigerator before reheating.

Reheat carne guisada gently on the stovetop over medium-low heat until it’s warmed through. Add a splash of broth if the sauce has thickened too much.

You can use beef shoulder, bottom round or beef stew meat for carne guisada. The key is choosing a tougher cut with connective tissue that breaks down during the long, slow cooking time. This gives you that tender, fall-apart texture.

Whether you serve carne guisada on tortillas or rice, it also pairs beautifully with black beans, fresh salsa or even a side of warm cornbread.

It’s prebaked to mitigate sogginess but doesn’t require pie weights. Mascarpone keeps the whipped cream firm and fluffy for a full 24 hours.

Don’t be tempted to skip the cold-brew concentrate. You don’t want regular cold brew, and definitely not brewed and cooled coffee from your coffee machine at home, no matter how fancy. The concentrate (highly recommend Grady’s Cold Brew Coffee Concentrate) is consistent every single time with exactly the right strength to stand up to the dairy and eggs in the filling.

Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

Place a rack in middle of oven and preheat to 350°. Butter pie dish with unsalted butter. Pulse 2 cups (180 g) old-fashioned oats, ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour, ¼ cup (packed; 50 g) dark brown sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a food processor until oats are coarsely ground. Drizzle in 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled; pulse just until mixture comes together. Transfer to prepared dish (such as East Fork Ceramic Pie Plate); wipe out and reserve food processor. Press crust firmly and evenly across bottom and up sides of dish with a flat-bottomed measuring cup. Bake until golden and surface looks dry, 25–30 minutes. Transfer crust to a wire rack; reduce oven temperature to 325°.

Pulse 1 cup (packed; 200 g) dark brown sugar, 2 Tbsp. all-purpose flour, 2 Tbsp. instant espresso powder, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in food processor until no lumps remain, about 1 minute. Add 3 large eggs, ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, and 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and pulse until smooth. Add 1 cup cold-brew coffee concentrate and 2 cups heavy cream and pulse until well combined.

Pour custard into crust (it’s okay if crust is still warm). Bake pie until edges of filling are set and slightly puffed but center still wobbles a little when gently shaken, 40–50 minutes (filling will continue to set after baking). Transfer to a wire rack; let cool at least 3 hours, or, preferably, chill 12 hours.

Using an electric mixer, beat ½ cup mascarpone, 4 Tbsp. granulated sugar, remaining 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ⅔ cup heavy cream, and 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract in a medium bowl until soft peaks form. Spoon whipped cream mixture over pie; swirl lightly to create divots and peaks.

Just before serving, dust with instant espresso powder if desired; sprinkle generously with flaky sea salt.

Do ahead: Pie (without espresso powder and sea salt garnishes) can be made 1 day ahead. Cover loosely and keep chilled.

#6584. I Tried the New Bentgo Lift Water Bottle—And the Ring Handle Makes It So Easy to Stay Hydrated

The new Bentgo water bottle is easy to use, carry and clean, plus it comes in gorgeous, candy-colored hues.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

For someone who works and works out at home, I’ve amassed quite the collection of reusable water bottles. Maintaining the healthy habit of drinking more water is always my excuse for adding yet another to the mix. After all, the cuter the water bottle, the more likely I am to reach for it and take a swig.

So when I saw the new Bentgo Lift Chug Lid water bottle, I knew I had to try it. As much as I love my Stanley Flowstate, I like to ditch the straw every so often, even if it does save me from dousing myself every time I go in for a sip. But with the Bentgo’s unique lid and leakproof design, I had high expectations that this strawless bottle would become a regular in my hydration rotation. And it has! Here’s why I’m toting around the new Bentgo Lift water bottle like it’s my favorite purse.

The major draw of the Bentgo Lift Chug Lid water bottle is the soft-grip ring handle that’s attached to the lid. It does double the work by keeping the flip top securely closed and offering a comfortable way to tote it around. My major gripe with other water bottles has always been that their handles and/or straws make them unwieldy for carrying and commuting. But not the Bentgo. Just lift the handle and carry it like a bag. I’ve even hung it from the handle of my Peloton Bike during a ride!

It did take me a moment to get used to drinking from the bottle, only because it’s different from others I’ve had. But all you have to do is lift the ring handle and push the little lever with your thumb to pop open the cap (you could also wedge your thumb in under the handle to hit the button so it lifts the cap and the handle at the same time, but I found it easier to open the handle first). I like that the handle folds flat against the bottle so everything stays compact. The mouth is wide enough to comfortably drink from, although I do turn the bottle so that my nose doesn’t bump the edge of the ring handle.

At first I thought the smooth cylindrical shape of the bottle might be a problem because, other than the handle, there is nothing to grip the bottle when you’re actually drinking. But the powder-coated exterior offers plenty of grip so it won’t slip in your hand.

The lid twists off easily from the wide-mouth bottle, which makes it easy to fill with liquid and ice. It also makes it very easy to clean. The Bentgo is top-rack dishwasher friendly, although the manufacturer does recommend handwashing to protect the exterior. I’ve definitely popped the lid in the dishwasher several times already but I’ve been handwashing the bottle itself, at least for now.

The Bentgo Lift Chug Lid Bottle is available in 24-, 32- and 40-ounce sizes in a host of colors. I chose both the 24-ounce in Bubblegum and the 32-ounce in Denim, but soon found myself gravitating toward the more petite 24-ounce bottle. It wasn’t only because of the candy hue—I just prefer a smaller bottle!

With all this talk about design and color, you’re probably wondering: Does it even keep your water cold? Yes, it sure does. The Bentgo Lift water bottle features a stainless steel interior with triple-layer insulation (BPA-free with no PFAs) that keeps liquids cold for up to 24 hours. And yes, I can confirm this to be true: I left ice water in a bottle on my desk after the work day and came back the next morning to surprisingly cold water!

You can purchase the Bentgo Lift Chug Lid Water Bottle right on the brand’s website, as well as on Walmart and Amazon. It comes in 24-, 32- and 40-ounce sizes, which cost $29.99, $34.99 and $39.99, respectively. The two smaller sizes come in six colors: Bubblegum, Denim, Latte, Blanc, Back to Black and Amalfi Coast. The 40-ounce is currently available only in Blanc and Back to Black. These will make great gifts for the holidays, so shop soon for the best size and color availability!

Live Science spoke with comparative psychologist Christian Frings to discuss a new theory for why orcas are attacking yachts.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Over the past six years, orcas have made headlines for a unique behavior: Some individuals have repeatedly damaged or destroyed rudders on boats. The behavior has prompted a wide range of explanations, including that it's playful, a form of revenge, a warning against getting too close to the pod, or even a type of cultural transmission, in which one orca observes another interacting with a boat and then imitates it.

But Christian Frings, a cognitive psychologist who studies how humans control their actions, thinks it could be deliberate.

While Frings, who is also chair of general psychology and methodology at Trier University in Germany, does not study orcas directly, he believes that theories developed to explain human behavior could provide insight into this orca behavior. Orcas (Orcinus orca), he said, may be a "test case" for whether a wide variety of species can anticipate how their actions will change the environment and then take those actions deliberately, with the goal of making those changes.

He published his theory as a commentary Sept. 8 in the journal Animal Cognition.

This doesn't necessarily mean orcas have wicked motives or are ramming boats with the goal of sinking them and scaring or harming people. It may be that orcas just like the sensation of smashing into a rudder or being in the water with a wonky, disabled boat. Once they learn this, they anticipate the effect — for example, how a boat moves or feels when the rudder is damaged — and then carry out the learned action sequence that creates that effect.

Frings' theory doesn't attempt to explain why orcas (also called killer whales) would seek to damage a boat or rudder. "Why they want this effect is a secondary question and while of course interesting it touches a quite different topic," Frings told Live Science via email.

Christian Frings is a cognitive psychology professor at the University of Trier in Germany and the director of the Institute for Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience. His research explores how the human mind turns perception into action and why our recent experiences can shape what we do next, often without us noticing.

Live Science spoke with Frings about his hypothesis and why theories that describe how humans execute a series of motor behaviors — called action control frameworks — might help us understand how other complex animals behave in the wild.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry: Why is it important to study orca behavior, and what can studying orcas tell us about animal cognition?

Christian Frings: In truth, I'm the wrong person to get that question because I should mention right from the start that I'm a cognitive psychologist. So usually, I'm studying human behavior. So, it's not really that I'm interested in orcas, per se, more in the question of what is actually comparable between human action control, human cognition and animal cognition.

KHC: Can you explain the action-control framework for our readers?

CF: It's a group of theories. The most important point is that agents — humans and maybe orcas — control their actions by actually anticipating the behavioral and the sensory consequences of their actions.

So let's take the example of turning the light on. The action starts with anticipating how it will look when the light is turned on. It does not start with pressing the light switch. It starts with the visual effect you're going to produce. This visual effect then actually retrieves from memory a motor program, and this motor program actually produces the anticipated effect. So it's all about anticipating action effects.

In the human action-control literature, that is the most dominant view from different theories of how humans actually control their behavior: by anticipating the effects they're going to produce.

KHC: How does that apply to the orca behavior?

CF: The typical explanation for [the boat-attacking behavior] is more stimulus response or cultural transmission. Stimulus response would mean, in this case, the rudder elicits an approach or attack behavior. So any rudder should just elicit this behavior. [Editor's note: Stimulus-response theory is a psychological concept in which a stimulus triggers a particular response from an individual. Examples include a cat being sprayed with water when on the couch and jumping off the couch in response, or a dog salivating when it smells food.]

Cultural transmission would actually be observational learning. That means one orca sees how another orca is attacking a rudder and then just imitates the behavior.

I'm not saying that these explanations [stimulus response or cultural transmission] are wrong, by the way. I just want to add an additional layer of explanation.

I suggest that they actually anticipate the sensory consequences of their action. So maybe they anticipate how it would look and how it would feel if they destroy the rudder. I would not call it [their behavior] play, but maybe they're just testing or probing what kind of effect they're going to produce.

It's a little bit like human babies, when they start to move — or move their arms or move their legs — they're also typically trying to produce effects, right? It's also when they develop language, this kind of babbling, right? That is a kind of testing or probing action effects.

Maybe this is something the orcas also do. I don't know. But at least it's [another theory].

Whale-watching tours help the public see orca behavior from a close-but-safe distance.

KHC: So would the orca be anticipating something like the boat becoming impossible to steer?

CF: Actually, no. Let's assume for a moment it [that a broken rudder is] what they want to produce — because they somehow anticipate how it would look and how it would feel if this yacht cannot be steered anymore.

If they can anticipate, then this anticipation of this effect will retrieve from their memory what they have to do to actually produce this effect. And it's not about [higher-order] thinking. That is a very important thing.

So we do not need human-like intentions to impose that on the orcas. I'm not saying that, because I really think it's, in a way, comparable with turning a light on. When you turn your light on, you also do not have big thoughts about that. You just want to turn your light on. So you want to produce an effect, and you do not think about all the different, quite complex muscle movements you have to do if you actually press the light switch.

I would say, again, it does not really need higher-order cognition or something like that. We do not have to impose motives or complex thoughts on the orcas for that.

My point is just to look at this behavior from this somewhat different angle, adding this layer about action effects.

KHC: What are the bigger implications if your theory is correct?

CF: My point is just to look at this behavior from this somewhat different angle, adding this layer about action effects. Because if you, for a moment, take my ideas for granted and say, "OK, maybe he has a point," then this opens up the possibility to manipulate the orca behavior.

Because if the orcas anticipate effects and this action effect produces a certain behavior, if you change the effect — let's say the rudder [material] or the shell of the boat so that the orca thinks he's producing a certain action effect — then he shows his behavior, but this behavior does not produce the action effect anymore. So the orca will probably change the behavior. It might be dangerous because it might elicit somewhat different — maybe even more dangerous — behavior of the orcas, but it might also stop it.

But it gives you a natural angle to manipulate the orca behavior. [Editor's note: In a follow-up email, Frings noted that this could involve testing a different version of the boat rudder. If the original rudder, when damaged, leaves the boat floating in a "helpless" way, a second one could be tested that allows the boat to be maneuverable even when attacked. If Frings' hypothesis is right, then by breaking the link between the orcas' planned actions (ramming the boat) and the outcome they want (helpless boat), you could change the orcas' behavior.]

But again, if you try to change it this way, it might be a little bit dangerous. So I would not suggest doing that with a boat with real people on it, because if you change the environmental consequences, they [the orcas] might actually go a little bit crazy. Maybe they might try to produce this effect with a different kind of behavior, and that could be even more aggressive. But I don't know. I can't predict that.

KHC: So the orcas are a case study to test this framework, right?

CF: Exactly. And for the general approach, it's important to try to find action frameworks that can travel across species that are not specific for one particular species. Because at the moment, we might have action-control models for humans or action-control models for the great apes.

But maybe we can just have a family of action-control frameworks, because maybe orcas and humans, and at least the great apes, control their behavior concerning action effects in quite the same way, to be honest.

Another important point here that makes it, for me personally, very interesting: This is behavior in the wild. So a lot of the research on action control is typically in the lab under very controlled conditions, so in a way, this is moving from humans to orcas but also from lab into wild behavior.

I think one misconception is actually that the models from the lab are not applicable to behavior in the wild. That's not only true for orcas; it's also true for humans. And I don't like that.

And again, this paper is a nice showcase that lab models can actually be used to explain behavior in the real world.

This interview has been condensed and edited lightly for clarity.

#6581. ‘The Gilded Age’ Is Back! Here’s What to Eat While You Watch the Show

The good china is coming out, but the sweatpants are staying on. The Gilded Age season four is back on Nov. 1, and this is everything I'm eating for the series return.

I can be persuaded to watch almost anything that promises extravagant set designs and beautiful costumes. If there’s history and a little mischievous social maneuvering involved, even better. My coworkers recently recommended The Gilded Age, and within two weeks, I’d watched all three seasons just in time for season four to drop.

There’s plenty to admire: Bertha Russell’s determination, Peggy Scott’s writing career and rooms furnished with a reassuring disregard for minimalism. I love the history, too, from the railroad fortunes and New York bankers to Lewis Latimer’s work in electric lighting and the woman who helped bring the Brooklyn Bridge to completion. Every episode gave me another reason to keep watching.

My husband is often still at the restaurant in the evenings, so once the kids are asleep, I have a few hours to settle in with a show. While I watched The Gilded Age, I usually poured a glass of wine (some of my favorites are under $25 at Walmart) and enjoyed the fire as Christine Baranski made an art of Agnes’s disapproval. But with the new season arriving on Nov. 1, I’m borrowing a few ideas from the show to make a watch party spread.

I have a decidedly romantic streak when it comes to my surroundings, so the show’s interiors have my full attention. I’m particularly taken with the glassware and china that can make even a small supper feel indulgent. With a few soft lamps and the fire going, I’m looking forward to borrowing a little of that grandeur for my own evening.

Dan Roberts for Taste of Home, Courtesy Barbra Nitke/ Courtesy Hbo

I’m more than happy to borrow the show’s habit of pouring wine into crystal glasses. Mine usually contains Champagne, but Ada’s season-three temperance campaign gives us a reason to put some thought into an alcohol-free option too.

Agnes’s feelings about wine appear to be settled, but there’s room for both sisters.

Jonathan Melendez for taste of Home, Courtesy Barbra Nitke/ Courtesy Hbo

The Russells may require a meticulously planned succession of courses, but I’d be content with a small selection of savory bites. Oysters, warm crab dip or little sandwiches would make a perfectly elegant dinner by the fire.

Mark Derse for Taste of Home, Courtesy Alison Cohen Rosa/ Courtesy Hbo

For something more substantial, you can look to the show’s luncheons as much as its elaborate dinner parties. A bowl of soup or a sandwich can feel quite grand when the ingredients are good and someone else is responsible for the evening’s drama.

Dan Roberts for taste of Home, Courtesy Karolina Wojtasik/ Courtesy Hbo

A pot of tea and something sweet would be enough for me on an evening when dinner is already behind us. I like having dessert ready before I sit down, whether that means a trifle waiting in the fridge or a few pastries brought home in a paper bag.

#6579. French Onion Stuffing

Recipe by Susan Bronson, Rhinelander, Wisconsin

This recipe for French onion stuffing takes caramelized onions, beef broth and Gruyere, and transforms them into a holiday-ready side dish.

Every year at Thanksgiving, I consider filling my plate with all the sides and foregoing the turkey altogether. (That’s what I did during my decade as a vegetarian—and I did not miss the meat.) Give me all the cranberry sauce, green bean casserole and mashed potatoes. But my absolute favorite Thanksgiving side dish is the stuffing. Since my vegetarian days, I’ve preferred the stuffing cooked outside the bird. Not only does this prevent common food-safety issues, it also ensures the stuffing cooks evenly and crisps up on top. Although I’m partial to my mom’s (a classic stuffing with celery, onions and day-old bread), I also like to experiment with new recipes and flavor combinations.

This recipe for French onion stuffing is a real crowd-pleaser. It takes the ingredients of classic French onion soup—caramelized onions, beef broth and Gruyere cheese—and transforms them into a savory stuffing recipe. The most important ingredient you need for this recipe is patience. Caramelization is a process that cannot be rushed, but the results are oh-so worth it. The sweet-savory onions truly take this stuffing recipe to the next level. Just like in a bowl of French onion soup, a generous amount of grated Gruyere cheese melted over top ensures each bite is mix of sweet and savory flavors.

Preheat the oven to 350°F. Spread the bread cubes in an even layer on two baking sheets. Bake them for 10 minutes, then flip the cubes and rotate the baking sheets. Bake them until they’re very dry and golden brown, about five to eight minutes. Remove from the oven and set aside to cool.

Meanwhile, in a Dutch oven, heat the butter and olive oil over medium heat. Add the onions, and cook them until they’re softened, 10 to 15 minutes, stirring frequently. Stir in the salt and pepper. Reduce the heat to medium-low, and cook the onions until they’re deep golden brown, 40 to 50 minutes, stirring occasionally. Add the garlic, and cook until it’s fragrant, 30 to 60 seconds. Add the dry sherry, and use a wooden spoon to scrape up any browned bits. Stir in the thyme. Remove the pan from the heat.

In a large bowl, whisk the eggs until they’re smooth. Stir in the cooked onions and bread cubes. Stir in the beef broth until the bread is evenly moistened.

Editor’s Tip: The stuffing should be moist but not soggy. If the mixture seems too dry, add more broth in 1/4-cup increments until evenly moistened.

Spoon the stuffing into a greased 13×9-inch or 3-quart baking dish. Cover it with foil, and bake the stuffing for 30 minutes. Uncover the dish, and bake the stuffing until it’s crispy and browned, 15 to 20 minutes.

Remove the stuffing from the oven, and increase the oven temperature to 425°. Sprinkle the cheese on top. Bake the stuffing until the cheese is melted and bubbly, three to five minutes. Garnish the stuffing with thyme before serving it.

After allowing the French onion stuffing to cool completely, store any leftovers in an airtight container in the fridge for up to four days.

Absolutely! Caramelizing the onions requires low and slow cooking, and the process can’t be rushed. If you don’t have the time or the space to dedicate to making this dish all at once, you can make the caramelized onions up to four days in advance.

After caramelizing the onions, allow them to come to room temperature, then store them in an airtight container the fridge until you’re ready to use them. You can also prep the entire stuffing in advance up to a day in advance. Follow the recipe until it’s ready to bake, then cover and refrigerate it. Allow it to sit at room temperature for about 30 minutes, then bake it as directed, adding an extra 5 to 10 minutes to the baking time.

Or, you could try something new and use the microwave to caramelize onions. Yes, we tested it and it works!

Stuffing actually freezes really well. Cut the stuffing into large squares and wrap in a layer of storage wrap followed by a layer of foil. Freeze the stuffing squares for up to one month.

While there is a way to safely bake stuffing inside a turkey, this stuffing recipe is not an ideal candidate. By cooking it in the bird, it won’t be able to crisp up like it does when cooked it separately in a casserole dish.

You can start out with fresh bread for this recipe, but you will need to dry out the bread cubes in the oven before using them. Doing so helps to ensure the bread will soak up all the flavors of the stuffing without getting too soggy.

This stuffing recipe is baked both covered and uncovered. Covering the dish tightly with foil traps in steam, locking in moisture and allowing the stuffing to cook through without over-crisping the top. Cooking it uncovered allows the top to crisp up to golden brown.
