The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has found what might be a new dwarf planet in our solar system, orbiting the sun on an inclined plane past Pluto.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has found what might be a tiny new world in the far reaches of our solar system, hidden beyond the orbit of Neptune — and it is among the largest and brightest objects ever discovered beyond Neptune.

If confirmed, the miniature world would increase the number of officially recognized solar system dwarf planets to six. Upper estimates of the object's size place it at more than half the diameter of Pluto, the largest known dwarf planet.

"My first reaction was one of excited disbelief," Matthew Holman, an astrophysicist at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory and member of the Rubin team who wrote the code that helped discover the prospective dwarf planet, said in a statement. "Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong."

The potential dwarf planet, designated 2026 ED138, orbits the sun at roughly 46 times the distance between Earth and the sun. The potential new planetoid has been hiding behind galactic camouflage; with its orbit tilted at a 25-degree angle from the solar system plane, it's at just the right angle to get lost in the light from the inner Milky Way, the researchers said.

Many telescopes struggle to see past the millions of stars making up our galaxy's bulge. The Vera C. Rubin Observatory, however, images the entire southern sky every few nights with the largest digital camera ever built, sending out millions of nightly alerts for every object that has changed brightness or position. This makes it exceptional at identifying anything that moves, from solar system objects to transient events like supernova explosions.

The observatory had only just begun its 10-year mission of scanning the sky in July, and ED138 stood out in the data.

Holman works on the software algorithms that process the extreme amounts of data the observatory collects. The code he developed with his colleague, Kevin Napier, compares billions of observations to determine which ones are detections of the same moving object. Running data from Rubin through the code revealed the unusually large object.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

By looking at past data from Rubin and archival images from the Dark Energy Camera mounted on the Victor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (both in Chile), the team was able to map out ED138's orbit over the past 10 years.

The Kuiper Belt is a region of the solar system beyond Neptune that is a wild frontier of small, mostly icy bodies made from frozen methane, ammonia, water and rock. It ranges from roughly 30 to 50 times the distance between Earth and the sun, and is home to most of the known dwarf planets, including Pluto. Thousands of Kuiper Belt objects have already been discovered. These space rocks can be frozen time capsules that hold clues about the early solar system's formation.

A model of the solar system showing the five dwarf planets officially recognized by the International Astronomical Union (IAU) and the orbit of the newly discovered dwarf planet candidate 2026 ED138.

Dwarf planets are the largest Kuiper Belt objects that we know of. Bigger than asteroids but not quite planets, dwarf planets are big enough to be rounded under the force of their own gravity but too small to clear their orbits like planets do. While the International Astronomical Union (IAU) has officially confirmed five dwarf planets — Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake — astronomers studying dwarf planets often recognize at least nine, with several more candidates whose properties are still unknown.

Depending on which astronomer you ask, there could be anywhere from a handful to hundreds of dwarf planets in this part of the solar system. Identifying which Kuiper Belt objects are dwarf planets is tricky because they are often very dim and move very slowly from Earth's perspective, since their orbits are so large and distant. The likeliest candidates have high albedo (surface reflectivity) and diameters greater than roughly 370 to 500 miles (600 to 800 km).

What makes ED138 special is its size, inferred from its brightness, albedo and distance from the sun. It's estimated to have a diameter between 370 to 930 miles (600 to 1,500 km). For comparison, Pluto — the largest dwarf planet recognized by the IAU — is 1,477 miles (2,377 km) in diameter. Ceres, the smallest IAU-recognized dwarf planet, is 595 miles (958 km) in diameter. Future observations of ED138 will give researchers a more accurate idea of its diameter and density to determine if it's round enough to join the dwarf planet club.

"If confirmed as a dwarf planet, ED138 would join a very small family of worlds," Holman said in the statement. "Rubin will image the whole southern sky again and again for ten years, so any others hiding in the places earlier surveys skipped are now within reach."

He has a degree in mechanical engineering from the University of Connecticut, and he gets really excited every time he sees a cat.

#6468. I Love Hosting—These Easy Home Upgrades Make My Small Space Party-Ready

From better hand soap to smarter shelves, these quick upgrades help your home feel party-ready.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

We’re fast approaching the most joyous and stressful time of the year—hosting season. Back-to-back-to-back holidays mean parties, festive dinners, and other assorted gatherings, most of which happen at home.

I’m an unabashed fan of hosting and will find any reason to invite friends over in the name of ceremony. My fiancée and I have a prime hosting space (for Brooklyn), complete with a backyard, a guest bathroom, and a gallery wall. Beyond prepping snacks and filling coolers with booze, I enjoy getting the apartment ready for company. I’m not just vacuuming the floors and cleaning the grill; I’m talking about small projects like hanging new prints, finding a better solution to the pile of jackets in the study, and expanding kitchen storage. It’s a chance to spruce up the place and field some compliments on our digs. Here's what we’ve done in anticipation of holiday hosting, broken down by room.

People come together around food, and our small kitchen can only handle so much, which is why it’s been the most challenging and most rewarding to arrange. There’s a decent amount of storage, but exposed shelves with deep capacity can look cluttered fast. We bought Yamazaki Shelf Risers to maximize space and keep dishes and spices organized. They’re built solid to hold large, heavy dishes and look good doing it.

I was most excited about this Mustard Made The Kit locker, which now holds mugs, tea, and coffee gear. Wall-mounted storage is the way to go in small spaces—the more floor space you have, the bigger the room feels. I had to use molly bolts since my walls have no studs, but overall the assembly and installation were straightforward. The all-metal locker has tempered glass doors for a cleaner look and freed up shelf space in the kitchen.

Feeding a crowd has been easier with this Breville Oven and Air Fryer. I was against air fryers for the longest time because they’re cumbersome and ugly, but I finally gave in and got one; I’m now their biggest advocate. The Breville boosts cooking power, cooks faster than a standard kitchen oven, and is easier to clean.

The bathroom isn't a glamorous place for guests, but they’ll need it at some point. Our guest bathroom is tiny—I can touch the walls with barely extended arms—and storage has been an issue since we moved in. The walls are tiled, so drilling shelves or hanging a cabinet wasn’t an option. Most over-the-toilet storage cabinets are ugly, but I was glad to find this Yaheetch one for under $100. It immediately solved my storage issue, and the engineered wood construction feels surprisingly sturdy (not particle board!).

One of the easiest bathroom upgrades? Better hand soap. Seriously, it’s the one thing almost everyone mentions after using the bathroom. The Homecourt Hand Soap costs more than the typical grocery-store option, but it also makes everything else in the bathroom a little nicer. Same goes for the Tushy Bidet. In contrast, no one leaves the bathroom talking about how much they love it, but its presence elevates the space (and it rocks).

The liminal space between outside and inside can also be the most inviting. I like when an entryway looks lived in—jackets hanging, boots neatly lined up, etc.—but not in disarray. The Sicotas shoe cabinet saved my fiancée from even more arguing over the bedroom closet space. We moved most of our shoes into the cabinet outside our door. Now we have floor space in the closet for luggage and extra bed sheets.

Winter meant breaking out heavy coats and jackets we didn’t want stuffed into our one closet. We hung two of these coat hooks, one in the apartment hallway and one just outside our door, and they hold all our outerwear.

Like hand soap in the bathroom, a welcome mat is an unexpected hit in the entryway. Don’t overthink it; just get one for guests to wipe their feet, and they’ll probably say something nice about it.

Danny Perez is a Reviews Editor for Popular Mechanics with a focus on men's style, gear, and home goods. Recently, he was coordinator of partnership content at another product journalism outlet. Prior to that, he was a buyer for an independent men's shop in Houston, Texas, where he learned all about what makes great products great. He enjoys thrifting for 90s Broadway tees and vintage pajama sets. His spare time is occupied by watching movies and running to impress strangers on Strava.

#6467. Scientists Uncover Why Breast Cancer Becomes Deadlier As We Age

Scientists have uncovered a biological mechanism that may help explain why breast cancer becomes more dangerous with age.

In older mice, breast cancer was far more likely to spread to the lungs, even when the original tumors grew at roughly the same rate as those in younger animals. Researchers at Georgetown’s Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center have identified an inflammation-related receptor that appears to play a central role in this age-related increase in metastasis.

The researchers found that genetically removing the receptor, known as RAGE, almost completely eliminated the increased spread of cancer in older mice. Published May 15, 2026, in Communications Biology, the findings suggest that changes occurring throughout the body during aging can influence how aggressively cancer behaves.

The study focused on RAGE (Receptor for Advanced Glycation End-products), a receptor on the surface of cells that amplifies inflammatory signals. Aging increased levels of molecules that activate RAGE, including the proteins S100 and HMGB1. These molecules were found in both primary tumors and metastatic sites, where the resulting inflammatory activity helped cancer cells invade surrounding tissues and spread.

“Our study addresses a major gap by showing that aging dramatically increases breast cancer metastasis and that this effect depends on RAGE, a receptor on the surface of cells that fuels inflammation,” says Barry Hudson, PhD, associate professor of oncology at Georgetown Lombardi and corresponding author for this article. “Most laboratory studies rely on young mice, which has limited our understanding of how aging itself alters the host environment, including immune function and chronic inflammatory states that, in turn, influence cancer behavior.”

“These findings show that aging doesn’t just increase cancer risk — it actively changes the body in ways that help tumors spread,” says Hudson. “RAGE appears to be a key mediator of these harmful age-related pathways.”

The research benefited from an unusual circumstance during the COVID-19 pandemic. Reduced laboratory activity meant some mouse colonies were allowed to age longer than originally planned. Because maintaining older laboratory mice is expensive and time-consuming, the situation gave researchers a rare opportunity to examine how aging affects cancer progression. They compared younger and older animals across three mouse models of triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive form of the disease.

The team also investigated whether the findings had parallels in humans. An analysis of breast cancer data from more than 1,000 patients showed that higher expression of AGER (the gene encoding RAGE), along with elevated activity in related inflammatory genes, was associated with poorer outcomes. Although these associations do not establish that RAGE causes metastasis in patients, they support the potential clinical relevance of the animal experiments.

RAGE is being studied as a therapeutic target in several diseases associated with aging. Earlier research from the Georgetown team showed that the RAGE inhibitor TTP488 (azeliragon) could suppress breast cancer metastasis in preclinical models. In the latest experiments, the drug also reduced the invasiveness of cancer cells exposed to blood serum from aged mice, which otherwise promoted more invasive behavior.

A clinical study at Georgetown Lombardi is now evaluating TTP488 in breast cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy, with particular attention to safety and cognitive outcomes. The drug has previously demonstrated a favorable safety profile in humans, although its ability to prevent breast cancer metastasis in patients remains unproven.

“This study highlights the importance of the host environment in cancer. While cancer is often viewed as driven primarily by mutations intrinsic to tumor cells, systemic factors such as aging and inflammation play a critical role in shaping how cancers behave,” says Hudson. “Most deaths due to cancer occur because tumors spread to other organs, so understanding these influences may help identify new strategies to limit metastasis.”

Reference: “Aging promotes a RAGE-dependent increase in breast cancer metastasis” by Philip Miller, Sunita Chopra, Melinda Magna, Jiaxiang Tao, Carlos Benitez, Thomas Heist, Nanette H. Bishopric, Jeanne S. Mandelblatt, Julia Panov, Joyce M. Slingerland and Barry I. Hudson, 15 May 2026, Communications Biology. DOI: 10.1038/s42003-026-10022-4

Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter.Follow us on Google and Google News.

Assuming the new research applies to both humans and mice, as just a senior lay American male I’ve known of a couple of differences between young and old females for a long time; estrogen and uric acid levels. And, postmenopausal women not on hormone replacement therapy are as likely to get gout (a high blood serum level of uric acid) as younger males. For those who’ve never had to deal with gout, you should also know that serum uric acid is a product of inflammation. Medical testing and my lay findings of forty-five years and counting assure me that still medically unrecognized food allergies (Dr. Arthur F. Coca, by 1935) aggravated with still medically unrecognized FDA approved food poisoning (soy, tBHQ and added MSG, minimally) are the primary causes of most chronic inflammation, chronic diseases and premature disability and/or mortality. Statistically, for human females, soy being mostly processed with hexane (by the early 1970s) is likely still to be a major contributing factor in US breast cancers. Old, old news.

#6466. How brain implants turn thoughts into speech

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Casey Harrell, here at home in the summer of 2026, uses a brain-computer interface to communicate with his family.

Regents of the University of California, Davis

Casey Harrell lost his voice to ALS or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. As a volunteer in a clinical trial, he’s helping scientists test a brain-computer interface. Electrode arrays that are implanted in Casey’s brain send signals to nearby computers, where those signals are translated into words he intended to say.

Casey uses this system every day to talk with his wife, daughter, friends and work colleagues. The moment he realized that it worked was “pure joy,” Casey says. Even though the researchers scripted his words for that first test, “it was a profound moment,” he says. “The possibilities for the near future for me and the rest of humanity were overwhelming to realize.”

This episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me follows Casey and the fast-moving neuroscience that enables him to speak.

Patients paralyzed from the neck down can manipulate robotic arms with their thoughts. The woman in this video is controlling a robot with her mind. The so-called BrainGate system relies on a sensor of electrodes implanted in the motor cortex of the brain. Researchers hope by implanting electrodes in the brain it can read the brain signals meant to move the muscles involved in speaking, and translate the person’s intention to speak into comprehensive speech produced by a computer.

Laura Sanders: Controlling things with your mind. It sounds like science fiction, but it’s definitely real. Today, we’re going to explore what it’s like to communicate with a brain implant that decodes your thoughts and turns them into words.

[voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? The voice is absolutely an integral part of your identity. Hello? That added layer of it being you. Do you want to talk? Your voice. Hi. Your voice is you.

Sanders: From Science News, I’m Laura Sanders, and this is The Deep End, Talk to Me. Okay, so what is BrainGate? It’s an experimental system that connects electrodes that are implanted in a person’s brain to a nearby computer. It’s called a brain-computer interface, or BCI. The goal here is big: to help people with paralysis or brain injuries or missing limbs regain control over their world.

Leigh Hochberg: BrainGate clinical trials have now been going on for nearly 22 years. It’s 21 point something at the moment.

Sanders: Leigh Hochberg is the director of the BrainGate Consortium and Clinical Trials. He also has a job at Massachusetts General Hospital, Brown University and the VA.

Hochberg: People who may have had a brainstem stroke and suddenly lost the ability both to move and to speak, or for somebody with ALS who is progressively losing the ability to move or to speak, there’s long been a hope that particularly implantable brain-computer interfaces could restore communication and could restore mobility.

Sanders: In 2004, a BrainGate device was implanted into a person’s brain for the very first time. That person was a man named Matthew Nagle, and he had been paralyzed in an accident. With BrainGate, he could control a computer cursor with his thoughts. Here’s a 2008 report from IT World.

Technology gave him hope. He was one of four testing BrainGate, a new technology where a chip is implanted in the brain that picks up electrical impulses. A computer then interprets those impulses as actions.

Hochberg: Those early studies have been really encouraging, and I think speaks to the potential for the field.

Sanders: Over the years, there’s been amazing examples of people using BrainGate. People have used it to click around on the internet, play video games, one woman who was paralyzed was even able to drink a cinnamon latte with a robotic arm.

Hochberg: And she was able to think about using her own arm and reach out with a robotic arm and pick up that thermos and bring it to her mouth, and tip it towards her mouth, and then put the straw in her mouth and then to take that sip. And while it wasn’t the first time in nearly 15 years that she had had something to drink, it was the first time that she was really able to do so solely of her own volition. I remember the smile on her face when she did that.

Sanders: Over the decades, BrainGate has had a lot of research success in a lot of ways. But what about talking? Hochberg says that when it comes to decoding speech, the science here is still very, very young.

Hochberg: We are at early days, just to be super clear. This is the very beginning of this field. There are only a small handful of people in the world who have had any type of implantable BCI that has been decoding speech.

Sanders: Where does the science stand when it comes to decoding the intention to talk? In the past few episodes, we’ve heard the stories of people who have lost their ability to speak. One of those people was Casey Harrell, and Casey also happens to have a BrainGate device implanted in his brain.

Casey Harrell: My name is Casey Harrell and I am 47 years old.

Sanders: Casey wakes up in the morning, and plugs in.

Casey: The first thing I will usually do after getting out of bed is to plug into the Matrix, so to speak.

Sanders: By that, he means attaching two wires to two pedestals that come out of the top of his head. These two black wires then snake down to nearby computers. Collectively, these electrodes in Casey’s brain, wires from his head, and computers are called the BrainGate 2 neural interface system. So Casey gets it all fired up and then he’s off.

Casey: Unless I have a medical appointment or something that will move me out of the house, I will sit in this position for most of the day, with specifically small breaks in between.

Sanders: All the while, Casey is generating brain signals as he thinks about saying words. These are small, precise electrical pulses made by Casey’s neurons, specifically the cells in his speech motor cortex. Remember how we learned there are over 100 muscles that are involved in speech? These are the parts of the brain that control those muscles.

Casey: I am using a decoder for about ten to 14 hours a day, seven days a week, for the past almost two years, making me the world’s biggest power user of the brain-to-computer interface known to man.

Sanders: Like Jules, Casey has ALS. The disease has slowly taken away his ability to move and to talk.

Casey: I began to lose my ability to talk shortly after my diagnosis in 2020. Then it became a slow motion car crash of multiple years before almost no one would be able to understand me.

By the time of my surgery, only my assistant and my wife, Levana, could really understand me fully. A few other friends who were around often would be able to understand some of what I was saying. I relied upon my assistant and my wife to basically serve as my translators to other people. I did not go anywhere, even a video call without them, either one or both.

Sanders: In July of 2023, Casey volunteered for a clinical trial called BrainGate 2. A UC Davis neurosurgeon put four small electrical arrays onto the left side of Casey’s brain. I wanted to know more about how these arrays worked, so I talked to the neurosurgeon who put Casey’s devices into his brain.

David Brandman: My name is David Brandman, and I am the co-director of the UC Davis neuroprosthetics lab, developing next-generation neurotechnology to help people with paralysis. A brain-computer interface is a device that records brain signals from people that are paralyzed and then translates those brain signals to allow people to control objects in their environment using their minds.

Sanders: Casey’s implant is made of four arrays. Each of them are square and they’re about as wide as a peppercorn. Each array has a bunch of pointy ends that go down into his brain. They look a little like those metal cat brushes. Altogether, the four arrays contain 256 electrodes. These electrodes are all listening to Casey’s brain activity when he thinks about saying a word.

Brandman: The way this device works is by recording the electrical activity of the brain as he tries to speak.

Sanders: The wires from Casey’s head carry those neural signals to nearby computers. That’s where machine learning algorithms attempt to do a very complex sort of matching. The algorithms match Casey’s brain activity patterns to the patterns that predictably occur with certain sounds called phonemes.

Brandman: We translate his brain signals into one of 39 different English phonemes. Now, a phoneme is a building block of language. So if I say the word hello, the word hello can be broken down into ha, uh, uhl, and oh. Hello.Sanders: Next up, those algorithms assembles these phonemes into words by making its best guess about what Casey wants to say.

Brandman: So I translate this brain activity into a phoneme and then, using artificial intelligence, turn phonemes into words, words into sentences, and sentences into paragraphs.Sanders: So that’s the process, and it allows Casey to type messages on Slack, text his friends, and send emails. Sometimes in his emails to me, he includes a tagline at the bottom: “Sent from my brain,” with that cute little pink brain emoji. His setup also lets him convert these typed messages into spoken words. These words show up on a screen for him where Casey proofreads them. If everything looks good, Casey gives the go-ahead and the system speaks the words out loud. Brandman tells me that when Casey tries to speak naturally, he can say about six understandable words per minute. That’s pretty slow.

Brandman: Using this prosthesis, he’s in the ballpark of 50 words per minute. Now, as I’m speaking to you right now, I’m speaking on the order of 120 to 150 words per minute, depending on how excited I am, right? So we’ve got him back to about a third of how quickly he spoke as an able-bodied person.

Sanders: I had emailed Casey some questions a few days before our talk. But he didn’t answer them by email. He used his brain-computer interface to answer my questions in real time just by thinking about the words he wanted to say to me. As we introduced ourselves, I saw how the timescale had stretched.

Casey: It’s a challenge because we can have this conversation, but I am slower than the average Joe, even where we grew up.Sanders: Casey and I both grew up in the south, Casey in the Atlanta area and me in middle Tennessee. But he’s lived in the Bay Area for over 20 years now. And like me, his accent had faded.

Casey: And yes, I do not have much of a Southern accent anymore. But I love my roots, and I would love to show my daughter where and how I grew up. But it is exceedingly difficult to travel when you cannot move.

Sanders: Before his mobility was limited, Casey did a lot of cool things.

Casey: I spent most of my professional career as a climate campaigner and have went all over the globe, fighting companies who are destroying the Earth and trying to bring some justice to our planet and the people who inhabit it. I am very fortunate because I have been able to do something that I love and also develop some deep friendships and relations with other phenomenal people.

Sanders: My interview with Casey was unlike any I’ve ever had. I’m used to being flexible for interviews. There’s time zone problems, language barriers, mathematicians who sometimes answer my questions in symbols and formulas. But when I logged on to Zoom to talk with Casey, I quickly realized this conversation would be different. I was self-conscious at the beginning of our talk. I fumbled around too much. I’d ask Casey a question and then another one before he had a chance to answer. I accidentally interrupted him a few times. Sometimes I wasn’t sure if he was composing an answer or just waiting for me to say something else. This poor performance on my part wasn’t unusual for Casey at all.

Casey: It is hard for people in your position to stay focused because you were not used to the cadence of a conversation this slowly.

Sanders: He’s right. I was not used to it. And timing, in conversations and in life, is everything. Here’s Greg Bryant of UCLA.

Bryant: Turns, conversational turns, happen at the level of hundreds of milliseconds at the longest. Two hundred milliseconds is a long turn. That’s a fifth of a second. I mean, that’s really fast. So if you are slow at all, it’s noticeable. We have to coordinate our talk so our terms make sense. I can’t take too long or be too quick to respond to your questions. I have to know when to stop and start. We get into this flow, kind of a dynamic, and that is hugely consequential for how we feel about the conversation, the other person, ourselves. You know, it’s all timing.

Sanders: Let’s turn to Jules. His words start in his brain too, but then they take a different route. He types them by looking at letters on a screen, then his voice clone says them. It’s also a slow process and one that takes a lot of mental power, too. At one point in our conversation, MA describes the effort this requires of Jules.

MA: And in his brain, you know, you can imagine he’s doing all these mental gymnastics, to, right now, he’s listening to us. He’s writing something with his eyes, like letter by letter to contribute to the conversation. Plus, he has the answers that he pre-wrote, of the questions that you asked. So it really is like, there’s a whole lot happening behind the scenes that of course anybody who doesn’t have to think about their voice takes for granted. So I’ll pause to let him complete what he’s saying.Sanders: MA and I wait here for Jules to weigh in. So far you’ve heard ten seconds of the pause. The full length of the pause was a minute and 18 seconds.

Jules: It is a challenge to communicate with people who don’t interact with me on a daily basis. I have a major bottleneck from my thoughts to actually speaking.

Sandes: And as with Casey, these pauses can introduce difficulties. Here’s speech pathologist Jessica Pietrowski with more on that.

Pietrowski: Humans are not very comfortable with silence, especially communication. And when we’re talking to one another, we fill in the silences, it’s less awkward. And so, someone who’s communicating with a device is probably very used to those latency periods and some more silence and they’re comfortable with it. Whereas the person they’re communicating with is like, let’s keep it going, like this is, I want to help, I want to fill in the blanks, I don’t want this to feel awkward, but in turn, might make it a little more awkward than they think.

Sanders: Jules hates when people read his screen before he’s ready to say what he wants. This particular hate inspired a joke in his stand-up routine.

[Jules audio]: People read off my screen while I’m typing and try to finish what I am saying. It’s like having to constantly deal with an over-competitive charades partner.

Sanders: Jules and Casey encounter other people’s impatience constantly. Not that it isn’t well-intentioned but still, it does not help. Even worse, they face other people’s misconceptions about what they’re capable of. Casey is an interesting, funny and compelling conversationalist. That might not be apparent to everyone who doesn’t slow down to hear him. And that’s an assumption that really bothers him.

Casey: It is incredibly undignified and a terrible consequence of the health care system to treat me like this very quickly.

Sanders: Brandman has seen this dismissal, this mistreatment too. It happens with some of the volunteers he works with on the BrainGate 2 project I mentioned earlier. That’s the same trial Casey’s in.

Brandman: I think as healthcare professionals, we conflate the inability to communicate with the lack of understanding. And I’ve witnessed this firsthand as I’ve watched doctors and nurses interact with my BrainGate participants and then treat them as if they are invalid. Or they’re not there because they’re unable to express themselves. And in fact, I go out of my way in the intensive care unit on the wards and dealing with anyone who’s dealing with my participants to say, look, you know, they’re inside. They’re there. They can understand everything that’s happening. They just happen to not be able to speak. And so please treat them with the respect and dignity that they deserve. And it’s a constant challenge for the participants that I work with. And it’s the reality of which we face and it’s the bias that we have against people that can’t speak for themselves.

Sanders: Casey and the other people with ALS are not alone. Many people who have trouble talking or who just need more time can be judged this way. Here’s Karina Nagin from Bridging Voice.

Nagin: It’s how people see you. And so when you have ALS and you cannot move and you don’t even have facial expressions and you’re hooked up to machines, people assume you’re not there. And we see this every day where people either don’t talk to the person with ALS, assuming that they can’t respond. They speak really loudly and slow. Their mind is completely working.

Sanders: For now, Casey’s words may be slow. But despite all the drawbacks, they are still an absolute marvel. Remember Hochberg from the start of this episode? He’s one of the neuroscientists who works with Casey, and he told me a story from the first few days of testing after Casey’s BCI was implanted.

Hochberg: We gave him a 50-word vocabulary on day one. And even on day one, he was able to say some key sentences from those 50 high-value words.

Sanders: At this point in the testing, Casey was asked to say some pre-specified sentences so researchers could test their system out.

Casey: Most of the sentences were what we called closed loops.

Sanders: That means that the researchers already knew what brain activity patterns should go with the words Casey thought about saying. It was a test to see if the system was working.

Casey: The decoder would be able to verify whether I was right or wrong, giving me short preloaded sentences to say. I was asked to say, “What good is that?”

Sanders: “What good is that?” is not the most poignant sentence ever uttered, but it had a big effect both in the room and for researchers joining remotely by video.Casey: “What good is that?” Everyone is crying after I am successful.

Sanders: Later on, there was time for Casey to actually express himself.

Sanders: Things only got better from there. To set the scene here, during this session, Hochberg was in his office and Casey was at his home, sitting in his living room. Hochberg was watching Casey on a screen.

Hochberg: On the second session, came back and gave him the full 125,000 plus word English dictionary to be able to select from. That is, the decoders and the AI and the machine learning language models would be able to select from basically a full dictionary. And the first thing that he said was something along the lines of, “Is this thing on?” Kind of a funny statement.

The next thing that he said on the second day of using brain-computer interface, or the second thing that we decoded was, “I’m looking for a cheetah.” And it’s the second day. We know there’s all kinds of opportunities for decoding errors. And when I saw that, I said, you know, there’s no way that the second sentence on the second day of using an implanted brain-computer interface is going to say anything about a cheetah. You know, that’s obviously a decoding error and that’s fine.

Sanders: Hochberg could see Casey on the screen, but he couldn’t see something really important that had just happened in the room.

Hochberg: His four-year-old daughter had just walked into the room dressed as a cheetah.

Sanders: Here’s Casey remembering the same moment.

Casey: Yes, I remember this time very well. It was the second session of talking that I experienced early in August 2024. My daughter was incredibly cute in her cheetah outfit. This was one of her favorite animals. They were going through a phase where everything they did was super fast, running from thing to thing. Everyone was thinking that it must have been a mistake that I could not use this language. It was so random. This was only from the people like Leigh who were not in the room with us. The researchers who were there could validate that, yes, I said this. I meant it because of the unique context.

Sanders: It’s one of those moments that many parents have. A kid does something cute, a parent plays along. But in this moment for Casey and his child, it was anything but ordinary.

Hochberg: And she was born around the time that he was diagnosed with ALS. And one could imagine that because the voice that was coming out of the computer was a version of his own voice, and then the rest of the interaction was between dad and daughter. And it was between parent and child.

Sanders: The BCI had given Casey something priceless, a minute to play with his sweet little cheetah.

Casey: I was quietly confident that it would work the way it ended up working for me. I had done a lot of research and the thing was that the technology was on the cusp of a breakthrough. And why not me? I asked myself.

Sanders: Early on in the research project, Casey and his wife had been told not to expect it to work. This was an experiment and the outcome was far from certain. Casey, however, was optimistic.

Hochberg: So to me, seeing it work that quickly and that powerfully really, really emphasized that these are technologies that are going to be able to restore not only activities of daily living, not only key kind of instrumental activities of daily living, but they’re going to restore communication between parent and child. They’re going to restore communication between friends and family and care partners and health care providers.

Sanders: Because this is a podcast about the human voice, I’ve been asking people I interview what their voice means to them. Here’s Casey’s answer.

Casey: It means so much. I think it is the most important thing that I have lost in this whole disease.

Sanders: Getting it back, even in a limited form, is everything.Casey: It was so amazing to be able to be understood right from the get-go and to be able to talk and respond, respond to my daughter, especially because that was lacking completely from my life up to that point.Sanders: Casey’s restored voice changed his life.

Casey: It is the ability to parent my daughter. It is the ability to connect with my wife. It is the ability to make a wry joke with my friends. Timing is everything, and that is why having nothing, this is completely revolutionary. And to look back on my previous answer, it is something that really can still improve.

Sanders: At the beginning of the experiment, the research team had told Casey and his wife that they’d be able to try using the BCI for casual chats just a few hours a week. Those hours felt like a huge gift at the time, considering that they hadn’t been able to talk meaningfully for a long time. Here’s Brandman.

Brandman: As we kept coming to his house two or three times a week, things kept getting better and better. And it got to a point where Casey wanted to use the system to say all the things that he wanted to say.Sanders: Early on, only the researchers could set Casey up with the system, plugging him into the Matrix, as he puts it.Brandman: And so our research technologist would start coming to his house three, four, five times a week to don and doff the system to enable him to communicate so that he could go about his day. And so at a certain point, we saw, well, he really wants to use the system. Can we streamline this for him? And so we petitioned the FDA to actually allow us to change the clinical trial protocol slightly so that we could train his care partners to don and doff the system without us being there. And so since then, he’s been a near daily user of the system.

Sanders: That’s a far cry from a few hours a week. I’m going to read you some numbers from a research paper Brandman and his colleagues published about Casey’s BCI in Nature Neuroscience in June of 2026.“Over nearly two years, the participant, that’s Casey, used the BCI for more than 3,800 hours at home with no researchers present to maintain rich, interpersonal communication with his family and friends, independently control his personal computer, and sustain full-time employment, despite being paralyzed. He communicated 183,060 sentences, totaling 1,960,163 words, at an average rate of 56 words per minute. He labeled 92 percent of sentences as being decoded at least mostly correctly.”

Those numbers in this very bare-bones science kind of way are dry, if we’re being honest. But when you stop to think about it, each sentence, each of those nearly two million words, is a tether that connects Casey to his life. They’re messages to his daughter, jokes with his partner, texts to his friends. They’re games of Wordle with his wife and kid. Here’s Casey and his family in a video shot by UC Davis Health.

Okay, so no A, but we got an E. M-I. O. M-I. Good job, team. We are almost there.

Sanders: We’ve talked a lot about words here and the fundamental ways that Casey’s BCI has restored his ability to say them. But Casey’s BCI goes a little bit farther than that. It gives him the ability to add some extras. He’s got some bells and whistles up his sleeve.Casey: It is really a communication device, first and foremost, and less of a tool that I use to make funny remarks. But I do have that as well in my repertoire. For example, I have the ability to add sound effects to what I am saying.

Sanders: For instance, Casey has a sad trombone sound.

Casey: So if I find something funny and want to say, LOL, the theme from the TV show, Seinfeld, will play.

[theme song]Sanders: This is what he means. These jokes make me think of Jules, which made me wonder if Casey, like Jules, could also swear with his system.

Casey: To answer your question of whether I can curse with this device, I most certainly [beep] can.

Sanders: So for all your inquiring minds, there you have it. Looking ahead a bit, there’s a lot happening on the horizon. The science here is moving fast and many companies are working on similar systems. We’re going to cover that in a few episodes. But for now, Casey is alone. He is an N of 1, as the scientists say – the only person using a brain-computer interface for communication this heavily.

Casey: I hope to have this changed very soon because I feel like everyone who wants this should have the opportunity to have it, especially those who are with my disease.

Sanders: Hochberg tells me that this drive to help others is common among people who volunteer for these sorts of clinical trials.

Hochberg: Each participant in the trial has been just so generous and so clear that they recognize that it’s early days in the research, but they’ve told us that they want to help other people with paralysis. They want to be able to allow people with brainstem stroke or cervical spinal cord injury or ALS or other paralyzing illnesses or injuries to have improved function, to be able to regain control over that computer or regain the fluent speech and communication that they had previously. So it’s that generosity of spirit that has really defined the participants in our BrainGate studies.

Sanders: Casey’s generosity, his drive to help other people, really shines through as we talk. But I want to get back to him. I ask Casey what it’s been like to have this technology in his home, in his brain. He tells me how precious our voices are, and how easy it is for many of us to forget that.Casey: We take them for granted. The ability to scream when you are running and want to get out some stress. The ability to say sweet nothings into your partner’s ear. These are the things that life is all about. And when you are robbed of those times, you want them back at all costs. And this is why this is good enough for now, and we should have accelerated approval for devices like this.

Sanders: Casey’s BCI is slow compared to the pace of a normal conversation. And it gets things wrong occasionally.Casey: Sorry, I am trying to answer you. And it is changing what I want to say. And I am being stubborn instead of trying to say it another way, which I will do now.[Sanders audio] I’m not in any rush. You take as much stubborn time as you want.

Sanders: And it needs an internet connection and power. And let’s not forget that Casey has an adapter coming out of the top of his head. But these are solvable problems, one that scientists are actively working on. So not perfect, but as Casey puts it, good enough for now.

Scientific efforts to restore voices have been transformative for Jules, Casey, and others. But the ability to separate a voice from a body also raises new possibilities for our societies and for our lives.

MA: His voice will live on in whatever videos or things we’ve captured, whatever he’s left us intentionally, and that’s as far as that goes.

Sanders: On the next episode, we’re stepping out of the lab and into a strange new digital world where voices might not be what they seem.

Hany Farid: And so we are living in, I think, in equal parts an exciting time and a terrifying time. And somehow those are coexisting.

Sanders: What changes are coming in a world where voices can be so easily cloned?Farid: Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, anybody doing or saying anything.

#6465. Don’t Visit Ko Lipe

After 19 years, I finally went back to Ko Lipe, the Thai island I spent close to a month on in 2006. Back then, it was one of those super off-the-beaten-path destinations that few but the most intrepid travelers visited, where electricity only ran a few hours a day, basic bungalows right on the beach cost something like $2 USD, and there really was a last boat for the season.

There was much to do here but that was the point. You hung out on the beach, read a book, went snorkeling, went back to the beach, drank beers at the one beach bar on the island, rotated meals between the five restaurants there, and went to bed early.

It was paradise – and a place a lot of people got stuck. Days easily turned into weeks here.

If you asked me what the highlight of all my travels was, I would be the time I spent on Ko Lipe. I made incredible friends, lounged around, got to know the locals, learned a bit of Thai, and, overall, lived that idyllic backpacker life we all dream about.

Over the years, I’ve avoided going back to Ko Lipe because the memory of my time there is so strong that I didn’t want to ruin it. Any re-visit would simply be trying to recreated a magic that couldn’t be recreated because the people that it special wouldn’t be there. I’d be chasing travel ghosts. And, since I know my sleepy paradise has been developed greatly over the years, I was also too afraid seeing that would make me sad.

Tourism in Thailand tends toward the unsustainable. No island really develops in a good way. It’s all build, build, build.

And I didn’t want to see my Ko Lipe like that.

But as I was planning my recent trip through Southeast Asia, returning to Ko Lipe made sense. I was heading down the Indian Ocean side of Thailand on my way into Malaysia and I’d pass by it.

And, since I was looking for a lively place for New Year’s Eve, it seemed liked the best choice. I knew there would be travelers there and there were no other nearby islands that would work, especially since Ko Lipe has a boat to Langkawi, which was my next stop.

And I’m sad to report that Ko Lipe took the Ko Phi Phi model of tourism and is now extremely overdeveloped.

Most of the island is now paved over, the old dirt footpaths having become concrete for the cars and construction trucks. Swaths of palm trees are now the sites of high-end resorts with pools (on an island with no natural water supply). Construction of more resorts continues at a fast pace. The coral around the island is dying, a victim of all the boats, anchors, pollution, and overfishing. Beaches are now lined with boats, their exhaust spilling into the ocean, leaving a shiny film you can see as you swim. And the restaurants cater to tourists looking for bad Western food, not great Thai cuisine.

The island’s boom has displaced many locals, who were forced to sell to mainland developers, and much of the island’s workforce is now from the mainland. They see little of the benefits this tourism boom.

So lies Ko Lipe, another victim of Thailand’s all too common overdevelopment and exploitation of limited resources.

I met lots of people there who loved the island. If it’s your first time, I can see why you would love it. After all, the area is postcard perfect, the water is perfectly an azure blue, the sand is a beautiful white, and since you’re surrounded by a national park, a lot of tours take you to some secluded islands.

And, in comparison to Ko Phi Phi, Krabi, or Phuket, it is less developed so I can’t fault someone stepping here for the first time going “wow!”

But, as I reflect on the island and its overdevelopment, I have come to the same conclusion I have about Ko Phi Phi: people shouldn’t visit.

I’m not against growth, but I’m against this kind of growth. It’s not sustainably managed and going there will only tax the island’s limited resources even further. You can’t put the genie back in the bottle and no local is going to say “sure, I’ll stay broke so you can an idealized vision of the world.”

And, with so many other islands to visit that are well managed (Ko Lanta, Ko Jum, and Ko Mook, to name three nearby), I think you should skip Ko Lipe.

A visit there will only make things worse.

It pains me to say that, because it was such a beautiful place, and my original visit had a huge impact on my life. But if we’re going to be good stewards and travelers, sometimes you just have to say enough is enough.

And Ko Lipe is a place where enough is enough.

Go somewhere else that is better managed.

Riding elephants in Thailand went away when consumers became more conscious of it. Eco lodges got big because of consumers. Overtourism is talked about by consumers as much as it is by locals.

Maybe if enough people start to do something, Ko Lipe will change.

But, at the very least, by not going you are at least no contributing to the problem.

#6464. Do Spiders Dream? Scientists Discover a Mysterious Sleep State

Scientists have discovered that spiders experience REM-like sleep, complete with twitching muscles and moving eyes, raising the intriguing possibility that they might dream.

Spiders may have more in common with sleeping humans than scientists previously realized. Researchers at the University of Bonn have discovered that Australian jumping spiders experience two distinct stages of sleep, including a state that closely resembles REM sleep in humans. During this stage, the spiders move their eyes and twitch their muscles, behaviors that raise intriguing questions about the origins of sleep and whether spiders might experience something resembling dreams.

The findings provide the first comprehensive experimental confirmation of regulated sleep in spiders. They also suggest that complex sleep patterns may be far more widespread throughout the animal kingdom than previously understood.

In humans and other vertebrates, sleep involves multiple stages, including REM (rapid eye movement) sleep. This stage is associated with rapid eye movements, changes in muscle activity, and vivid dreaming in humans. Scientists have long wondered whether animals with very different nervous systems, including spiders, experience comparable sleep states.

To investigate, researchers from the Institute of Organismic Biology at the University of Bonn turned to an unusual subject: the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata.

The spider belongs to the genus Portia, a group of predators known for their sophisticated hunting techniques. Unlike many spiders that primarily capture insects, Portia species specialize in hunting other spiders.

One of their most remarkable strategies involves manipulating the webs of their prey. By producing vibrations that imitate insects struggling in silk, these spiders can lure web-building spiders toward them. Such complex hunting behavior suggests an unusual capacity for learning and adapting to different situations.

Despite their impressive abilities, these predators are quite small. A fully grown Portia fimbriata is roughly the size of a one-euro coin.

Their sophisticated behavior made them particularly interesting subjects for investigating sleep. Scientists wanted to determine whether these spiders simply become inactive at night or enter a genuine, biologically regulated sleep state similar to those observed in vertebrates.

The researchers found convincing behavioral evidence that Portia fimbriata does more than rest. The spiders exhibit regulated sleep with two clearly distinguishable stages.

One of these stages closely resembles REM sleep, a well-known phase of human sleep characterized by rapid eye movements and muscle twitches.

During the spiders’ REM-like periods, the researchers observed eye movements and twitching muscles, suggesting that certain features of sleep may be shared by animals whose nervous systems are dramatically different from our own.

The discovery is especially significant because most scientific knowledge about sleep has come from studies of vertebrates, including humans, other mammals, birds, and reptiles. Until now, comprehensive experimental evidence establishing true sleep behavior in spiders had been lacking.

Although the REM-like movements are intriguing, they do not demonstrate that spiders dream. Determining whether spiders experience anything comparable to human dreams would require evidence beyond the behavioral observations available in this study.

To examine the spiders’ nighttime behavior, the scientists monitored individual Portia fimbriata specimens over multiple days and nights.

Each spider was kept in a small plastic dish measuring 12 centimeters in diameter. The researchers exposed the animals to different lighting conditions to investigate their daily activity cycles and determine how their behavior changed between day and night.

High-resolution video recordings allowed the team to examine the spiders’ movements in detail. During nighttime observations, infrared cameras captured their sleeping positions, periods of inactivity, and episodes of REM-like behavior without requiring visible light.

But remaining motionless is not necessarily proof of sleep. Animals can become inactive for several reasons, so the researchers needed additional evidence to distinguish actual sleep from ordinary rest.

They tested the spiders’ responses to sound and measured how quickly the animals reacted. These experiments helped determine whether the spiders became less responsive to external disturbances during their resting periods, an important characteristic of sleep.

The team also investigated a phenomenon known as “sleep rebound,” which occurs when an animal compensates for interrupted or insufficient sleep by sleeping more afterward. Testing for this response helped establish whether the spiders’ rest was regulated by an underlying biological need.

Together, these observations and experiments provided evidence that the spiders experience genuine sleep rather than simply remaining inactive.

Studying sleep in spiders presents difficulties that researchers do not typically encounter when investigating humans or other mammals.

One major obstacle was identifying a stimulus that would reliably awaken the spiders during experiments. Spiders perceive their surroundings very differently from humans, making it challenging to design tests that could consistently measure their responses.

The researchers also had to be careful when interpreting the unusual movements recorded during the REM-like stage. Although eye movements and muscle twitches resemble behaviors associated with REM sleep in vertebrates, similar outward movements do not necessarily indicate identical processes inside the nervous system.

Another important limitation was the inability to directly measure the spiders’ brain activity. Instead, the researchers had to base their conclusions entirely on observable behavior.

To overcome these challenges, they collected extensive high-resolution video recordings over long observation periods. This provided the detail needed to examine subtle movements and sleep patterns, but it also generated enormous amounts of data that had to be analyzed.

By combining behavioral recordings with experiments measuring responsiveness and recovery from interrupted sleep, the researchers were able to build a much stronger case for true sleep in spiders.

The discovery could have important implications for understanding how sleep evolved.

REM sleep is one of the most fascinating and still incompletely understood aspects of human biology. Although it is closely associated with dreaming in humans, scientists continue to investigate its broader functions and evolutionary history.

Finding REM-like behavior in spiders raises the possibility that some features of complex sleep are shared across a much wider range of animals than previously established.

Spiders and vertebrates have very different nervous systems, yet both appear capable of entering distinct behavioral sleep states. Understanding these similarities could help researchers identify fundamental properties of sleep that have persisted through evolution or developed independently in different animal groups.

The findings also open new opportunities in behavioral biology, neuroscience, and chronobiology, the study of biological rhythms and internal clocks. They may be particularly valuable for understanding how sleep functions in animals with relatively simple nervous systems.

Rather than limiting sleep research to humans and traditional laboratory animals, the scientists recommend studying a much broader diversity of species, especially those with unusual nervous systems or highly specialized adaptations.

Such comparisons could help reveal whether sleep serves a universal biological purpose and whether some of its essential features originated very early in animal evolution.

Despite decades of research, many basic questions about why animals sleep and what happens during different sleep stages remain unanswered, even in humans.

The University of Bonn researchers are now extending their investigations to other spider species to better understand how sleep and REM-like states evolved across this diverse group of animals.

They also plan to compare spiders sleeping in laboratory environments with those living in the wild. These studies could reveal whether natural surroundings influence sleep patterns in ways that controlled laboratory conditions cannot fully capture.

Another major research direction involves exploring the relationship between sleep and intelligence. Because Portia spiders display sophisticated hunting and learning abilities, they provide an interesting opportunity to investigate whether sleep contributes to cognitive processes in animals with very different brains from humans.

Future studies will also examine what happens inside the nervous systems of spiders and insects during sleep. Direct measurements of neural activity could help determine whether the REM-like behaviors observed in spiders involve processes comparable to those found in vertebrates.

The researchers are additionally interested in how environmental changes influence sleep. In particular, they hope to investigate the effects of climate change and human activities, including artificial light at night (ALAN), on the sleep behavior of spiders and other small animals.

Artificial nighttime lighting can alter the natural cycle of light and darkness that many organisms use to regulate their daily rhythms. Understanding how spiders respond to these disruptions could provide new insights into the broader ecological consequences of human activity.

For now, the findings establish something remarkable: even a tiny jumping spider can experience distinct, regulated stages of sleep, including one that resembles REM sleep in humans.

Whether those sleeping spiders actually dream remains an open question, but their unusual nighttime behavior offers scientists a new way to investigate one of biology’s oldest mysteries.

Reference: “Behavioral evidence for two-stage sleep in spiders” by Nadja Geiger, Maxim Q. Capelle, Phillip Rosentreter, Marie E. Herberstein, Armin Bahl, Massimo De Agrò, Barrett A. Klein and Daniela C. Rößler, 26 October 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2618030123

This work was supported by the Emmy Noether Program of the German Research Foundation (DFG).

Researchers hope recursive self-improvement could tackle the skyrocketing costs of developing advanced AI models. But is it viable?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists in China are exploring what it would take to develop "the last AI built by humans" — a powerful, self-improving artificial intelligence (AI) system capable of creating its own successors.

In a new paper, researchers examine how approaches to recursive self-improvement (RSI) could help tackle the rising financial and computational costs of developing ever-more advanced AI models.

RSI refers to the idea that future AI models could direct their own training and development, using what they learn from each round of improvements to guide subsequent rounds of development.

This recursive feedback loop could eventually enable AI systems to develop newer, more powerful generations of models with minimal human input.

The study, which was uploaded to the preprint database arXiv Sept. 10 but has not been peer-reviewed, proposes a framework for classifying AI systems based on their self-improvement capabilities, from Level 1 (lowest) to Level 5 (highest).

At the lower levels, development remains largely human-led. As AI systems move up the scale, they become increasingly capable of identifying their weaknesses and deciding how to address them, eventually gaining the ability to make their own “meta-improvements” — improving how they improve themselves.

Whether AI could ever achieve this level of sustained self-improvement remains an open question. Previous experiments have, however, demonstrated more limited forms of RSI.

In one study earlier this year, an AI system called A-Evolve-Training was tasked with improving the performance of a 30 billion-parameter large language model (LLM).

Over four rounds, A-Evolve-Training modestly improved the LLM's benchmark performance by testing different training techniques and using the results to change how it approached subsequent experiments.

Peter Bentley, a professor of digital biology at University College London, questioned whether such experiments offer a credible route to RSI.

"This idea that some AI is magically going to start generating better and better AIs by themselves [is] nonsense," Bentley told Live Science in an email.

Bentley pointed out that self-improving computer systems have been around for decades. Evolutionary computation and reinforcement learning, for instance, are both based on the principle of systems refining their performance over time in response to feedback.

Could AI really self-improve? Some experts are skeptical.

The much greater challenge, he said, is developing AI systems capable of autonomously conducting the research needed to create more powerful successors — not to mention overcoming their dependence on human expertise and physical computing infrastructure.

"You can't 'recursively self-improve' unless you can also enhance your own training, enhance your hardware, and test it exhaustively in real world settings," Bentley added.

The study's authors acknowledged some of these challenges. Developing RSI-capable systems could require enormous investments in computing power, as well as human supervision to ensure successive improvements delivered meaningful gains. All of this becomes effectively redundant if the resources needed to develop and test subsequent AI models outweigh any benefits they offer, the authors noted.

Scientists would also need a reliable way to determine whether an AI system was genuinely becoming more capable over iterations, rather than exploiting weaknesses in tests used to measure its capabilities. This is a known problem in AI development, where models can achieve higher benchmark scores by exploiting testing methods or cherry-picking results.

Kayla Blomquist, an AI researcher at the University of Oxford and co-founder of the Oxford China Policy Lab, said that, while the paper doesn't provide a practical road map to RSI, it could help developers and policymakers understand the technical challenges and safety risks associated with increasingly autonomous AI systems.

She also questioned whether there would ever be a clear point at which AI became completely independent of human development. "The paper describes a gradual handover of responsibility rather than a single moment, so there may never be an obvious 'last' model built by humans," Blomquist added.

#6462. The 8 Best Slim Wallets to Keep Necessities Secure

Quality materials and sleek designs make these functional and stylish.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Whipping out a Costanza wallet overflowing with years-old receipts and foreign currency is less than ideal when it comes time to pay. The solution is simple—get a slim wallet. Slim wallets come in a variety of styles, from tactical to traditional, and are made of leather, aluminum, or ripstop nylon.

They’re designed to condense your everyday carry to the necessities with a couple of card slots, bill pockets, and sometimes extra stash pockets for business cards. And if you're worried about identity theft, many options include RFID-blocking technology. They fit comfortably in your back pocket or backpack without adding unwanted bulk, and they won’t feel like you’re on half a booster seat when you sit.

We shopped around dependable retailers to find minimalist wallets that combined functional design with durable materials. We then checked user reviews to see which products held up over time to daily wear and tear. Pooling together a variety of styles and price points, we determined that these slim wallets are the best. There’s something for anyone who wants to declutter without compromising on capacity (too much) or quality.

This attractive wallet opens like a traditional bifold, but with a more streamlined design. The inside has a money clip bar to secure your bills—rather than an oversized pocket—and two card slots.

It keeps your information safe with RFID-blocking tech and fits comfortably in a front or back pocket. There’s a slot with a pull-tab on the front, making it easy to access your most frequently used cards. The other side has a clear slot for photo I.D. and can fit a card and a folded bill or two.

Along with the practical design, this wallet is made with longevity in mind. Full-grain leather maintains its shape better than low-grade leather and polyester, so the slots won’t stretch anytime soon. You can tighten the money-clip bar on the inside, too, so don’t worry if it starts to work loose.

The James Brand started with pocket knives and now makes pretty much every aspect of EDC you can think of. This wallet is one of its newest offerings that uses machined aluminum and a sleek design for a minimalist wallet option.

The card slot isn’t expandable so it keeps you honest in only carrying what you really need.

Another intriguing design from Bellroy, this flip case features rounded edges and integrated organization slots for easy access to your bills and plastic. The hardshell case is durable without being bulky and secures shut with a magnetic closure.

One side has slots for cards, while the other is a large pocket to stash things on the fly; both sides can be flipped open with your thumb or finger. The streamlined design is best suited for those who rarely carry cash, so if you prefer to have more than a couple of bills on you, you should opt for a model with more capacity.

The Parliament can hold over 10 cards comfortably without compromising its slim profile. Each side of the wallet accommodates up to six cards, and the right side has a button at the bottom to fan out your cards for easy access.

There’s an interior cash strap for holding a couple of bills or ID, though there’s no dedicated clear ID card slot. We like that the cash strap is on the inside, though, since we’re wary of money clips and straps on the outside. If anything comes loose, at least it’s sandwiched inside.

The Ridge is built to last. But if it doesn’t, the company’s lifetime warranty ensures you’ll get another one ASAP. This wallet has replaceable parts, so if anything goes wrong, Ridge can replace them, from the plates and screws down to the elastic strap. Luckily, this isn’t a frequent occurrence thanks to the anodized aluminum plates that resist corrosion and the stainless-steel hardware.

The wallet holds plenty of cards, as well as some cash, in the money clip, and it can expand without stretching too much, unlike a fabric or leather wallet. If you’re not into the money clip, it comes with an elastic band you can attach.

The only downside is there’s no separating cards inside—it’s all just one space. So if you like an organized wallet, this isn’t the one for you.

There are multiple color options to suit your style. It’s a bit expensive, but if it lasts a lifetime, it’s probably worth it.

If you’re looking to buy a slim wallet on a budget, this no-frills option from Herschel might be right up your alley. The Charlie has two card slots on each side and one up top to hold some folded bills. The elastic band gives some extra security and keeps your cards from sliding out.

This was our gateway to slim wallets and card cases, and it's a good starting point if you feel like you’re carrying too much and want to make a change. If you plan on carrying more than a couple of cards, it’s going to get pretty tight. But it’s a good way to help you figure out what you need on the day to day. If you find you prefer extra space, this option isn’t a costly trial-and-error.

Many of our picks can fit comfortably in your front pocket, but only the Rogue Industries Front Pocket Wallet is specifically designed for this purpose. This is ideal for anyone who feels nervous about keeping valuables out of sight in their back pocket or simply doesn’t enjoy sitting on their billfold throughout the day.

This wallet’s bison leather is super soft and durable, and it can hold up to 6 cards along with some cash. It’s longer than the others on our list to fit the standard-size card while maintaining a slim profile.

The Ranger has only one main compartment, one pocket, and a cash strap, but they’re well placed so things stay organized. The outer pocket keeps your frequently used cards handy, while the cash strap is on the back.

The center slot holds up to six cards, which fan out when you pull the leather tab at the bottom. The full-grain leather is oiled for water-resistance and will patina over time to develop a unique look.

A slim wallet should comfortably fit in your pocket, even when it’s full of your essentials. This kind of wallet is meant to reduce bulk by being only slightly larger than a standard credit card while holding the must-haves: credit cards, an ID, and maybe some cash. Remember, maximizing storage capacity isn’t the goal here—whichever you choose should have enough room for what you need. We came across some online reviews that harped on size and capacity, which was counterintuitive, especially for a slim wallet. It may force you to pare down your usual contents, but that’s why you’re here.

Slim wallets are made from a variety of materials to suit a range of functions and aesthetic needs. Leather options are good if you want something more classic, with full-grain leather being the best you can buy. If you want something on the modern side, you can find wallets made of aluminum and carbon fiber, though these may look too tactical for some people’s taste. Slim wallets made of textiles like nylon or polyester are a good middle ground if you just want something simple. All of our picks have RFID-blocking capabilities, which prevent thieves from scanning your credit cards through your pocket and wallet.

Some of our picks have a button or trigger to deploy your cards from the pocket, making them easier to access. The addition of these mechanical devices is convenient, but they can break after repeated use. An alternative is a pull tab that raises cards from the pocket. The downside there is that they can limit space in your wallet.

#6461. A Last Refuge: Australian Waters Could Save a Critically Endangered Ocean Predator

Despite decades of research, major gaps in scientists’ understanding of green sawfish could complicate efforts to save the species.

Green sawfish have disappeared from large parts of their former range, but northern Australia still supports some of the last relatively intact populations of this critically endangered species. A new scientific review suggests these waters could be central to the animal’s survival, although major gaps in researchers’ knowledge continue to complicate conservation efforts.

Green sawfish are a type of ray with a sharklike body and a distinctive, tooth-lined snout resembling a saw. Overfishing and habitat loss have driven their decline worldwide. Researchers at Murdoch University’s Centre for Sustainable Aquatic Ecosystems, part of the Harry Butler Institute, have now brought together decades of scientific findings to identify the species’ remaining strongholds and determine where further research is needed.

“Although the species has disappeared from large parts of its historic range, including parts of Africa and southern Asia, northern Australia still supports some of the last intact populations left anywhere on Earth,” said Dr. Jack Ingelbrecht, a postdoctoral research associate who led the review alongside Associate Professor David Morgan. Ingelbrecht added, “We’re fortunate that the main factors responsible for the global decline of sawfish are less severe in northern Australia.”

Western Australia’s Pilbara region is particularly valuable because it contains important green sawfish habitat and populations that remain relatively healthy. “The Pilbara region in particular has become one of the world’s most important areas for green sawfish research, as it still supports relatively healthy populations of this species and provides critical habitat,” said Morgan, who has studied Australian sawfish for more than 25 years. “It gives us a rare opportunity to understand how green sawfish use their environment, and identify which conservation measures would best facilitate their recovery.”

The survival of green sawfish in Australian waters has also shaped the global scientific understanding of the species. “To research something, you first need specimens to study. Naturally, opportunities for green sawfish research will be greater in areas where this species still occurs in relatively high numbers,” Ingelbrecht explained.

“Our review found that, for decades, Australia has been the global leader in green sawfish research. This is partly because green sawfish populations have been wiped out in many countries, but still exist in Australia,” he said. Australia’s contribution extends across many different areas of scientific investigation. “Interestingly, when we looked at the specific types of information that have been produced, we found that Australia has also been at the forefront of almost every major sub-discipline of research relating to green sawfish.”

The research team compiled existing studies into a single resource intended to support conservation planning and future investigations. “Renowned zoologist Ferdinando Boero said it best: ‘you can’t protect what you don’t know,'” Ingelbrecht said. “It’s incredibly difficult to stay up to date with research on any topic, particularly when there’s a lot of information to cover. Ultimately, if conservation experts don’t fully understand the species they’re trying to protect, they can’t implement the most-suitable recovery initiatives.”

Despite Australia’s extensive research history, the review identified substantial gaps in the information needed to protect green sawfish. “By synthesizing the current knowledge of green sawfish, we wanted to provide an all-in-one resource to guide conservation efforts and researchers, alike,” Ingelbrecht said.

The most pressing uncertainties concern how many green sawfish survive, where their most important habitats are located, and how many individuals are old enough to reproduce. “Sadly, when it comes to the research areas most relevant to conservation – the size of remaining populations, the locations of critical habitat, and the number of mature individuals present in the wild – we realized that there’s very little information currently available.”

These missing data make it difficult to design conservation strategies suited to the species’ biological needs. “Research is the lifeblood of conservation. In order to be successful, recovery efforts often need to be tailored towards the species they’re intended for. To do that, you need scientific input,” Ingelbrecht said.

As green sawfish disappear from more of their historical range, Australia’s role in protecting the species could become increasingly significant. “Conservation biologists bear the responsibility of enhancing recovery initiatives through research. If green sawfish populations continue to decline, that responsibility – that burden – will fall more and more towards Australia,” Ingelbrecht warned.

The researchers nevertheless believe extinction can still be prevented if scientific research and conservation measures receive sufficient support. “It’s not over yet. There’s still a genuine opportunity to turn things around. With the right support, the right research, and the right conservation measures, we can ensure the survival of green sawfish. I hope Australia sets an example the rest of the world can follow,” Ingelbrecht said.

Reference: “The Critically Endangered green sawfish (Pristis zijsron): current knowledge and future directions” by Jack Ingelbrecht, Barbara E. Wueringer, Tyler N. Dornan, Penelope T. Dantas, Travis Fazeldean and David L. Morgan, 11 September 2026, Reviews in Fish Biology and Fisheries. DOI: 10.1007/s11160-026-10088-7

Funding: BCI Minerals, Western Australian Marine Science Institution, Leichhardt, Chevron Australia, Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development, Save Our Seas Foundation, Ecological Society of Australia
