#6460. Why This Company is One of the Best for Finding Work

Most travel is extractive and passive. You show up somewhere, take photos of the same landmarks everyone else takes photos of, eat at a restaurant the guidebook recommended, and hit up some bars. You take some tours to learn about the place and, if you’re lucky, get to meet some locals on your trip. You don’t really go deep.

Even long-term travelers who talk about how they “aren’t tourists” do the same – just at a slower pace and while trying to spend less money.

And there’s nothing wrong with that. That’s just the nature of travel. While we all imagine dropping into a place, befriending locals, and having this crazy time like we’re in some movies. But that doesn’t happen. Because we’re just passing through and, for the most part, locals don’t want to become friends with tourists. In fact, most locals don’t interact with tourists. (I mean it does happen but it’s not the norm.)

If you really want a deep travel experience, you need to stay. If you want to understand a place, you need to stay. The most transformative travel experiences I’ve ever had involved contributing something and staying somewhere long enough to build real relationships. It was being embedded in a place rather than just passing through.

I think that more travelers should give back when they travel. In the old days, it was hard to find out what organizations and opportunities were legit, vetted, and actually made the lives of locals better.

Even for experienced travelers, moving abroad can be difficult. For the past decade, “digital nomad” has been the aspirational version of long term travel. Work remotely, earn in a strong currency, live somewhere cheaper, repeat.

But that model only really works for a small subset of people. You need a remote job, a certain income level, and often a level of career stability that most younger travelers simply don’t have yet.

Instead of bringing a job with you, you get one when you arrive. You integrate into the local economy instead of floating above it. You meet people through work, not just coworking spaces or short-term hostels. And you build a life somewhere, not just a temporary routine.

In a lot of ways, working holiday makers are having a more grounded and accessible version of what people think digital nomad life is. You’re not just passing through, you’re actually living there. #6459. Comets probably didn’t deliver life’s building blocks to Earth

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The speed and angle of impact would have destroyed most organic compounds from comets

Comet McNaught shines over Australia a safe distance from Earth in this photo taken in 2007. Most comets that collided with the early Earth would have been moving too fast and at too steep an angle for prebiotic molecules to survive the collision and kick off chemical processes that gave rise to life, a new study suggests.

The chemical building blocks that gave rise to life on Earth probably didn’t come from comets.

Most comets would have been traveling too fast and at too steep an angle to Earth for prebiotic compounds to survive impact with the planet, researchers contend October 28 in Scientific Reports. While the study doesn’t completely rule out the possibility that comets brought these molecules to Earth, it contradicts the long-standing idea that comets seeded Earth with the chemicals necessary for life to arise.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“Even though we see that comets contain all of these molecules in really high concentrations, it’s not straightforward to go from there to saying we’re going to have all of these available for prebiotic chemistry on the surface of the Earth,” says Richard Anslow, a planetary scientist at the Met Office, the national meteorological service for the United Kingdom in Exeter.

Comets carry carbon- and nitrogen-containing molecules left over from early in the solar system’s formation. These molecules can react to form biologically important compounds like sugars and DNA. Scientists have long thought that comets could have delivered these building blocks to Earth when they collided with the planet during its first billion years.

But it’s important to revisit these ideas as our understanding of both comets and the early solar system improves, says Nicolle Zellner, a physicist at Albion College in Michigan who was not involved in the study.

In the new work, Anslow and colleagues used computer simulations to predict the likelihood that a chemical called hydrogen cyanide would survive a comet’s journey through Earth’s present atmosphere and its impact with the planet’s surface. The early Earth’s atmosphere was probably much denser, so would have been even more destructive.

The strong chemical bond between the carbon and nitrogen atoms in hydrogen cyanide can release energy that drives later chemical reactions necessary for life. It also makes the molecule particularly stable compared to other carbon-based chemicals.

“It’s probably one of the more robust molecules to surviving impacts,” Anslow says. “So if things look bad for hydrogen cyanide, then we think it’s going to be much harder for other, more complicated molecules that are more likely to be broken down during these impacts.”

Based on the simulations, a comet impact that kept hydrogen cyanide intact would be extremely unlikely, the team found. On average, the simulations suggest that only one impact would have been able to deliver a meaningful amount of hydrogen cyanide to the planet’s surface over more than a billion years. For hydrogen cyanide to survive the crash, the comet would have to be larger than 100 meters across, slow moving and traveling at an oblique angle to Earth.

A comet that met those narrow criteria would also have had to crash into land, rather than an ocean, to kick off any biologically useful chemistry. If the comet landed in the ocean, any hydrogen cyanide that survived would be diluted too quickly to trigger those reactions.

While still improbable, comets may have been more likely to deliver carbon-based molecules to Mars than to Earth, the simulations showed. Mars’ thinner atmosphere and smaller size meant that comets would impact at lower speeds. That could mean that more compounds could survive the collision.

If Earth’s carbon-based chemicals didn’t come from comets, they may have come from carbon-rich asteroids called carbonaceous chondrites, says Gordon Osinski, a planetary geologist at Western University in London, Canada, who was not involved in the study. Other sources might have included volcanoes and hydrothermal vents.

The study “definitely will make people think twice about comets being the originator for the delivery of organics,” Osinski says. “I hope other people will try to reproduce these results [and] then potentially try something similar with carbonaceous chondrites as well.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

R. Anslow et al. Cometary impacts an unlikely pathway towards the origins of life on Earth. Scientific Reports. 2026. doi: 10.1038/s41598-026-74214-y

Skyler Ware was the 2023 AAAS Mass Media Fellow with Science News. She has a Ph.D. in chemistry from Caltech, where she studied chemical reactions that use or create electricity.

#6458. A Natural Compound Found in Everyday Foods Shows Surprising Power Against Lung Cancer

Quercetin, a compound found in citrus fruits, onions, and buckwheat, slowed lung cancer cell division and movement in laboratory experiments. At the highest dose tested, cell migration nearly stopped.

The findings come from researchers at Universitätsklinikum Erlangen at Friedrich-Alexander Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU), who examined the compound’s effects in laboratory-grown lung cancer cells, mouse lung tissue sections, and living mice. Their study appeared in Cell Death Discovery.

Lung cancer is the most common cancer worldwide and causes more cancer deaths than any other type. Available treatments do not work for everyone, prompting researchers to investigate additional approaches, including plant compounds such as quercetin, which is known for its anti-inflammatory properties.

The team in the hospital’s Department of Molecular Pneumology found that quercetin affected several processes involved in cancer growth. “Many drugs against lung cancer target a single molecule,” explains Prof. Dr. Susetta Finotto. “Quercetin, by contrast, attacked at several points simultaneously in our experiments.”

Treated tumor cells divided more slowly. In one of the two lung cancer cell types examined, quercetin also lowered oxidative stress. This occurs when reactive oxygen compounds overwhelm cells’ defenses, potentially causing damage that contributes to cancer development.

The effect on movement was particularly striking because migration helps cancer cells spread and establish new tumors, known as metastases. “The higher the quercetin dose, the fewer cancer cells migrated. At the highest dose, the migration almost completely stopped,” reports Christine Carvalho, the study’s lead author.

Quercetin also reduced levels of two proteins, EGFR and PD-L1, in the cancer cells studied. EGFR passes growth signals into cells, while PD-L1 can help tumors evade immune defenses.

In mouse lung tissue sections, quercetin increased levels of interferon-alpha-2, a signaling molecule that helps the immune system defend against tumors. The researchers also observed changes beyond the lungs, involving the community of microbes living in the gut.

“In the mice that received quercetin, the gut microbiome also changed,” explains Prof. Susetta Finotto. “Bacteria that produce certain short-chain fatty acids were more common.” These fatty acids can enter the bloodstream and reach the lungs, where they can inhibit cancer cell growth.

The mice given quercetin also showed signs of fewer tumor sites. However, only a few animals developed tumors, leaving too little evidence to confirm that finding. Further studies are needed, and whether the effects seen in cells and mice extend to people remains unknown. The experiments also do not establish whether eating quercetin-containing foods would reproduce these results.

“Our results suggest that a quercetin-rich diet could support treatment for lung cancer,” says Prof. Susetta Finotto. “We also think it may have preventive effects. We want to investigate that next.”

Reference: “Immunoregulatory role of quercetin in lung cancer” by Christine Carvalho, Elvedina Nendel, Susanne Mittler, Sonja Trump, Adriana Geiger, Jonas Willar, Mircea T. Chiriac, Stefan Wirtz, Carol I. Geppert and Susetta Finotto, 14 September 2026, Cell Death Discovery. DOI: 10.1038/s41420-026-03312-7

In two new surveys, U.S. adults report lying to their doctors and their children's doctors about symptoms in hopes of being prescribed antibiotics.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nearly 30% of U.S. adults have lied to doctors in an effort to obtain antibiotics, either by exaggerating their actual symptoms or by fabricating symptoms, the results of a new national survey suggest. Additionally, in a second survey, about one-quarter of children's caregivers reported lying about their kids' symptoms to get antibiotics on their behalf.

"As clinicians, we know that patients lie to us sometimes," Dr. Jeffrey Linder, a general internist and primary care clinician-investigator at Northwestern Medicine, wrote in a commentary about the survey findings.

However, the results are still important because the inappropriate use of antibiotics can contribute to the mounting problem of antibiotic resistance, in which bacteria build up a tolerance to the drugs designed to kill them. Recent data released by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) highlight the extent of the problem: In 2023, drug-resistant bacteria and fungi caused about 9.7 million infections in the U.S., up from 2.8 million in 2017. In turn, the estimated number of deaths caused by drug-resistant germs rose from 35,000 to 50,800 between the two years.

A major factor driving resistance among bacteria is the misuse of antibiotics — in other words, using antibiotics for ailments like viral infections, which the drugs do not treat. For individual patients, such prescriptions don't cure their illness and can result in an upset stomach or issues with the gut microbiome, the community of microbes in the intestines. Simultaneously, they place extra pressure on bacteria to evolve resistance, granting the germs opportunities to pick up new strategies for thwarting antibiotics.

Doctors play a big role in ensuring that the antibiotic prescriptions they write are necessary. Part of their decision-making process comes down to what patients say about their symptoms, some of which may be fabricated, the two new surveys suggest.

The new surveys were published Friday (Oct. 30) in the journal JAMA Network Open.

The first survey was completed by nearly 960 adults from across the U.S. in January and February 2026. It asked whether the respondents had ever told a healthcare provider that their symptoms were worse or more long-lasting than they were in order to get antibiotics, as well as whether they'd ever made up symptoms for the same reason. It then inquired about what motivated a given patient to lie — or avoid lying, if they were truthful — as well as posed contextual questions about their demographics, health behaviors and beliefs.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Overall, about 28% of the respondents reported misrepresenting their symptoms, including 26% who exaggerated their existing symptoms and 17% who fabricated symptoms. They most frequently lied about cold-like symptoms, such as fever, cough and sore throat. About two-thirds of these patients were at least moderately confident that their lie would motivate a clinician to prescribe them antibiotics, and 77% said the strategy worked for them at least once.

Often, patients' motivations for lying centered around feeling very sick, holding strong beliefs that antibiotics would help them recover quickly and get back to their responsibilities, and wanting control over the treatments prescribed to them. Compared with people who didn't lie, those who lied were also more likely to feel that clinicians didn't take them seriously or more likely to endorse statements suggesting that antibiotic resistance is a hoax.

"Greater antibiotic knowledge and aversion to taking antibiotics were associated with lower odds of misrepresentation," meaning lying about symptoms, the study authors noted.

Less than 30% of these patients regretted their lies or taking the antibiotics prescribed to them. Those that did express regret noted experiencing side effects, noticing that the treatment didn't help or feeling that the lying itself was morally wrong.

The second survey was much smaller; it included 236 parents and other guardians of children and teens under 18 years old. It posed similar questions but asked whether the caregivers had lied about their children's symptoms and, if so, what motivated them to lie.

About 27% reported lying about a child's symptoms to get antibiotics, with 87% of these caregivers believing that their lying worked at least once. Their reasons for lying were very similar to those expressed by the respondents in the first survey.

"These findings suggest that symptom misrepresentation may contribute to antibiotic overuse in pediatric care," the study authors concluded.

Ideally, antibiotics should be used only when truly needed, to help relieve the pressure on bacteria to gain resistance.

The surveys reached a diverse group of people, including a range of ages, demographics and locations within the United States; however, the respondents were not necessarily representative of the whole U.S. population, the authors noted. The prevalence of lying should therefore be seen as a tentative measure to be checked in future studies, rather than an unbiased, population-level metric, they wrote. It's also possible that not all the respondents who lied disclosed that they did so or remembered that they had done so.

Especially in outpatient settings, which account for most antibiotic use among U.S. patients, it can be difficult for doctors to quickly determine whether a patient needs an antibiotic.

One factor is that there's a lack of fast, surefire diagnostic tests for many bacterial infections. Outpatient appointments are also extremely short, so doctors sometimes worry about overlooking an infection that could then get worse, Julia Szymczak, a medical sociologist at the University of Utah School of Medicine, previously told Live Science. Another major factor is that clinicians can face pressure to prescribe antibiotics from their adult patients or from children's caregivers, as the new surveys reflect.

But in the face of these pressures and patients' occasional lies, Linder argues that it's still up to the clinicians to do the right thing. "While clinicians might interpret patients' symptom maximization and questions as demands for antibiotics, symptoms do not determine the indication, a diagnosis does," he wrote in the commentary.

"It does not track that approximately 80% of respondents who reported misrepresenting their symptoms obtained a prescription," he added, "unless prescribers were being willfully deceived or, more likely, just getting worn down with what they perceive as patient demand, regardless of actual clinical appropriateness."

When it comes to making decisions about individual patients, Linder argued that doctors don't necessarily need to think about the big picture of antibiotic resistance and how their patient's case fits into that global trend. Rather, providers should simply ask whether a given prescription is more likely to help or hurt that patient, he said.

"Clinicians' obligation is to act in patients' best interest," he said, "even if patients are hoping we do something different, even if patients do not like it, or even if patients lie about their symptoms."

#6455. How the Antigravity 360 Drone Will Change Your Travels

Drones are huge. And, while there’s lots of restrictions around them, a lot of travelers take them on road because they produce some amazing sweeping aerial shots.

There’s lots of amazing brands out there but one that I think is super cool is the Antigravity A1. Released in late 2025, attempts to render the traditional gimbal obsolete for a vast segment of creators. By leveraging a dual-lens 360-degree capture system, the A1 records everything in every direction simultaneously. The result is a “fly now, frame later” experience that feels less like piloting a drone and more like directing a virtual camera in a pre-recorded digital environment.

I was sent one to use and want to share my experience and why I like this product so much.

What make’s Antigravity 360’s so special is the two lenses. Most drones feature a single lens that points forward. However, the A1 features two ultra-wide-angle lenses positioned on the top and bottom of the central fuselage that each captures a 200-degree field of view. When those images are combines, they overlap to create a seamless 360-degree sphere.

And, in the final exported footage, the drone itself is digitally removed, creating the illusion of a camera floating in mid-air with no visible means of support.

The sensors themselves are 1/1.28-inch CMOS units. While smaller than the 1-inch sensors found on some “Pro” level photography drones, they are massive compared to typical 360 action cameras. This allows for significantly better low-light performance and a higher dynamic range, capturing details in the highlights and shadows that would typically be lost in the harsh contrast of a midday sun.

Most countries require drones weighing 250 grams or more to be registered and subject to stricter flight rules. Antigravity clearly understood the importance of this threshold because they made the A1 to weigh exactly 249 grams with its standard battery meaning it’s not considered a commercial drone so you don’t have to register it.

And the drone feels remarkably sturdy. It utilizes a high-grade carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer that offers a better strength-to-weight ratio than the standard ABS plastic found in cheaper models. The folding mechanism is satisfyingly tactile, clicking into place with a precision that suggests long-term durability. When folded, the drone is roughly the size of a large smartphone, though about three times as thick.

The Vision Goggles: These are sleek, lightweight, and feature dual 4K micro-OLED displays with a 120Hz refresh rate. The latency is nearly non-existent and they have integrated head tracking. Because the drone is recording in 360 degrees, you aren’t limited to seeing what is in front of the drone. When you turn your head to the left, the goggle feed pans to the left. If you look down, you see the ground passing beneath you. This provides a sense of presence and spatial awareness that is simply impossible with a traditional fixed-camera drone.

The drone uses a single-handed motion controller. You point the controller where you want to go and pull the trigger to accelerate. Tilt your wrist left to bank, or raise the nose of the controller to climb. It is an incredibly intuitive system that allows even a novice to fly through complex environments within minutes. For professional FPV pilots who prefer the precision of manual acrobatic flight, the A1 does support a traditional “Mode 2” stick controller, but the motion controls are so fluid that most users will likely never switch back.

The marketing for the Antigravity 360 proudly displays “8K Resolution.” In a traditional camera, 8K means every pixel is packed into a 16:9 rectangle. In 360 video, those pixels are spread across a full sphere. When you “reframe” that 8K sphere into a standard flat video, you are looking at a “crop” of the total image.

The color science is noticeably improved over previous 360 cameras. The A1 features a “Vivid” profile for those who want punchy, social-media-ready colors, and a 10-bit “Log” profile for professional editors who need to match the footage to other cameras in a color-grading suite. The stabilization, powered by Antigravity’s “FlowState” algorithms, is nothing short of miraculous. You can fly in 20mph winds, and the footage remains as steady as if the camera were on a tripod.

The “Antigravity Studio” app allows you to download footage wirelessly (at speeds up to 80MB/s) and reframe your video using your phone’s gyroscope. You simply watch the video and move your phone around to “film” the scene in real-time. The app also features “Auto-Frame,” an AI tool that identifies subjects and automatically generates a cut that keeps them in focus. For a solo creator, this effectively provides a virtual camera crew that never misses a shot.

Battery technology remains the bottleneck for all small drones. The A1’s standard Intelligent Flight Battery provides a theoretical 24 minutes of flight. In real-world conditions with moderate wind and constant recording, expect closer to 19 or 20 minutes.

While 20 minutes sounds short, the “work per minute” is much higher than a traditional drone. Because you don’t need to re-fly a path to get different angles, a single 20-minute flight can yield the same amount of usable footage as three flights with a Mavic. For those who need more time, the “Pro Battery” (which pushes the weight over 250g) offers a staggering 39 minutes of flight time, though it does compromise the drone’s agility slightly.

In terms of flight dynamics, the A1 is a “cinewhoop” style flyer. It is stable and predictable rather than aggressive and twitchy. It has a top speed of roughly 36 mph, which is plenty for following bikes or cars, but it won’t keep up with a professional racing drone. The “Turtle Mode” is a life-saver; if you crash and end up upside down, the drone can flip itself over using its propellers, allowing you to take off again without a “walk of shame” to recover the aircraft.

The Antigravity 360 is a niche product that is rapidly becoming mainstream.

The Antigravity 360 (A1) is the most exciting drone I have tested. By removing the need for a gimbal and the stress of manual framing, it allows the pilot to focus on the one thing that truly matters: the story they are trying to tell.

While the image quality isn’t quite at the level of a high-end cinema drone, and the lenses are admittedly delicate, these are small prices to pay for the creative liberation the A1 provides. It bridges the gap between traditional cinematography and the immersive world of VR.

If you are a creator who is tired of the same old “drone shots” and want to push the boundaries of what is possible in the air, the Antigravity 360 is an essential addition to your toolkit.

#6454. Alzheimer’s-Linked Proteins Have a Hidden Role in Human Reproduction

Proteins commonly associated with Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease may have a surprising function in human reproduction. Researchers at Columbia University’s Zuckerman Institute have discovered that amyloid fibrils, tiny protein fibers found in semen, can help transport RNA into sperm cells. The findings suggest a previously unknown pathway for moving genetic material into sperm and could eventually lead to new methods for delivering gene therapies.

Published in Molecular Cell, the research shows that amyloids can serve a useful biological purpose despite their association with neurodegenerative diseases. The scientists also demonstrated that these protein fibers can carry RNA molecules large enough to produce functional proteins in developing embryos.

The investigation grew out of earlier research showing that amyloid fibrils in semen can help HIV enter cells in the reproductive tract. Anthony Fitzpatrick, PhD, a Columbia researcher who studies amyloids in brain diseases, wondered whether these same structures might help transport the body’s own genetic material into sperm.

His team focused on RNA, a molecule involved in converting genetic instructions into proteins and regulating gene activity. Seminal fluid contains numerous small RNA molecules that may influence gene expression during embryonic development. However, scientists have not fully understood how these molecules move from semen into sperm.

HIV provided a potential connection because the virus uses RNA as its genetic material. If seminal amyloids could facilitate viral entry into cells, researchers reasoned, they might also help deliver free RNA molecules.

William Mallen, PhD, the study’s lead author, investigated whether amyloid fibrils could attach to RNA. The two have complementary electrical properties: amyloids carry a positive charge, while RNA is negatively charged. Using fluorescent markers, Mallen confirmed that the molecules bind together.

The researchers proposed that amyloids might also protect RNA during transport. RNA is relatively fragile and can be broken down by enzymes, whereas amyloid fibrils form highly stable structures. Encasing RNA within these fibers could potentially help preserve it, although that protective function has not yet been established.

To determine whether the fibrils actually enter sperm, the team used cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), a powerful imaging technique that creates detailed three-dimensional views of frozen biological samples. Amyloid fibers marked with tiny gold particles were found inside sperm cells, confirming that they could cross the cell boundary rather than simply attach to its surface.

“Seeing those amyloid fibers inside sperm cells was just so extraordinary to me,” said Mallen, who is now a medical student at the University of Vermont. “There were hints of this happening earlier in our other experiments, but actually seeing this just totally blew us away.”

Additional experiments using fluorescent markers showed that amyloid fibrils greatly increased the amount of RNA entering sperm. The researchers also identified a possible mechanism for releasing the transported material: a protein called clusterin could help separate RNA from its amyloid carrier once inside cells.

The team tested whether the fibrils could deliver larger RNA molecules capable of directing protein production. Sperm exposed to amyloid-bound RNA encoding green fluorescent protein were used in fertilization experiments. The resulting embryos produced at least 10 times more of the fluorescent protein than embryos fertilized with sperm exposed to the same RNA without amyloids.

Previous studies have suggested that RNA carried by sperm can influence gene activity in offspring through epigenetic mechanisms, which regulate how genes are used without altering the underlying DNA sequence. Research in mice has also linked paternal transmission of certain metabolic conditions, including insulin resistance, to RNA-mediated processes.

Beyond reproduction, the findings could have implications for RNA delivery in medicine. Technologies such as CRISPR rely on RNA to guide gene-editing machinery toward specific DNA sequences, but getting these components safely and efficiently into cells remains a major challenge.

Some gene therapies use modified viruses to transport genetic material into cells. Although effective in many applications, viral delivery systems can provoke immune responses. Amyloid fibrils derived from human proteins might eventually provide another approach, although their safety and effectiveness as therapeutic carriers still require investigation.

“Since the amyloid fibrils we looked at are human-based, hopefully the immune system won’t react in the same way they do to the repurposed viruses often used in gene therapy,” Mallen said.

Reference: “Amyloid-mediated RNA uptake by sperm for embryonic delivery” by William S. Mallen, Nataliya Zabello, Susan Brenner-Morton, Simone Sidoli, Feng-Xia Liang, Joseph Sall, Jason Yin, Priyanka Mathews, Mengmeng Zhu, Guoan Zhang, Carolyn L. Lee, Ya-Cheng Liao and Anthony W.P. Fitzpatrick, 26 October 2026, Molecular Cell. DOI: 10.1016/j.molcel.2026.10.004

This work was funded by the Hevolution Foundation, the ERC-CFAR Center for AIDS research, the Einstein-Mount Sinai Diabetes center, the NIH Office of the Director (S10OD030286), the Vagelos Precision Medicine Fund, and the NYU Langone Health Microscopy Laboratory (RRID: SCR_017934), which is partially funded by NYU Cancer Center Support Grant NCI P30CA016087.

#6452. Scientists Discover How Dead Stars Could Break One of Physics’ Most Famous Limits

New simulations suggest that powerful internal magnetic fields could allow some white dwarfs to grow far beyond a long-established stellar mass limit.

New research suggests that some white dwarfs, the incredibly dense remnants of dead stars, could grow far heavier than a fundamental limit in astrophysics predicts. Computer simulations show that powerful internal magnetic fields may allow these objects to reach about 2.4 times the Sun’s mass, well beyond the conventional limit of roughly 1.4 solar masses.

The findings, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, offer a possible explanation for unusually bright stellar explosions and could have implications for how astronomers measure the expansion of the universe. They also demonstrate a potential evolutionary path through which these exceptionally massive stars could form.

White dwarfs form when stars exhaust their nuclear fuel and lose their outer layers, leaving behind compact cores typically about the size of Earth. Despite their small dimensions, these remnants can contain a substantial fraction of the Sun’s mass. For white dwarfs without strong magnetic fields or rapid rotation, the maximum stable mass is approximately 1.4 solar masses, a threshold known as the Chandrasekhar limit.

Researchers at the Department of Physics, Indian Institute of Science (IISc), and their collaborators found that strong magnetic fields could change this restriction. As a white dwarf draws material from a companion star, its increasing mass causes it to become denser and contract. This compression strengthens its internal magnetic field, generating additional pressure that helps counteract gravity and allows the star to support more mass than conventional models predict.

The simulations also suggest that magnetic fields can alter the relationship between a white dwarf’s mass and radius. This effect could help explain observations of certain low-mass white dwarfs that appear larger than expected.

To investigate whether such objects could actually develop through stellar evolution, the scientists modified STARS, a computer program developed at the University of Cambridge. They incorporated the effects of magnetic fields and white dwarf cooling, allowing them to follow a star from its main-sequence phase, when hydrogen fusion powers its core, through its transformation into a white dwarf. They then modeled how the remnant would evolve as it accumulated material from a companion star.

In one simulation, a star initially eight times the Sun’s mass produced a carbon-oxygen white dwarf weighing approximately 1.02 solar masses. When the remnant gained material at a rate of 10⁻⁹ solar masses per year, its magnetic field strengthened enough to support a modeled mass limit of approximately 2.4 solar masses. Under comparable conditions without magnetic effects, the limit remained near 1.4 solar masses.

“The important question was not simply whether a super-Chandrasekhar white dwarf is possible, but whether a star can actually evolve into one,” says Zenia Zuraiq, first author of the study and PhD student at the Department of Physics. “Our simulations allowed us to follow that evolutionary pathway from the main-sequence star to the white dwarf, and show that under certain conditions, such a pathway is possible.”

The possibility of white dwarfs exceeding the Chandrasekhar limit has been explored theoretically for decades. Astronomers have also observed unusually luminous Type Ia supernovae, raising the possibility that some originate from white dwarfs substantially more massive than expected. Previous interpretations have suggested progenitor masses, and possible upper limits, approaching 2.8 times the Sun’s mass.

The new study builds on an investigation that began more than a decade ago. “The idea started in 2011, when a summer student came to me and I gave him a problem quite casually: to check whether the Chandrasekhar limit can be violated by a magnetic field,” explains Banibrata Mukhopadhyay, Professor at the Department of Physics and corresponding author of the study published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Unlike calculations that examine whether an unusually massive white dwarf could remain stable, the new simulations follow the process by which such a remnant might develop. The results support the theoretical possibility of magnetically sustained white dwarfs, although they do not establish how commonly these objects occur in nature.

Type Ia supernovae can occur when carbon-oxygen white dwarfs undergo runaway thermonuclear burning. As a white dwarf approaches the Chandrasekhar limit, conditions in its interior can become extreme enough to ignite carbon and potentially trigger a catastrophic explosion.

Astronomers use Type Ia supernovae as standardizable candles to estimate distances across the universe. Although their intrinsic brightness varies, relationships between their luminosity and how their light changes over time allow scientists to calibrate these explosions. Such measurements have played a central role in understanding cosmic expansion.

If some Type Ia supernovae originate from unusually massive, strongly magnetized white dwarfs, differences in their progenitors could influence the properties and brightness of their explosions. Understanding those effects may help astronomers interpret exceptionally luminous supernovae and improve the physical models underlying cosmic distance measurements.

Reference: “Super-Chandrasekhar White Dwarfs by the Evolution of Magnetized Main-sequence Stars: New Mass Limits from STARS Simulation” by Zenia Zuraiq, Banibrata Mukhopadhyay, Achal Kumar, Arnab Sarkar, Alexander J. Hackett, Projjwal Banerjee and Christopher A. Tout, 8 October 2026, The Astrophysical Journal Letters. DOI: 10.3847/2041-8213/aea97e

A new study revealed that people who rely on AI for basic tasks become less motivated over time. Live Science polled its readers on whether they have experienced this situation.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

While people use artificial intelligence (AI) tools to help with tasks like learning new skills or answering questions, a new study suggests that these benefits may come with a downside.

The findings, presented at the 2026 Conference on Language Modeling in San Francisco earlier this month, revealed that people who used AI assistance for reading comprehension or math problems were more likely to struggle or give up when the AI assistance was removed. The results suggest that relying too much on AI could lower people's motivations to overcome challenging situations.

In the wake of this study, Live Science recently polled its readers on whether they felt AI was making them less motivated after using it.

More than 140 readers voted in the poll, with 30% of voters picking "No, I don't use AI at all, so this situation doesn't apply to me."

"If AI were only a tool, controlled by those who use it I might give it a try," said one commenter in response. "But it isn't under control at all. It gets into your bank accounts and moves money without authorization. It encourages suicide and self-harm. It is addictive and makes people lazy. I know someone who uses it to answer questions and while it is detailed, it makes her lazier, asking one question and getting the answer without her searching for it. AI Is a danger. It should not be allowed."

Other comments reflected this sentiment, with one reader writing, "Use of all automatic aids decrease[s] attention and retention. I see it in the use of navigation devices where drivers ought to recognize routes after a couple of times. AI helps research and cuts down lengthy searches, but over use of summaries weakens critical faculties."

Other commenters questioned whether AI is the problem, or if people are just inclined to take the easy option, asking "Would you get the same results if the answers to all but a few problems were provided on separate sheet of paper?" and another writing, "I think researchers should also investigate whether shovels decrease motivation to dig holes with one's hands. AI, like a shovel, is only a tool."

Do you agree with these readers? Let us know in the comments!

#6450. Uranus and Neptune May Have Been Cosmic Strangers All Along, New Research Reveals

Uranus and Neptune have long been considered planetary twins, but new research suggests their similarities may conceal surprisingly different origins.

Neptune may have formed from material that originated much closer to the young Sun, challenging the long-standing belief that it and Uranus developed from the same reservoir of cosmic ingredients. New research suggests the two ice giants, despite their striking similarities, have significantly different chemical histories.

An international research team, including scientists from Southwest Research Institute (SwRI), found evidence that Neptune’s deep atmosphere contains substantially more oxygen than Uranus’s. Published in the September 2026 issue of Astronomy & Astrophysics, the study uses atmospheric observations and computer models to investigate how the planets acquired their chemical compositions roughly 4.5 billion years ago.

Uranus and Neptune have comparable sizes, masses, and atmospheric conditions, making them appear almost like planetary twins. Neither has a solid surface like Earth. Instead, their atmospheres extend thousands of miles into their interiors, with water, ammonia, and methane among the compounds present. Methane in their upper atmospheres helps produce their distinctive blue-green colors by absorbing red wavelengths of sunlight.

“Uranus and Neptune may resemble twins today, but their chemistry is telling us that they are more like cousins with very different histories,” said Dr. Olivier Mousis, a program director in SwRI’s Solar System Science and Exploration Division in Boulder, Colorado, and a co-author of the study. “Their atmospheric compositions may be connected to different regions of the protoplanetary disk where the planets formed, which would make their similarities a noteworthy coincidence.”

To investigate the planets’ chemical differences, researchers analyzed carbon monoxide measurements, including recent observations from the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA). Although scientists cannot directly sample the deep atmospheres of Uranus and Neptune, carbon monoxide concentrations in their upper atmospheres can help constrain the chemistry of the layers below.

The team combined these observations with atmospheric chemistry models to estimate oxygen abundances and carbon-to-oxygen ratios. Their results indicate that Neptune’s deeper atmosphere is considerably more oxygen-rich than Uranus’s, suggesting that the two planets incorporated different proportions of carbon-bearing and oxygen-bearing materials during formation.

“We can’t directly access the deep atmospheres of Uranus and Neptune, but chemical tracers allow us to probe the conditions hidden beneath their visible clouds,” Mousis said. “Studying carbon monoxide, or CO, is particularly useful because of its abundance in the upper troposphere. Using this data, we can model the chemical evolution of the protoplanetary disk and the origins of its materials.”

The researchers then examined how these chemical differences could have developed within the protoplanetary disk, the rotating collection of gas and dust surrounding the young Sun. As the disk cooled, volatile compounds condensed into solids at different temperatures and distances. This process created reservoirs of material with distinct chemical compositions, providing different ingredients for growing planets.

By comparing the planets’ inferred carbon-to-oxygen ratios with models of the evolving disk, the team identified a possible explanation for Neptune’s unusual composition. Rather than forming entirely from materials available near its present orbit, Neptune may have accumulated building blocks that originated closer to the Sun and subsequently migrated outward. This would give Neptune a different chemical history from Uranus, even if the two planets formed during roughly the same period.

“Neptune’s chemistry is difficult to reconcile with the idea that it formed where we see it today, pulling from the same reservoir of cosmic materials as Uranus,” Mousis said. “Instead, our models lead us to believe that its building blocks traveled a long way to where Neptune could accrete them. In short, two superficially similar worlds may have reached their present locations and formations through two very distinct evolutionary paths.”

The proposed formation scenario remains dependent on atmospheric and planetary formation models. Without direct measurements from deep within Uranus and Neptune, scientists cannot fully determine their internal compositions or reconstruct the movement of materials that shaped them. Future spacecraft observations and atmospheric probes could provide more precise constraints on their chemistry and formation histories.

“Our findings have implications beyond Neptune and Uranus and even far beyond our Solar System,” Mousis said. “Planets comparable in size to Uranus and Neptune are common around other stars, which is why Uranus and Neptune are essential benchmarks for understanding how planets form and evolve throughout the galaxy, and it is precisely why missions like NASA’s planned Uranus Orbiter and Probe, expected to launch sometime in the next decade, are so important.”

Reference: “Contrasting C/O ratios in Uranus and Neptune from disequilibrium chemistry: A clue to distinct evolutionary pathways?” by T. Briand, V. Hue, O. Mousis, T. Cavalié, T. Benest Couzinou, A. Schneeberger and M. D. Hofstadter, 19 October 2026, Astronomy & Astrophysics. DOI: 10.1051/0004-6361/202660770

#6449. Why do flamingos dance while they eat? This scientist found out

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Erin Garcia de Jesús, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

On a family trip to Atlanta, Víctor Ortega Jiménez spent time taking pictures and videos of flamingos as they fed in their pond. It wasn’t to admire their long legs or flamboyant pink color. Instead, he noticed the “beautiful” ripples spreading across the water as the birds ate under the surface. But he didn’t know why the waves were happening.

It took “more than four years to answer that question,” says Ortega Jiménez, of the University of California, Berkeley. “But I think the answer was fascinating.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Ortega Jiménez’s focus is biomechanics, or the study of how mechanics applies to animal movement and structure. His goal is to understand how animal behaviors might lead to human-made engineering feats.

He discovered that, by retracting their heads, flamingos produce vortexlike traps with water to scoop up algae. They stomp around — or dance, if you will — amplifying the vortex. The series of motions brings the food to their crooked beaks. The beaks then filter in food, releasing silt and mud.

The impressive process can weed out particles the size of a single cell. This kind of self-cleaning filter for extremely small particles can be applied to remove microplastics and so-called forever chemicals called PFAS from water, Ortega Jiménez says.

“Nature is always full of secrets,” he says. “And I think that’s the riddle that keeps me going, trying to understand nature. That’s my way to see science: by observation and trying to be inspired and trying to solve a problem.”

#6448. Two Trains Collided in Spain—and Killed 69 People. The Terrifying Truth? It Could Also Happen in the U.S.

The deadly crash exposes a dangerous gap in automated train safety systems.

When a high-speed Renfe AVE train traveling from Madrid to Seville, Spain, suddenly stopped on the morning of Wednesday, October 28, passengers were told that the line was busy with other trains. But then their train started moving again—and soon, a violent jolt sent people grabbing for their seats, according to passenger accounts.

The AVE had slammed into the back of another high-speed train, operated by Iryo and also bound for Seville, that was stopped on the tracks near Urda, in Toledo province. Passengers broke open windows to escape. By Thursday morning, at least 69 people had died, and more than 100 people were reported injured as a result of the violent collision.

On the Iryo train, the driver had also received instructions to restart her train-protection equipment and resume normal running. But she called the control center run by Spain’s rail infrastructure manager, Adif, to report that the equipment wouldn’t boot back up—and her train stayed stopped, according to radio transcripts published by Cadena SER, a Spanish broadcaster.

The obvious question: Why was one train traveling toward another that was stopped on the same track?

Earlier that morning, a computer malfunction had knocked out a train-protection system called LZB, according to Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente. Around 8:30 a.m., the malfunction caused six trains to stop automatically, Puente said. Six minutes later, the control center authorized the Renfe train to resume normal running, even though a red warning was showing that the Iryo ahead was occupying the track, he said.

LZB helps a train driver know what’s coming up ahead. If a train is equipped with LZB, it sends its position and braking characteristics to equipment near the tracks through a cable along the railway. That equipment then sends information back to the driver’s compartment, including how fast the train can travel and how far it is from the point where it has to slow down or fully stop. If the train reaches LZB’s automatic-braking threshold, the system hits the emergency brake.

But when LZB goes down, drivers still have other ways to navigate. Trains can keep going under trackside signaling, where drivers obey signals positioned along the line. The Madrid–Seville line also uses a system called ASFA, which picks up information from devices on the track and can automatically apply the brakes if the driver doesn’t respond as required. Investigators are examining whether additional failures in the train-protection equipment contributed to the collision near Urda.

Under trackside signaling, a red light tells the driver to stop. But depending on the conditions, drivers can still pass the signal with specific authorization and compliance. Under what’s called “on sight” instructions, the driver must travel slowly enough to stop short of another train or obstacle. Puente said the Renfe train should have been limited to 40 kilometers per hour, or about 25 mph. On Wednesday afternoon, Euronews reported that authorities were still examining data to establish how fast the Renfe train was going.

Another driver whose train had stopped during the outage questioned the same instruction to resume normal running, Puente said after listening to recordings of the exchanges. The driver reminded the controller that the train needed to proceed on sight. Investigators still need to learn why the Renfe train was told otherwise and what happened after it resumed travel.

The collision near Urda came just nine months after another deadly crash involving trains operated by the same two companies near Adamuz in southern Spain. That January collision began when an Iryo train derailed into the path of a Renfe train traveling in the opposite direction, rather than one approaching from behind.

In a situation where continuous train-protection systems were interrupted and drivers were forced to rely on signals and instructions, it’s fair to wonder: Could a similar collision happen in the U.S.?

American railroads use a system called Positive Train Control (PTC), which can automatically slow a train to help prevent collisions. Like LZB, it provides automatic protection, though the technologies and operating rules can vary. But even when PTC is working, railroads sometimes allow a train onto a stretch of track where another train is already traveling—or has stopped.

That’s exactly what happened near Easton, Pennsylvania, on March 2, 2024, when an eastbound Norfolk Southern freight train had stopped because of traffic ahead. A second freight train approached from behind and passed a trackside signal that gave it permission to enter the same section at restricted speed.

But why was it allowed in at all? As the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) explained in its final report, it’s because keeping trains closer together can help a railroad move traffic through a busy area—as long as the crew of the approaching train can stop short of the train ahead.

In Easton, the engineer knew another train was ahead, but as he later told investigators, he thought it was still moving. As his train came around a curve, elevated ground and vegetation obscured the track ahead. By the time the engineer saw the stopped freight, it was about eight railcar lengths away. He tried to slow down, primarily using the locomotive’s dynamic and independent brakes, but they didn’t do much to reduce speed in the final 17 seconds. His train hit the other one at 13 mph.

The collision derailed cars from the approaching train onto the neighboring track. Just over a minute later, a westbound freight struck them, derailing locomotives and more cars. Four crew members suffered minor injuries in the two collisions. The approaching train’s PTC was enforcing the maximum speed permitted by the signal—but that signal also meant the engineer had to go slowly enough to stop within the distance the rule required.

A crew operating at restricted speed must be able to stop the train within half the distance of clear track visible ahead. This helps ensure it can stop before reaching another train, a worker, or an obstruction. Let’s say a curve leaves 400 feet of clear track in view. The train must then be able to stop within 200 feet, even if that means going slower than the federally defined 20-mph maximum—or a lower limit set by the railroad.

At Easton, while the engineer did keep his train below the speed limit, he was still going too fast to stop. The NTSB identified his failure to follow the restricted-speed rule as the probable cause of the crash. Investigators also found that while PTC could enforce the speed limit, it couldn’t prevent this restricted-speed collision.

The accident in Easton wasn’t the only time a train couldn’t stop under a restricted-speed rule. In September 2026, the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) described seven recent collisions involving failures to follow those rules or related signals. The FRA warns that PTC can often enforce an upper speed limit during restricted-speed operation without ensuring that the train can stop within half the distance the crew can see.

Back in Spain, the Renfe driver was told to resume normal running. But we still don’t know the cause of the collision, as investigators are examining the instructions given to the trains and whether additional safety failures contributed to the crash.

Here in the U.S., the FRA has urged railroads to check whether crews following other trains into occupied sections are staying below the speed limit and can stop within half the distance of clear track ahead.

#6447. “The Closest Thing to Magic” – Researchers Create an Invisible Pipe That Moves Liquids Through Thin Air

Scientists have developed an invisible tube made entirely of ultrasonic waves that can guide liquids through mid-air without physical contact.

Researchers at the University of Helsinki have created a pipe with no physical walls, using ultrasound to guide a stream of liquid horizontally through open air. The technology could provide a new way to transport corrosive, sticky, or contamination-sensitive substances without exposing them to the surfaces of conventional pipes.

“Of all the experimental setups I have seen, I would say this is the closest thing to magic,” says Ari Salmi, Professor of Electronics at the University of Helsinki, who led the development of the device.

The system uses 256 miniature speakers arranged in a cylinder around the flowing liquid, approximately five centimeters (2 inches) away. They produce ultrasonic waves at a frequency of about 40 kilohertz, beyond the range of human hearing. By carefully coordinating these waves, the researchers create an acoustic field that confines the liquid to a narrow path without any solid walls.

Unlike conventional piping, the ultrasonic channel can change direction without requiring physical adjustments. Researchers can electronically reshape the path, redirect the liquid toward another destination, or control its release with single-drop precision. “By changing how the speakers are controlled, we can reshape and turn the tube as needed,” explains postdoctoral researcher Dmitry Nikolaev, who led the project team.

https://youtu.be/qmslDZWmiaE Video material of the ultrasound tube transmitting liquids, powder, mist and electricity. Taken from the article Contactless continuous guidance of matter in its main states using curved elongated Bessel-like acoustic fields. Credit: Dmitry Nikolaev

The approach can also be adapted for different materials. “Transporting a solid substance, for example, requires a different field configuration than transporting a liquid or a gas.” Beyond moving matter, the ultrasonic tube can guide an electrical discharge along a controlled route.

Salmi first conceived the idea four years ago, following earlier research into using ultrasound to clean the inside of pipes. “We had been developing a device that cleaned the inner surfaces of pipes with ultrasound. At a lunch with a colleague, we discussed that it would be handy if a pipe had no surface for dirt to stick to.”

The discussion stayed with him. During an evening walk with his dog, he realized that ultrasound might be used to form the walls of a pipe rather than simply clean them. Turning the concept into a functioning device required extensive experimentation to determine how the speakers should operate together. The University of Helsinki researchers worked with collaborators at the Public University of Navarre and the University of Michigan to develop the system.

The completed prototype produces an ultrasonic tube just eight centimeters (3.1 inches) long, shorter than the diameter of the surrounding device. Nikolaev says multiple modules could be connected to extend the channel to greater lengths. Each eight-centimeter section consumes approximately 50 watts of electricity, comparable to a traditional incandescent light bulb.

Although the device operates beyond human hearing, its ultrasonic field is extremely intense, and dogs may find the sound unpleasant. “At the core of the device, the intensity of the ultrasound is comparable to a continuous roar of gunfire right next to your ear,” Nikolaev says. “Even right here next to it, the sound could be compared to a jet engine if you were standing right beside it. But it is too high-pitched for the human ear.”

Reference: “Contactless continuous guidance of matter in its main states using curved elongated Bessel-like acoustic fields” by Dmitrii Nikolaev, Denys Iablonskyi, Alexander Martinez-Marchese, Marika Sirkka, Mikel Aldea, Chinedum Okwudire, Edward Hæggström, Asier Marzo and Ari Salmi, 23 October 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2614959123

#6445. New X-Ray Technology Captures 4.6 Times More Light Without Losing Sharpness

Scientists have developed a new approach to X-ray imaging that captures significantly more light without sacrificing image sharpness.

A major obstacle to sharper X-ray images is that much of the light generated inside detectors never reaches the camera. Researchers have developed a nanostructured surface that increased average light output by 4.64 times and improved the imaging signal-to-noise ratio by 13 decibels. The experimental system also maintained spatial resolution finer than 25 μm (about 0.001 inch).

Developed by scientists at Chongqing University, the 26th Institute of CETC, and Stevens Institute of Technology, the approach could help X-ray detectors produce clearer images when very few photons are available. Potential applications include medical scans using lower radiation doses, security screening, and detailed industrial inspections.

X-ray imaging relies on materials called scintillators to convert invisible X-ray radiation into visible light. These “photosensitive” components act as a “translator,” converting the “language” of high-energy radiation into optical signals that cameras or photodetectors can capture and turn into images.

High-density inorganic scintillators (such as GAGG) are particularly effective at absorbing X-rays and generating light, but much of that light cannot escape. Because these materials have a substantially higher refractive index than their surroundings, light striking the surface at certain angles undergoes total internal reflection. Up to 90% of the generated photons can become trapped in guided optical modes, reducing the amount of light available for imaging.

This problem becomes more severe when detectors operate with weak X-ray signals. Increasing scintillator thickness can improve X-ray absorption, but it also allows light to spread sideways before detection, reducing image sharpness. Thinner scintillators preserve fine details but can produce weaker signals.

The researchers addressed this trade-off by modifying how light escapes the scintillator rather than increasing its thickness. Their design uses a photonic crystal, a regularly repeating nanoscale structure that changes how light travels through a material.

Through a process known as Bragg diffraction, the periodic structure provides additional momentum that allows previously trapped light to escape into free space. This increases the amount of visible light reaching the detector without requiring a thicker scintillator.

Manufacturing such structures over large areas has been difficult. Conventional lithography offers precise patterning but requires costly equipment and complicated processing, particularly on brittle scintillator surfaces. Simpler self-assembly techniques can cover larger areas, but cracks, missing particles, and poorly aligned crystal regions can reduce light extraction and introduce imaging artifacts.

The team developed a self-assembly technique that uses the Marangoni effect, in which differences in surface tension drive liquid movement. By combining ethanol and water, the researchers created surface tension gradients that helped organize polystyrene nanospheres into a highly ordered layer.

Surfactants helped pack the particles more tightly, while a vibration-free drainage process transferred the assembled structure onto a 25 mm (about 0.98 inch) diameter GAGG scintillator wafer. The resulting photonic crystal consisted of a continuous monolayer of nanospheres arranged in a hexagonal close-packed pattern.

The research was led by Associate Professor Feng Peng of Chongqing University, working with Dr. Ding Yuchong of the 26th Institute of CETC and PhD candidate Kaifeng Liu of Stevens Institute of Technology. Their paper was published in Opto-Electronic Advances.

The experimental findings demonstrate that modifying the scintillator surface can substantially improve light extraction while preserving fine image details. This approach could be particularly useful in photon-starved conditions, where limited X-ray exposure makes it difficult to distinguish weak signals from background noise.

Further development is still needed before the technology can be widely adopted. Residual structural defects can affect spatial resolution, and the researchers plan to refine the assembly process and investigate compatibility with other scintillator materials.

This study was financially supported by the Natural Science Foundation of Chongqing, China under grant CSTB2025NSCQ-LZX0041, the Development Foundation of 26th Institute of China Electronics Technology Group Corporation under grant K2605ZZ2025002, the Beijing Natural Science Foundation under Grant L242114 and the National Key Research and Development Program of China under Grant 2019YFC0605203.

Some people in mainstream physics today have become obsessed with dogma. They have long been plagued by pseudoscience. They would rather admire an imaginary cat that is half dead than face the real physical reality. Their theories and thinking are lazy, and they no longer know what shame is.

The team developed a self-assembly technique that uses the Marangoni effect, in which differences in surface tension drive liquid movement. VERY GOOD. Self-assembly, liquid movement. WHY? WHY? WHY?………………………………………………………………………

The appearance of actors does not change the inherent material and structure of the stage itself. Just as the ocean gives birth to life, but the chemical nature of seawater (H₂O) remains unchanged; just as quantum vortices appear in a superfluid, the essential nature of the superfluid ground state persists. Similarly, the birth of stars and black holes are merely local excitations on the background of absolute space. In the vast regions of the universe far from these excitation points, the homogeneous, isotropic characteristics of absolute space still dominate, as confirmed by the high uniformity of the Cosmic Microwave Background radiation.

The thinking mode that opposes absolute space and relative space has negatively impacted the development of theoretical physics. In the pursuit of purely “background-independent” theories, we sometimes may overlook the most fundamental and stable levels of the physical world. This has led to some “pseudo-theories,” detached from physical intuition and untestable by experiment, spinning idly in mathematical games.

True progress lies in inclusion and synthesis, not in negation and severance. Topological Vortex Theory (TVT) provides us with a vivid metaphor: a stable, absolute background (the stage), together with dynamic, relative excited states (the actors), jointly constitute the rich and diverse physical universe. Acknowledging the foundational status of absolute space is not a regression in history; it is about retrieving the indispensable cornerstone for building a more complete and profound theory of the universe. The future theory of topological quantum gravity may precisely be the ultimate framework capable of describing both the “tranquil sea” and the “turbulent vortices” upon it.

The outer solar system will descend into chaos just a few billion years after the sun exhausts its fuel ‪—‬ much sooner than scientists previously thought, a new study suggests.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When the sun inevitably dies, not even the outer solar system will be safe from the resulting chaos, new research hints.Scientists have long thought the outer solar system ‪—‬ which comprises the four giant planets Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — would mostly retain its present-day appearance for hundreds of billions of years to come. But a new study suggests that the outer giants may develop weirdly shaped orbits as the sun runs out of fuel, causing the planets to cross paths and destroy themselves through collisions within three billion years of the sun's transformation into a red giant.

The findings, published Sept. 21 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, could change our understanding of what kinds of exoplanets orbit certain stars.

In about 5 billion years, the sun will balloon outward as a red giant after exhausting all of the hydrogen in its core. During this red giant phase, our star will swell to 100 times its present-day size, gobbling up Mercury, Venus and possibly even Earth in the process, Nathan Kaib, a planetary scientist at the University of Oklahoma who wasn't involved in the new research, told Live Science in an email. Following this violent swelling, the sun will crumple into a collapsed core called a white dwarf.

Until now, scientists thought the four outer planets would escape this phase relatively unscathed. A 1998 simulation-based study suggested that the gas the sun spews from its outer layers will push this planetary quartet outward, doubling the radius of each planet's orbit. Only the gravitational impact of a runaway star could destabilize this new order, and such events are thought to occur only once every billion billion years.

These predictions hinged on the assumption that the sun will eject its outer layers smoothly. However, recent observations of stars suggest a jerkier loss of mass, with gas clouds lofted by plumes of plasma in the sun — as though our star were spitting out mass blobs. "They're kind of like coronal mass ejections, except much larger," Jim Fuller, a professor of theoretical astrophysics at Caltech and co-author of the new study, told Live Science in an email.

Each "blob" pushes the star backward, similar to how a fired bullet causes a gun to recoil. Although every push is small, moving the sun just a few feet per second, many pushes can, over time, impart the equivalent of an enormous kick that alters the sun's speed by several hundred feet per second. In fact, astronomers have already seen white dwarfs suffer such kicks in other star systems.

An illustration of the sun releasing a giant mass of plasma. As such large explosions increase in the sun's dying days, the recoil could disrupt the gravitational balance of the outer solar system.

When Fuller, who studied these kicks, described them to Konstantin Batygin, a professor of planetary science at Caltech and the study's first author, Batygin "realized this would have important consequences for the evolution of our own solar system," Fuller said. That's because the kicks change the sun's gravitational pulls on everything around it.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

To determine how the sun's mass loss would influence the giant planets, Batygin created computer-based simulations of the sun and the outer planets. The researchers considered three scenarios: if the sun lost its mass smoothly, if it spit out distinct mass blobs during its entire time evolving as a red giant, and if the sun spewed the blobs only during its last stages. The researchers also varied each ejected blob's mass.

The first scenario produced results similar to those of previous studies, with the outer solar system retaining almost all of its features for billions of years. In contrast, the other two cases had drastically different results. Using 672 simulations, the researchers found that if the sun lost mass in blobs, the giant planets would be thrown into chaos, switching places, developing weirdly oval-shaped orbits, and even getting ejected out of the solar system entirely. Most dramatically, in 96% of the simulations with the heaviest ejected mass packets, the planets get destroyed as they crashed into each other.

These developments also happened much more rapidly — less than a few hundred million years after the sun transformed into a white dwarf, or even during the red giant phase, in the most extreme scenarios.

The study's findings hint that analogues of the present-day outer solar system around white dwarf stars are less likely to exist than previously thought. Kaib noted that the study's results suggest that planets with oval-shaped orbits should dominate instead. It's thought that habitable planets could exist around white dwarfs, but this study's findings show that our understanding of those distant star systems may be incomplete, and that such worlds may, in reality, be unstable.

Batygin, K., Fuller, J., & Adams, F. C. (2026). Terminal instability of the solar system triggered by stochastic solar mass loss. The Astrophysical Journal Letters, 1009(2), L22. https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/aea290

#6443. A Nutrient Found in Red Meat Could Make Dangerous Inflammation Even Worse

A nutrient known for helping the body burn fat may also cause inflammation when the immune system is in overdrive.

Yale researchers found that L-carnitine, a nutrient abundant in red meat and widely used in exercise and weight-loss supplements, could worsen severe inflammation in mice. After a bacterial component triggered inflammation and sharply lowered blood levels of L-carnitine, restoring the nutrient made the animals sicker, suggesting the decline was protective.

The findings were published October 19 in Cell.

L-carnitine is best known for helping cells turn fat into energy. The body produces it naturally, and skeletal muscle contains particularly high concentrations.

“L-carnitine helps transport fats into mitochondria so they can be broken down for energy,” says Eric Elliott, MD, PhD, assistant professor of medicine (infectious diseases) at Yale School of Medicine (YSM) and the study’s first author. “In simpler terms, it has become synonymous with fat burning, which is why it has also gained prominence as an exercise and weight-loss supplement.”

The team was investigating metabolic changes during sepsis, a life-threatening condition in which the body’s response to infection damages its own tissues and organs. Much of that damage can come from uncontrolled inflammation rather than a failure to contain the infection.

“Sepsis is incredibly challenging,” Elliott says. “Patients with sepsis can become critically ill, and among patients with sepsis treated in intensive care units, some studies report mortality rates approaching 40%.”

To model the inflammation associated with sepsis, the researchers exposed mice to lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a bacterial component. When L-carnitine levels in the animals’ blood dropped sharply, the team tested whether restoring the nutrient would improve their outcomes.

“We predicted giving carnitine back to these animals might improve their outcomes, but they actually did much worse,” Elliott says. “That told us the reduction in carnitine was an adaptive response.”

To understand why, the researchers conducted experiments in mouse and human immune cells. They found that L-carnitine activated part of the cell’s internal alarm system called the pyrin inflammasome. This triggered an inflammatory response involving the immune signaling molecule IL-17 and increased deaths among the mice.

“What was particularly striking was how detrimental IL-17 was in this model,” Elliott says. The team now wants to investigate whether blocking IL-17 might eventually help a subset of patients with sepsis, although that possibility remains untested.

The findings offer a potential research direction in a field where treatment advances have been limited. “We have made frustratingly little progress in improving sepsis treatment beyond learning how to better deliver fluids, antibiotics, and medications that support blood pressure,” Elliott says.

Because skeletal muscle contains high levels of L-carnitine, the researchers suspected that its release from damaged muscle could help drive inflammation. Senior author Andrew Wang, MD, PhD, associate professor of medicine (rheumatology, allergy & immunology) and of immunobiology at YSM, says the pathway may have implications beyond sepsis.

“There is tantalizing genetic evidence that the pathway we uncovered could be contributing to inflammation in a variety of diseases, particularly diseases in which muscle involvement has perhaps been thought to be a casualty of the disease rather than a potential driver,” Wang says.

The team found support for this idea in rhabdomyolysis, a condition in which skeletal muscle rapidly breaks down and releases its contents into the bloodstream, potentially causing acute kidney injury. In a mouse model, L-carnitine transport and pyrin inflammasome activation contributed to inflammation, suggesting that immune cells may interpret L-carnitine released from damaged muscle as a warning signal.

The pathway could also be relevant to cardiovascular disease, inflammatory bowel disease, and cancer. Further research is needed to determine whether it contributes to these chronic inflammatory conditions.

People who eat meat get most of their L-carnitine from food. Vegetarians and vegans tend to make more of it within their bodies, but their overall levels remain lower. The study examined L-carnitine on its own, so the findings do not directly show how eating red meat or taking supplements affects inflammation.

“We did not study red meat as a whole, and carnitine by itself did not induce inflammation,” Elliott says. “A substantial background of inflammation was required, and we do not yet know what inflammatory context might produce this effect in people. We cannot say that carnitine supplementation or heavy red meat consumption is always harmful. It is probably safe most of the time, but there may be specific circumstances in which it becomes a problem.”

Understanding those circumstances is a priority for the team. The researchers want to learn how individual food components interact with a person’s underlying health and inflammatory state and why the same nutrient might have different effects under different conditions.

“Food science currently exists in the realm of phenomenology,” Wang says. “I think that a deep understanding of all the elements that make up food, akin to a periodic table, will be required to understand what makes a ‘good’ or ‘bad’ diet for a particular individual in a particular health state.”

#6441. Three-quarters of NFL football players may end up with CTE

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

It’s the first population-level estimate for the neurogenerative disease among NFL players

The neurodegenerative disease CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, is diagnosed after death, during an autopsy. The condition has been identified most frequently among American football players.

An estimated three-quarters of NFL players who died in a 16-year period had the devastating neurogenerative disease called CTE.

Back in 2017, researchers reported that an estimated 99 percent of former NFL players developed CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, from an analysis of donated brains. But the families who provided the donations may have done so because their football-playing relatives had symptoms related to CTE, which could skew the results. A new study, which accounts for this potential bias, estimates that nearly 75 percent of former NFL players have CTE at death. It’s the first population-level estimate for NFL players, researchers report October 28 in JAMA Network Open.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The development of CTE is linked to repeated blows to the head over time. The disease can occur in people who play contact sports, experience intimate partner violence or engage in military combat. A study of American football players suggests that the longer the duration of repeated head trauma, the higher the risk of CTE and the more severe the condition. During life, people who are later diagnosed with CTE can experience symptoms including memory issues, difficulty concentrating, depression and poor impulse control.

A brain protein called tau, which usually helps nerve cells communicate and performs other jobs, goes awry in CTE. Brains with the disease are snarled with irregular, damaging clumps of the protein. The condition is diagnosed after death, during an autopsy, and has been identified most frequently among American football players.

The new study, by a Boston University research team, included all previous NFL players who passed away from January 2008 through December 2023. The more than 2,300 players included almost 400 with samples in the university’s UNITE Brain Bank, with the remainder identified from records in the U.S. National Death Index. The research team determined that families of NFL players who had CTE-related symptoms in life were five times more likely to donate their relative’s brain than families whose relative did not experience symptoms. Taking that into consideration, the team landed on a population-level CTE estimate for NFL players of 74.5 percent.

The research team notes that determining the true prevalence of CTE is important to understanding the public health impact of the disease.
